#6247. The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm

Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase

And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Big Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next big adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

There are just weeks left in 2026, and if you haven't quite reached the United MileagePlus elite status level you're hoping to secure for 2027, the clock is ticking.

From earning bonus Premier qualifying points with the right credit card to taking a last-minute flight, here are five ways to close the status gap before Dec. 31.

United's elite status qualification year runs from Jan. 1 through Dec. 31. Status earned in 2026 is valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

To qualify, you must fly at least four flights operated by United or United Express and meet one of two thresholds: a combination of Premier Qualifying Flights and PQPs or a higher PQP-only requirement.

You can check your progress in United's Premier Status Tracker, including how your upcoming flights will count toward qualification.

Some United credit cards offer bonus PQPs toward status as part of their welcome offers, in addition to redeemable United miles.

For example, the (see rates and fees) is currently offering 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 redeemable United bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, an additional 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

The card has a $350 introductory annual fee.

It's still possible to get bonus PQPs in 2026 as part of a new cardmember bonus on select United credit cards, but you should act quickly.

The good news is you can earn PQPs through everyday spending on United credit cards. The bad news is that most United cards earn them at a relatively slow rate of 1 PQP for every $20 spent.

That means $1,000 in purchases on most United cards would earn you just 50 PQPs.

However, the (see rates and fees) earns PQPs faster than the other personal United cards, at a rate of 1 PQP for every $15 spent. So, that same $1,000 in purchases would earn you about 66 PQPs with that card.

Every little bit helps, especially if you're close to your next status level.

Related: Why I charged $50,000 on my United card to earn status

If you already have United flights booked before the end of 2026, you may be able to earn additional PQPs by upgrading your seats.

Purchasing Economy Plus seats, United's preferred seating or paid upgrades to first class can earn 1 PQP per dollar spent (excluding taxes and fees).

You can also earn 1 PQP for every 100 MileagePlus miles redeemed for eligible seat upgrades on United and United Express flights.

Just remember that PQPs from upgrades purchased separately from your original ticket may post separately after you fly, so keep an eye on your account.

Related: What it's like in United's new Elevated Polaris business class

One of the most obvious ways to close the gap toward United elite status is to book another flight (or two) before the end of the year as part of a modern-day mileage run. Unlike in the old days, how far you fly doesn't matter if you're on United for status. It only matters how much you spend.

Ideally, you're going somewhere fun to see a friend, see some attractions or have a great meal. But if you turn around and don't leave the airport before your next flight, you won't be the first — or last — status-seeker to do so. I've certainly done it when I needed a few more segments at the very end of the year.

If you're chasing PQFs, remember that you generally earn one for each eligible flight segment on United, United Express or partner airlines.

For United-operated flights, you'll generally earn 1 PQP per dollar spent on eligible base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges, excluding government taxes and fees. You can see the estimated PQPs and PQFs a flight will earn when selecting a fare during booking.

If you need a lot of United PQPs and want to take this to the next level, it is possible to earn PQPs at a faster rate with some United partners. You can learn all about that strategy here.

Finally, if you have an upcoming United flight, you may be able to purchase additional PQPs through United's Premier Accelerator program.

To check, open an existing reservation and look for the Award Accelerator option, which lets you purchase additional redeemable miles.

Depending on your reservation, you may also see a Premier Accelerator option that lets you purchase PQPs along with redeemable miles, as shown below.

This isn't usually a cheap way to earn status, but it can be useful if you're just short of your goal and don't want to take another flight.

United is making some big changes to elite status qualification beginning in 2027, including eliminating the PQF-plus-PQP qualification pathway and raising the PQP-only requirement for Premier 1K.

That means earning status could get harder for some United travelers next year.

If you expect to rely heavily on United credit card spending to earn PQPs toward status, as I do, there's another reason to consider getting a United card before the end of 2026.

If you have an eligible United card by Dec. 31, 2026, you'll get a 5% PQP boost in 2027. For example, if you earned Platinum status in 2026, you'll get a 900-PQP boost to start 2027.

And remember, the earns PQPs faster than United's other personal cards, so it might be the best choice if every PQP is going to count.

It also currently offers an increased welcome bonus of 90,000 miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, an additional 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

But no matter what United status level you are going for or how you plan to get there, just remember that all of your activities must be completed by Dec. 31, 2026, to count toward status this year.

#6245. America Needs an Arsenal of Democracies

We must combine American and allied innovation and manufacturing to take on the threats we share.

A worker along the assembly line handles large caliber 155mm metal projectiles at the Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Scranton, Pa., April 16, 2024.

An Israeli-developed missile is now rolling off an American production line. On October 9, Raytheon-Rafael Protection Systems, an American Israeli joint venture, announced the first Tamir interceptors manufactured in Camden, Ark. They are intended for Israel’s Iron Dome missile-defense system, with plans to produce a U.S. variant for the Marine Corps.

The Camden facility builds on decades of allied weapons production, including the AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile with West Germany as well as the F-16 with multiple partners. But today’s conflicts require an industrial network that produces weapons at scale, maintains deliveries during disruptions, and replenishes forces across theaters. Co-production alone does not deliver that. It changes where a weapon is built; resilience depends on whether production can continue when something breaks.

#6244. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Even better, they're machine washable, so you can easily keep them in pristine condition all season long. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.

#6243. Frontier Begins First Class Ticket Sales

Frontier on Tuesday opened reservations for its upcoming First Class, which is set to debut in March 2027.

The new seats have up to 37 inches of pitch, the carrier said, and will be arranged in a two-by-two configuration at the front of the cabin. Installations are already underway. Reservations are available now for travel beginning March 5.

Frontier first announced plans to add a First Class product in late 2024.

The airline will also add extra-legroom seating, with up to 34 inches of pitch, in rows three through eight. These seats will be available with Frontier’s Premium bundle, which includes a carry-on bag and priority boarding.

Frontier plans to roll out two additional perks through 2027 – in-seat USB-C power at every seat in the first eight rows, and Starlink wireless internet service. The carrier decided on Starlink in July; it will be the first airline in the U.S. to use a new system managed directly by Starlink, officials said at the time.

“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” Bobby Schroeter, chief marketing officer at Frontier, said in a news release. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power, and fast, reliable Starlink Wi-Fi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us.”

#6242. JSX Adds Two Nonstop Routes From New City

JSX announced Tuesday that it will begin flying to New England for the first time in February 2027.

The carrier will operate from Jet Aviation’s terminal at Hanscom Field in Bedford, Massachusetts, northwest of Boston. Flights to Teterboro Airport in New Jersey will begin Feb. 8, with four flights on weekdays, two on Saturdays, and three on Sundays.

JSX markets the route as New York City service and requires passengers to sign up for its free Club JSX membership to book.

Service to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport will follow on Feb. 11, with one flight each day on Mondays and Thursdays through Sundays. JSX will use 30-seat aircraft on both routes.

“We’re excited JSX has chosen Hanscom to operate these flights to the New York and Florida markets,” Hanscom Field Director Chris Willenborg said in a statement.

JSX outlined its plans for Hanscom Field at an advisory commission meeting in September. At the time, the carrier was targeting a January launch and had also proposed flights to Naples, Florida. Naples was absent from Tuesday’s announcement.

#6241. These 9 Hotels for Broadway Lovers Put You in the Heart of NYC’s Theater District

As a Californian who discovered the wonderful world of Broadway by borrowing CDs from my local library, it was only fitting that the first trip I ever planned by myself was to New York City—and the entire itinerary revolved around collecting Playbills. Now, after living in the area for more than two decades, I’m that unlikely New Yorker who still claims Times Square as her favorite and most-frequented neighborhood. I just love the Theater District—where else can you find 41 venues featuring the world's best live theater all within a single mile?

In this age of event tourism, Broadway has remained a constant. And seeing a show is about more than just the storyline of a play or the numbers in a musical—it’s an experience that you’re a part of. Over my 20 years as an entertainment editor and journalist, I’ve interviewed numerous Broadway stars, and they always say they feed off of, and are fueled by, audience reactions. You’re not just a passive viewer; your presence drives the show. It's something special to take part in.

If you've got a Broadway trip in your future, chances are you're going to need a hotel that will help you maximize your experience. The list below features properties with themed suites, theater lore, and locations just steps from the Great White Way. Read on for the best places to stay in NYC for a show-stopping Broadway getaway.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to James Earl Jones Theatre and Lunt-Fontanne TheatreWhy we love it: Right across from Palace Theatre, pre- and post-show prix-fixe menus, Studio 54 history

These days, Studio 54 is one of Broadway’s most popular stages (currently home to The Rocky Horror Show ), but back in 1977, Ian Schrager opened it as a nightclub, and it has since come to epitomize celebrity culture for a generation. Schrager brought that same visionary spirit when he opened the 452-room Times Square Edition in 2019, just across the street from the Palace Theatre. One of my favorite spots in Times Square is the hotel's Terrace and Outdoor Garden, a lush dining oasis that offers three-course Broadway Express prix-fixe menus both pre- and post-show. For those looking for an upgraded theater experience, the Edition's Showstopping Stay package—which can be booked up to 10 days in advance—includes two premium tickets to select shows, dinner with Champagne, theater-themed amenities, and house-made snacks.

Closest theaters: 9-minute walk to Studio 54, 10-minute walk to Vivian Beaumont Theater, 11-minute walk to Broadway TheatreWhy we love it: Central Park views, Broadway VIP Experience

Though a few blocks north of the Theater District thrills, the Mandarin Oriental is still less than a 15-minute walk to most theaters—yet it feels a world apart. It overlooks Central Park in one direction, and its 75-foot lap pool has views of the Hudson River. Guests are pampered with a true five-star experience every step of the way, whether it’s raising a glass at The Bar speakeasy or lounging around at celeb-favorite MO Lounge. You can also rub shoulders with the stars via the hotel's Broadway VIP Experience package, which includes an hour-long meet-and-greet with a Broadway cast member over bites and Champagne at the lounge. Also included are orchestra tickets (choose from 13 shows, including Hamilton and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child) and show merch, as well as add-ons like a theater transfer in a Mercedes, a 90-minute guided tour of the Museum of Broadway, or even acting lessons or a private concert with a stage star.

Closest theaters: 3-minute walk to Belasco Theatre, 4-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, 5-minute walk to Stephen Sondheim TheatreWhy we love it: Official partner of the Tony Awards, recently refreshed, early check-in option

If hotels could earn Tonys, the Sofitel New York would be a clear winner. As a longtime partner of Broadway’s iconic awards show, many a theater star has walked through its doors. That includes George Clooney during his Broadway debut in Good Night, and Good Luck, Jonathan Groff during his turn as Bobby Darin in Just in Time, and Mia Farrow while she was in The Roommate. Just last year, the property underwent a full makeover, reimagining its 398 rooms and suites (some with Empire State Building views), as well as its lobby, fitness center, and dining options (including Social 45 Bar & Bistro), drawing on the Art Deco glamour of Paris and New York. While an exclusive Broadway package is currently in the works, the Sofitel does currently offer The Ultimate Manhattan Luxury Staycation experience, which includes a welcome drink, dining credit, signature pastries, and early check-in at noon, perfect for squeezing in an extra Wednesday or weekend matinee.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Longacre TheatreWhy we love it: Quiet, designed by a Tony-winning scenic designer, curated theater mementos

Despite being footsteps away from several Broadway theaters, Civilian Hotel manages to create a cozy boutique experience, starting with an entrance just around the corner from Eighth Avenue. One step inside, and you feel like you’ve earned a backstage pass— hotelier Jason Pomeranc teamed up with scenic designer David Rockwell (Hairspray, Legally Blonde, Elf) on a classic theater theme featuring everything from marquee-inspired lighting to dramatic curtains. Even its 203 guest rooms channel vintage dressing room vibes. Rockwell's goal was to create a space for NYC’s creatives—performers, designers, directors, producers, and writers—that paid homage to classic Broadway. Stop by the Blue Vault tasting room and lounge to spot some theater relics, and the Olio Collection rooftop bar for more than 250 pieces of theater-inspired art.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Palace Theatre, 3-minute walk to Marquis TheatreWhy we love it: Location across from TKTS booth, buzzy Sky Lobby

When it comes to Theater District locations, you can't find much better than the 661-room Tempo by Hilton New York Times Square. Making its debut in the dense area in August 2023, it snagged a prime spot right across from Duffy Square’s TKTS booth, the bright red discount ticket outlet that sells last-minute show tickets for up to 50% off (psst, check here for today’s offers). Even closer is the Palace Theatre, currently home to the musical The Lost Boys, which the property has partnered with on a themed suite, bookable through September 14, 2027. Inside the suite, you'll find an ’80s seaside feel mimicking the musical’s world of Santa Carla.

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to Eugene O’Neill Theatre, Walter Kerr, and Ambassador Theatre; half a dozen more a 3-minute walk awayWhy we love it: Vacation vibes at its Bar Sprezzatura, daily complimentary wine in the Living Room Lobby during Evening Social Hour, Roundabout Theatre Company partnership

The first time I stepped off the elevator into Kimpton Theta New York’s Bar Sprezzatura, I immediately craved an Aperol spritz. That’s how much I was transported to the Italian Riviera. The contrast between the lively Midtown streets below (the bar sits on the 15th floor) and the laid-back rooftop bar made me fall in love with the 364-key property instantly, and with multiple two- and three-bedroom suites, it's perfect for families and groups looking to book a foodie-friendly Broadway bonding trip. This November, the hotel launched the Roundabout Theatre Co. x Kimpton Theta package, giving guests 20% off tickets to Roundabout Theatre Co. shows (currently The Rocky Horror Show and Imaginary Invalid) plus pre- or post-show drinks at the bar.

Closest theaters: Attached to Marquis Theatre, 1-minute walk to Minskoff Theatre, 2-minute walk to Richard Rodgers TheatreWhy we love it: Ideal for Marquis Theatre shows, home to NYC’s only rotating restaurant, Broadway Bound Dining Package

For a mega-sized hotel smack dab in the middle of Times Square, the Marriott Marquis still has a sense of character. When I first moved to the area 23 years ago, I used to frequent its eight-floor Broadway Lounge, looking out at Times Square and marveling that I had finally “made it." Nowadays, I still pop in for a dose of nostalgia, gazing up at the 36-floor atrium’s elevators leading to the hotel's 1,900 rooms—a constant in a world that’s changed so much since it opened in 1985. But that throwback feel comes with a new spring in its step, most notably at its 48th-floor spinning restaurant, The View, reimagined by Danny Meyer in 2024. (Note: TodayTix members get free bubbly and bar snacks here, depending on their tier.) But what makes the property so unique for theater fans is that it’s the only hotel ever built with a Broadway theater inside—yes, the Marquis Theatre is literally on the third floor. Also special: The Broadway Bound Dining Package includes the chance to mingle with a theater star!

Closest theaters: 2-minute walk to the Nederlander Theatre, New Amsterdam Theatre, and Lyric TheatreWhy we love it: Themed rooms, located on 42nd Street, close to other attractions

Now here’s a hotel that reflects both “A Whole New World” and “The Circle of Life.” Through its partnership with Disney’s two long-running musicals, Hilton New York Times Square guests can go all in with themed rooms curated by Broadway designer Devin Sparkles Design. Aladdin's Times Square Palace Suite is decked out just like Agrabah, down to a genie lamp, Moroccan magic carpets, and Jasmine-inspired silks. Over in The Lion King’s Royal Suite, it’s all about the wonders of the Serengeti Pridelands, with hand-painted Rafiki-like patterns and bird puppets flying from the ceiling. Both include wake-up calls from each musical’s most iconic characters—the Genie and Rafiki—as well as themed drinks. But perhaps the most valuable part of the package, especially for those driving in? Parking in Times Square.

Closest theaters: 1-minute walk to Hudson Theatre, Belasco Theatre, and Lyceum Theatre

Why we love it: Passageway running between Hudson Theatre’s entrance and stage door, June 2026 refresh

Ever since my first Broadway trip to NYC in 2002, I’ve been stage-dooring shows. The Hudson Theatre shows can be tricky for this, as the theater’s entrance is on 44th Street, but its stage door is on 45th. It wasn’t until I discovered that the Millennium Hotel had a secret passageway—which is also the entrance to the hotel—that I started snagging spots close enough to get autographs (including from Daniel Radcliffe during Merrily We Roll Along). That said, I've always been jealous of those actually staying at the 751-room property, with a trio of theaters literally at their doorstep. Those eager to dive even deeper into the Theater District's history will love that the property is just across the street from the Museum of Broadway.

Is it expensive to see a show on Broadway?

Yes, price tags can be high—the year-to-date average per ticket for 2026 is $122.67. But there are also plenty of ways to find discounts through lotteries, TodayTix, Theatr, and the TKTS Booth. I’ve only paid more than $100 five times in my life—and never more than $200. (That’s why I haven’t been to a movie in nearly a decade, but have seen nearly 40 shows in the last year!)

What show should I see on Broadway this winter?

For last-minute trips, hot tickets right now include Bowen Yang’s record-breaking run in Cole Escola’s Oh, Mary! (Lyceum Theatre), plus A Few Good Men (Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Much Ado About Nothing (Winter Garden), Other Desert Cities (Hudson Theatre), and School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play (Samuel J. Friedman). And of course there are long-running hits like Wicked (Gershwin Theatre), Hamilton (Richard Rodgers Theatre), Harry Potter and the Cursed Child (Lyric Theatre), The Great Gatsby (Broadway Theatre), and Disney’s The Lion King (Minskoff Theatre).

Are there any shows I should plan a 2027 trip around?

As we’re standing on the precipice of one of the most anticipated Broadway seasons, there’s no better time to plan a theater getaway. Coming soon are Dolly: A True Original Musical (opening December 7 at St. James Theatre), the Julia Roberts and Paul Rudd–led Small Mouth Sounds (February 10 at Ethel Barrymore Theatre), Jonathan Groff’s The Amish Project (February 10 at Broadhurst Theatre), Dirty Dancing (February 12 at Lena Thorne Theatre), Evita on Broadway (February 27 at Winter Garden Theatre), Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Warriors (March 9 at Lunt-Fontanne Theatre), Purple Rain (March 12 at Majestic Theatre), The Sound of Music (March 23 at Vivian Beaumont Theatre), Damn Yankees (March 24 at Marquis Theatre), and the one I’m most thrilled about, the West End transfer Paddington: The Musical (March 30 at Al Hirschfield Theatre)—I already have my ticket for the first preview!

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

Despite the unfavorable transfer ratio, Hyatt is still a compelling transfer partner thanks to its fixed award chart pricing. And with a deep roster of airline and hotel partners, Chase still offers plenty of opportunities for valuable redemptions with other partners.

#6239. Why Russia Is Targeting European Freezers

Rearmament isn’t just for the battlefield — civil defense matters, too.

A woman walks past partially empty shelves at a SuperValu store in Blanchardstown, Dublin, Ireland, November 2, 2026.

Twice in the space of a few weeks, Russian hackers have managed to seize control of supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. It began with hundreds of French stores in mid-October, after which, in early November, hackers struck outlets in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, and elsewhere. The hackers remotely forced freezers and chillers into prolonged defrost mode, driving temperatures to more than 120 degrees Fahrenheit and spoiling large quantities of food. These attacks have revealed an underrated aspect of rearmament that has so far been almost completely overlooked: civil defense.

Hackers behind most ransomware attacks demand payment. These hackers simply disrupted Europe’s food supply and left without a message. Only a few days after the most recent (as of this writing) attacks, in early November, did a Russian group finally claim responsibility. European policymakers who may have wished that some random teenagers were behind the attacks instead had their fears confirmed: This was a Russian attack against Europe’s food supply.

John Gustavsson is a writer from Sweden and holds a doctorate in economics. He is Senior Editor of Nation & Citizenship at Restoring the West and a former adviser to the Sweden Democrats in the European Parliament.

#6238. Military Member Calls Alaska Airlines Employee “Anti-Military” Over Denied Free Upgrade

A military member and social media influencer has taken to Instagram to complain about a recent interaction with an Alaska Airlines employee, where he asked for a free upgrade, and was denied. He’s accusing an employee at the airline of being anti-military. Is that a fair complaint, or is this being blown out of proportion?

A military member posted a 2min35sec video online, outlining his experience with an Alaska Airlines representative at Portland International Airport (PDX), which he claims was his first time encountering an “anti-military” employee at the airline. To summarize his version of events:

You can see the video for yourself below. As you’d expect, this guy’s followers are mostly military related, so the 1,300+ comments on the post are almost entirely in agreement with the person who posted the video.

First let me say that I of course respect and appreciate the service of those who are in the military (even if I fundamentally disagree with the extent to which we get into conflicts that accomplish nothing — that’s the fault of our elected leaders, and not the fault of those who put their lives on the line).

Of course if the Alaska Airlines employee in question was rude, that’s not acceptable, and people expect polite service. Now, I’m a little skeptical of how much of a direct transcript this was, rather than how this guy chose to interpret it. That includes things like him suggesting that the Alaska employee accused him of lying. If that were the case, that’s unacceptable, but again, it’s not clear if that was actually said, or just how he was made to feel.

All that being said, this guy sort of strikes me as being rather entitled. Airlines are extremely generous with active duty military members, as they should be. The airline has a page that outlines military and veteran benefits, and upgrades isn’t among those perks. The airline offers all kinds of other things, ranging from special fares, to lounge access, to priority boarding. But it seems a little greedy to then be like “oh, they do all these things, but they should do more” (since he chooses to reference this page).

But here’s my bigger issue with this guy’s approach. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with asking for an upgrade, but be ready to be shot down. However, I feel like his approach is more one of entitlement than “it can’t hurt to ask.” Why do I say that?

The very example he gives is that for all these times he flies Alaska, either they say “sure, we’ll upgrade you,” or they say “sorry, it’s full, we can’t upgrade you.” In other words, he assumes he’s entitled to the upgrade as long as there are open seats, which just isn’t the policy. If he’s going to be rejected for something he’s not entitled to, he wants to be lied to, rather than told “sorry, that’s not our policy.”

And again, he emphasizes how he has no level of entitlement, but also then argues by pointing out that he has been upgraded for free in the past. It all sounds to me a little like being caught with a liquid that’s too large at the TSA checkpoint, and then trying to argue with them, and say “well last time they let me through.” Well, that’s fine, but that’s not the policy.

So my take here is that airline employees should of course always be professional. I think it’s perfectly fine to say “I’m sorry, that’s not our policy,” which is something this guy seems to take issue with. If the employee did actually accuse him of lying about being upgraded in the past, that’s of course not acceptable. But I’m also not convinced that actually happened.

A military member has accused an Alaska Airlines employee of being anti-military, after being denied a free upgrade to a seat with more legroom. He argues that there’s no harm in asking, but also seems to think that the only acceptable rejection is a claim that the cabin is full.

While Alaska offers lots of perks to military members (as they should), upgrades isn’t among them. Asking once is one thing, but I do find it a bit entitled to essentially believe that you’re entitled to the seats as long as they’re empty, and then to argue if you’re not upgraded.

What do you make of this “anti-military” Alaska employee?

Alaska Airlines is rolling out a new invite-only status level called Atmos Global Concierge. Like the other major U.S. airlines that have such a tier, Alaska is not publicly disclosing what it takes to earn an invitation — though you can be sure it will require a lot of spending.

News of Alaska's new invite-only tier began spreading across aviation blogs Tuesday, and the company confirmed the move to TPG.

"Atmos Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program," said Alaska in a statement, " ...  that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most."

For now, this is a beta program rollout, so it's likely to change over time.

In addition to published top tiers, like American Airlines' AAdvantage Executive Platinum, Delta's Diamond Medallion and United Airlines' Premier 1K, all three major U.S. carriers offer an even higher level of status generally saved for the elites who spend the most with the airline (and some travel providers and C-level executives and celebrities).

American Airlines has ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has 360, and United Airlines has Global Services. And now Alaska has Atmos Global Concierge.

None of these airlines publicly disclose the exact qualification requirements for their invitation-only programs, which makes pontificating about what it takes to qualify something of an unofficial pastime for loyalty die-hards.

Among the theories: Invites are tied not only to flight spending, but also to credit card spending and even to your home airport. For example, an American Airlines frequent flyer based at the carrier's Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) hub might have a harder time securing an invitation than a similarly high-spending traveler based in a more competitive market.

Alaska isn't revealing the full list of benefits that come with its new status, but it did share some details with TPG.

"Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences," Alaska said.

That means help with travel disruptions, such as a next-flight guarantee and dedicated, specialized assistance.

Reports suggest other benefits include the ability to gift Gold status, a free Clear+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. Those invited are also reportedly being given Atmos Titanium status, even if they haven't already qualified organically this year.

If Alaska follows the lead of its larger competitors, additional perks could include VIP airport transfers, higher upgrade priority and expanded lounge access. However, Alaska has not confirmed those benefits.

As for what it might take to get invited to this special club, it will likely require spending tens of thousands of dollars on tickets. Some reports suggest the invitations appear to be targeted at potential customers for Alaska's new international routes with lie-flat business class. On the flip side, some Titanium-level Alaska flyers haven't been invited even after earning as many as 250,000 Alaska Atmos status points and buying international business-class tickets.

"Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows," Alaska told TPG.

While this won't mean much for most of us, it's still exciting to see a new layer of potential perks for some of Alaska's most loyal flyers. Alaska has been one of the most innovative U.S. airlines when it comes to loyalty, so it's an interesting development to see the carrier recognize its highest-value customers with an invite-only tier that matches what the other big global U.S. airlines have done.

Alaska is also now the only major U.S. airline that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles (though you can choose to earn status by spending). A new top-tier status level is another way the airline is differentiating itself.

#6236. Atmos Global Concierge: Alaska Airlines’ New Invitation-Only Elite Status

Alaska Airlines is increasingly becoming like the “big three” US carriers when it comes to its route network, as the airline expands globally, following its takeover of Hawaiian Airlines. Now the airline is doing another thing you’ll find at competitors, which is introducing an invitation-only elite status. Let’s take a look at what we know so far about Atmos Global Concierge, which is the name of this new status.

Some Atmos Rewards members on Reddit are reporting receiving an invitation for the carrier’s new status tier that has no published qualification requirements, and it’s above the Titanium tier. Those who have been awarded the status can keep it through December 31, 2027.

So, what are the perks of Atmos Global Concierge status?

We’ll have to of course wait some time to get firsthand reports of the experience, but as you’d expect, this is a lot more about better “soft” treatment, plus having top priority for everything. There’s nothing particularly remarkable about this status otherwise, but that’s not surprising, since that’s typically not the focus on invitation-only elite status.

It’s anyone’s guess what exactly it takes to get an invitation, as it’s a bit of a mystery, much like with American Concierge Key, Delta 360, and United Global Services. It’s possible that criteria differ based on where you mostly fly out of. It does seem like frequent international travel in business class is something that increases odds of eligibility.

Based on the reports so far, it almost seems like this status is being dangled as a “carrot” for those who have maybe taken a few long haul business class trips, in hopes of keeping them flying on Alaska and Hawaiian.

There’s a reason that airlines offer invitation-only elite status, and it’s kind of brilliant. The idea is to keep people on the “hamster wheel,” and keep them booking high yield tickets on an airline over competitors.

Airlines of course have elite tiers with published requirements, and once you qualify for your planned tier for a year, you might consider branching out and booking another airline. But when there’s invitation-only elite status, you don’t know what you actually need to earn it, so you’re more likely to keep flying with the airline. And if you’re spending other people’s money, you’re also more likely to make sure that ticket is expensive as it should be.

At the end of the day, these kinds of status tiers aren’t really about the exact details of the perks. On some level, they’re intended to stroke the egos of travelers, and that works. People get excited when they get to board a flight first, etc., and this whole concept plays into that.

Alaska Airlines has introduced a new invitation-only elite status, named Atmos Global Concierge. The idea is that this is targeted primarily at those flying a lot internationally, and it offers perks like concierge assistance, upgrade priority, some partner elite perks, and more.

With the way Alaska has grown, it’s not surprising to see the airline also copying the “big three” with a status tier like this.

What do you make of Atmos Global Concierge?

#6235. Trump’s Amnesty Talk

President Donald Trump looks on as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller speaks about birthright citizenship in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., August 6, 2026.

Vice President JD Vance warned in his famous post-midterm X post that Republicans would begin advocating for amnesty in the aftermath of the election. He was right, although he didn’t mention that the president of the United States would be one of them.

In a 60 Minutes interview over the weekend, Trump said he’d like to find a deal with Democrats to regularize the legal status of good, hardworking illegal immigrants. Whenever Trump has talked in these terms in the past, or mused about increasing levels of legal immigration, his restrictionist aides have — rightly — pulled him back.

This will probably happen again, given that the president has just made the ur-immigration hawk Stephen Miller his chief of staff. Even if Trump persists, it’s hard to see how there’d be any deal in the offing with Democrats who think they won, in part, on the excesses of the president’s immigration enforcement and have a chance for a trifecta in 2028 that could roll back his immigration agenda entirely. Are they really going to make concessions on enforcement or legal immigration numbers?

There’s no doubt that the administration’s immigration regime hurt among Hispanics voters and the general electorate as well, although not nearly as much as corruption, prices, and the Iran war. With a vast illegal immigrant population in the United States and limited enforcement resources, the administration has understandably looked to self-deportation as a force multiplier. If there are high-profile apprehensions and deportations, illegal immigrants see that and decide to go home on their own. This dynamic has clearly contributed to a notable diminishment in the foreign-born population in Trump’s second term.

The political problem is that everyone else sees those apprehensions and detentions and may not like them, especially if they are needlessly combative for the sake of cable-news coverage and internet clicks. This was the approach of former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, whose subtraction from the administration was a net addition. Border czar Tom Homan took over the immigration portfolio and has tried to avoid headlines, but enforcement has still been overwhelming based on apprehensions in public places.

What’s been missing is an emphasis on what our friends at the Center for Immigration Studies call bureaucratic or briefcase enforcement, the nuts-and-bolts work to track down, warn, and punish as necessary employers who hire illegal workers. Ideally, we’d have a national E-Verify system to instantaneously flag such workers. Still, there’s much that can be done with currently existing tools, and Homan himself favors deploying them.

If we squeeze illegal workers out of the labor market, it creates an incentive for them to leave, since so many came here looking for a job. At the same time, such largely invisible enforcement doesn’t generate occasions for demonstrations and turmoil in the streets.

Yet the president is an obstacle to adopting this tactic. He has sympathy for employers desperate for immigrant labor — since he was one himself — and influential business constituencies will balk at intense workplace enforcement. So, we have the president wildly swinging from supporting splashy actions targeting specific cities to talking about throwing in the towel.

At some point, when the illegal population is down substantially and there’s an enforcement system in place that can’t be ignored or gamed, there will be a case for amnesty for specific categories of illegal immigrants. We aren’t there yet, and we shouldn’t be thinking of giving up after one election loss. Vance implied that it was GOP quislings who would immediately turn to amnesty after the midterm drubbing, but, alas, the call is coming from inside the house.

#6234. The Qantas Airbus A321XLR That Has 3 Fewer Economy Seats

In a move that puts traveler comfort ahead of scraping every shred of profit for a jetliner, Qantas pulled out three seats from its Airbus A321XLR that are requisite revenue-generating hardware for most shareholders. The aircraft, tail number VH-OGD, is the first delivery of a 48-seat subfleet that will include a fourth bathroom, using space that was reserved for the usual row of seats in the main cabin. The modification highlights a design tension inherent to the long-range narrowbody platform.

The cabin reconfiguration was designed in response to customer feedback that followed the first three deliveries of the type. The overarching tone from passengers, aviation commentators, and the media was scathing and derisive, often framing the issue as a ‘legacy stink’ left behind by the airline’s highly controversial former CEO, Alan Joyce.

Thus, instead of 180 economy and 20 business, the updated cabin of Qantas’ long-haul narrowbody now seats 197 travelers in ‘coach.’ The customer feedback Qantas received was immediate and highly critical of the airline's management, forcing a mid-stream redesign before the bulk of the fleet was even built. Consequently, the airline also committed to retrofitting the first three A321XLR aircraft already in its fleet with the extra toilet during future heavy maintenance checks.

Qantas ordered the new extra-long-range Airbus single-aisles in 2022 to replace aging Boeing 737-800s. In 2025, Qantas launched commercial A321XLR flights, beginning September service with Sydney and Melbourne. Sky TG24 noted that while marketing focused on cabin width and fuel efficiency, the media attention was honed in on the jet’s layout flaws. It was specifically highlighted that the first three aircraft of Australia’s flag carrier had fewer toilets in economy than its low-cost competitors, Ryanair, Scoot, and Jetstar.

For comparison, a standard Ryanair Boeing 737 carries 197 passengers with three toilets, like the new Qantas A321XLR. That ratio averages 66 people per facility. A Scoot Airbus A320 accommodates 180 passengers with three toilets, or 60 per facility. Meanwhile, a Jetstar A320 seats 186 with three units, averaging 62. In contrast, the original Qantas cabin provided just two toilets for 180 seats, at a 50% elevated ratio of 90 people per facility.

As Runway Girl Network reported, the airline stated that the first aircraft will be finalized in 2022 with three toilets to match outgoing 737 specifications. Management has since promised all 48 jets on order will feature four toilets following the updated design. The layout assigns three facilities to economy and one to business class. However, The Guardian has emphasized that the first three airframes will likely operate unchanged for approximately three years before undergoing a formal retrofit.

The first modified four-lavatory aircraft was currently scheduled for a December 2025 delivery. It didn’t ultimately reach Australia until late February of this year, according to Australian Aviation. The arrival resolved the initial cabin design crisis, shifting the industry conversation away from consumer complaints. Yet, analysts turned to the manufacturing choices and cabin design priorities that had led to the ill-equipped jets’ arrival in the first place.

Packing 200 passengers into a narrow fuselage turns cabin calculus into a test of passenger patience. While three total lavatories average one per 67-person full cabin, the forward facility is reserved for business class. That left only two rear toilets for 180 economy travelers, inflating the ratio to 90 people per facility. An arrangement that fell below the amenities relative to the legacy aircraft it replaced despite Qantas’ claims.

One Mile at a Time calculated that the outgoing Boeing 737-800 provided two toilets for a cabin of 162 economy seats, which equals 81 passengers each. The A321XLR added 18 coach seats compared to the 737 without expanding toilet capacity. Airline Geeks also reported that the legacy jet carried 174 total customers, increasing total flyer volume by 15%.

That design deviated drastically from the standard of the rest of the jets in the full-service airline’s fleet. While budget carriers maximize efficiency by allowing open passenger access to all facilities, AeroLOPA noted that Qantas' own standards typically maintain a ratio between 42 and 49 passengers per lavatory on long-haul airframes. This underscored the unusual deficit in the new narrowbody layout, which fell well behind the carrier's traditional passenger-comfort standard in its international widebody fleet.

General industry benchmarks added to the negative optics that resulted after the first three planes began service. Other prominent ‘legacy style’ operators of the Airbus A321 family, including Delta Air Lines, routinely equip their economy cabins with at least three dedicated lavatories on short and medium range routes.

What will the Australian flag carrier choose?

The A321XLR delivers a single-aisle operational reach of 4,700 nautical miles (8,704 km), supporting flight durations approaching 11 hours. This capability enables operators like Iberia to service long-haul routes like Madrid to Boston.

Many A321neos are equipped with Airbus' SpaceFlex module, which combines the rear galley and lavatory footprint which increases passenger seating capacity. Yet, according to AeroLOPA, mid-cabin restrooms were first rejected by all six of the original launch customers: Iberia, American Airlines, Aer Lingus, Air Canada, Qantas, and United Airlines. Due to that design choice, facilities were concentrated at the extremities of the aircraft, which caused serious bottlenecks during lengthy flights lasting eight to eleven hours.

The practical consequences immediately manifested during real-world operations for more carriers than just Qantas. Iberia’s configuration placed all three economy lavatories at the extreme rear of the fuselage, with one unit dual-functioning as a flight attendant jumpseat. This layout restricted active availability to just two units for 168 economy passengers. It resulted in persistent queues that routinely clogged the rear galley workspace, according to at least one Runway Girl Network review.

Even so, Qantas still implemented the most aggressive configuration among these initial operators at the outset. Deploying the dense 200-seat layout well exceeds the 182 seats found aboard Iberia and Air Canada variants or the 184 on Aer Lingus, 155 on American, and 150 on United jets.

Qantas will have one of the highest passenger capacities onboard its Airbus A321XLRs.

Tail number VH-OGD was the first A321XLR incorporating a mid-cabin product redesign driven by preliminary operational feedback. Eliminating a three-seat economy row contracted total cabin capacity from 200 to 197 seats, leaving 20 in business and 177 in economy. This adjustment reduced the economy passenger-to-toilet ratio from 90 to approximately 59, or a 34% reduction in demand.

The rear aisle congestion also caused significant disruptions to the crew's workflow. Flight attendants frequently had to pause meal services, back up their food carts, and manually clear crowds out of the aisle just to pass. Because the new front-economy toilet can accommodate a substantial portion of the cabin's passengers, the back aisle remains open and makes everything easier for the cabin crew, which also improves the customer experience in-flight.

While sacrificing three seats removes only 1.5% of the total aircraft inventory, the configuration change greatly impacted the amenity available on each flight. The cut marginally limits the maximum revenue potential on Qantas’ routes with high demand and slightly raises unit operating expenses per seat. On the other hand, the additional restroom reduces overall cabin congestion and even lessens the operational risk of a single component failure grounding a flight, and mitigates mechanical wear across onboard plumbing.

Larger fuel tanks and a lower passenger and cargo capacity are needed for Qantas' Project Sunrise flights.

Even after the cabin update for the vast majority of Qantas’ A321XLR fleet, the initial three airframes will remain with the original high-density layout for an extended period. The Guardian projected approximately three years of active service before modification. The remaining 45 aircraft within the 48-unit order book will arrive with four factory-installed toilets.

In February, Qantas also launched its highly anticipated Economy Plus product. The extra legroom addition heavily improves passenger comfort and recline dynamics on the Airbus A321XLR. The 36 Plus seats on the A321XLR feature a generous seat pitch of 34 to 35 inches (86.36 to 88.9 cm). Standard economy seats have a pitch of 30 inches (76.2 cm). When the traveler in front reclines, the space tightens significantly.

As the A321XLR flies transcontinental routes and mid-haul international segments, posture changes are essential to prevent fatigue. Qantas also designed the A321XLR economy cabin with a focus on streaming entertainment. The seats include built-in drop-down tablet holders with anti-slip mats.

Both Qantas and British Airways are reconfiguring their A380s to cut economy seating.

The Airbus A321XLR registered as VH-OGD arrived in Australia in late February. Although Qantas initially scheduled the aircraft's international debut from Brisbane to Manila for October 25, reports say its deployment was deferred to February 1, 2027.

The A321XLR's operational role runs completely parallel to Qantas's massive widebody modernization. The effort is internally split across Project Sunrise, which will debut in first-of-their-kind Airbus A350-1000ULR variants on what is projected to be the longest commercial flights in the world. The first locked-in route connects Sydney to London Heathrow starting in October 2027, followed shortly after by a nonstop link between Sydney and New York JFK in mid-2028.

Meanwhile, Project Fysh is in the works to introduce Boeing 787s and A350s intended to replace the retiring A330 and A380 fleets. The 787-10 fleet will fly medium-haul routes from Sydney and Melbourne to Singapore, Tokyo, Hong Kong, and Auckland. The standard A350-1000 will take over the long-haul routes that require maximum capacity but don't need the Sunrise range, such as Los Angeles, San Francisco, Johannesburg, and the traditional one-stop kangaroo route to Europe via Singapore.

#6233. Frontier Airlines’ Unique First Class Now On Sale (No Food, Drinks, Or Recline)

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale, with the product launching systemwide for flights as of March 2027. This is a major development for the Denver-based airline, as the historically ultra low cost carrier tries to move upmarket, and respond to consumer preferences. This is only one of several initiatives we’re seeing, along with the introduction of Starlink Wi-Fi, plus charging ports at select seats. Let’s cover all the details.

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027. For context, Frontier plans to reconfigure its entire fleet to add eight first class seats at the front of the cabin, with two rows of seats in a 2-2 configuration. Specifically, the airline has selected the Geven Comoda seating platform, with seats having up to 37″ of pitch.

Frontier has already started reconfiguring planes with first class cabins, and the idea is that by early March 2027, the entire fleet will have these seats, which is the point at which they’ll be sold as a separate product. So while the seats will already be in service, and some customers will luck out, that’s the formal launch plan.

Obviously this is a fast timeline for retrofitting cabins, but keep in mind most of the cabin will remain unchanged, so it shouldn’t take much time to reconfigure each aircraft. So, what should we expect in terms of the first class product? Here’s how the airline describes it:

First Class seats offer our most spacious seating experience, providing exceptional comfort and additional personal space at the front of the aircraft. These seats are pre-reclined and do not convert into lie-flat beds.

Complimentary food and beverages are not included with the First Class experience. However, a variety of food and beverage options are available for purchase by all passengers.

Frontier’s first class seats will be “pre-reclined” (meaning they won’t recline), and won’t actually offer complimentary snacks and drinks, so it’ll be just like economy in that regard. On the plus side, the seats are expected to feature USB-C charging ports, which will be the first time that the airline offers in-seat power. The carrier is also going from offering no Wi-Fi, to offering Starlink Wi-Fi as of mid-2027, so that’s pretty exciting.

The airline will also be introducing a dedicated extra legroom section in rows three through eight, with seats having up to 34″ of pitch. Not only that, but these seats will also have USB-C charging ports (while the remainder of economy seats won’t offer in-seat power).

With Frontier Airlines first class tickets now on sale, what is pricing like? The airline is increasingly leaning into the concept of bundles, so we’ll see the Basic Fare, Economy Bundle, Premium Bundle, and First Bundle.

The First Bundle includes a carry-on bag and personal item, two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds each, priority boarding, and no change or cancel fees.

Pulling up a random one-way flight from Denver (DEN) to Los Angeles (LAX), I see the Basic Fare starting at $119, the Economy Bundle starting at $142, the Premium Bundle starting at $172, and the First Bundle starting at $244.

Those are some incredibly attractive prices, especially if you intend to check bags. However, the airline emphasizes how it has promotional pricing at launch, so only time will tell how that pricing evolves.

There’s no single right or wrong way to offer a premium product. However, I feel like Frontier might be taking the wrong strategy here. What Frontier is offering is essentially more along the lines of the initial Spirit “Big Front Seat” — you get more space, and nothing else.

This just strikes me as a missed opportunity, because I feel like psychologically, willingness to pay is going to be substantially higher if you just include free alcoholic drinks and at least some sort of food. It’s not like I was expecting them to install ovens and have hot meals (JetBlue’s new first class will only have cold food).

But I feel like if the airline just invested $10 in drinks & snacks they could charge more, and would also expand the potential customer base. Whether logical or not, there are some number of passengers who would be more likely to even consider a product if it actually had a dedicated soft product, rather than just being a more spacious seat. At least that’s my take.

Obviously at the current pricing, this is an incredibly attractive proposition for customers. However, I also feel like the airline probably wants to be able to charge higher fares in the long run.

Frontier Airlines has started to reconfigure planes with first class seats, with tickets now being on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027 (at which point the entire fleet should be reconfigured). While Frontier first class will have first class-style seats (minus the recline), there won’t be any differentiation in terms of the soft product, as food and drinks will still be available for purchase.

I would’ve liked the airline to actually roll out a differentiated soft product, but it sounds like that’s not happening. Then again, between Starlink Wi-Fi and in-seat power, this will be a much more attractive proposition than flying with Frontier in the past.

What do you make of Frontier’s first class concept?

#6232. A350-1000ULR Sets New Distance Record

Airbus’ A350-1000ULR has been officially recognized for breaking the Guinness World Record for the longest flight by distance by a commercial aircraft.

The record-breaking flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France, took place in July and was widely reported on, but was only recently confirmed by Guinness using data validated by the International Aeronautical Federation and flightradar24.

The nonstop journey covered 12,503 nautical miles and lasted 24 hours and 24 minutes. The -1000ULR flew over Sydney and the Pacific on a north-easterly routing toward Los Angeles, crossed North America and the Atlantic, and passed over London on its way to Toulouse. According to Airbus, the 13 people on board witnessed two sunsets and two sunrises.

The crew included three Airbus flight test pilots, two pilots from Qantas, and five Airbus flight test engineers. Also on board were two Airbus design engineers and a representative from the IAF.

Airbus is developing the -1000ULR for Qantas’ Project Sunrise, a yearslong effort to connect the east coast of Australia with far-flung destinations such as New York and London. The manufacturer expects to deliver the first of the type in April 2027. Qantas is aiming to operate the first Project Sunrise flight, from Sydney to London, later that year.

The Australian flag carrier has ordered 12 -1000ULRs.

“In responding to the challenge laid down by Qantas, our teams came together to extend the range of the A350-1000 in an efficient and economically viable way to undertake the world’s longest ever commercial flights,” Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus, said in a news release. “Flying 12,503 nautical miles non-stop, we have fully proven the aircraft’s capability to fulfill its mission. And the world record was the icing on the cake.”

If you fly United Airlines regularly, you've probably considered adding one of its cobranded credit cards to your wallet. But with several options offering everything from complimentary checked bags to United Club lounge access, figuring out which one is worth the annual fee isn't always easy.

I carry the (see rates and fees) myself, and between its annual travel credit, award flight discounts and the boost it's given me toward Premier status, I've found plenty of reasons to keep it in my wallet. But that doesn't necessarily mean it's the right United card for everyone.

And with United's recent MileagePlus changes making cobranded cards more rewarding, it's worth taking a closer look at what each one offers.

Here's how the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards compare — and how to decide which is the best fit for your travel habits.

Here’s a quick look at four of the United cards:

Related: How the United Quest Card changed my airline loyalty

Best for: Occasional United flyers who want the core travel perks without a premium price tag

Current welcome offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

The covers the basics that matter most on a typical trip, such as a free bag, priority boarding and a couple of lounge passes, without asking you to pay a premium fee for perks you'd rarely use. It's the right fit for someone who flies United a handful of times a year and wants the card to pay for itself without overthinking it.

TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak says the two United Club passes alone tend to make the card worth it for her: "A day pass into a United Club costs $59, so if I use both of my passes, I've almost entirely covered my annual fee." She adds that the 9-miles-per-dollar-spent rate on standard United fares booked with the card is the other reason it's stayed in her wallet (earning rate may vary for those with United MileagePlus status and for those flying basic economy or with a base option ticket).

Compared to the United Quest Card, the Explorer is the more accessible option for less frequent flyers, while the Quest makes more sense once you're checking bags and chasing status often enough to justify the higher fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer Card.

Best for: Regular United flyers who check bags often and want a real head start toward Premier status

Current welcome offer: Earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQP: Earn 500 PQP after your first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

The is built for travelers who fly United often enough to want more than the free bag and priority boarding the Explorer offers — and who want a card that actively pushes them toward Premier status.

Between the $200 credit and the two free checked bags, much of the $350 annual fee can be offset for anyone flying United a few times a year, especially if you prefer to check a bag rather than tow a carry-on. For example, United charges $45 for a first checked bag and $55 for a second on domestic flights (when you prepay), so checking two bags on a round-trip flight could otherwise cost $200. Take a few similar trips each year, and those savings can quickly add up.

Clint Henderson, a principal spokesperson at TPG, says the $200 trip credit and elevated earning on United flights initially won him over, with "free checked bags and priority boarding" giving him reason enough to keep the card long-term.

One major shortcoming of the Quest, especially compared to the lower-fee Explorer, is its lack of lounge access — as a reminder, the Explorer offers two, one-time United Club passes per year. However, it makes up for that with a more robust collection of statement credits, an annual award flight discount and an additional complimentary checked bag.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest Card.

Best for: Frequent United flyers who want lounge access

Current welcome offer: Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles: Earn 90,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

The Club Card is for travelers who treat lounge access as a need rather than a nice-to-have. The unlimited visits for two can outweigh the $695 annual fee on their own for anyone who flies regularly with a plus-one, before factoring in the checked bags, Premier Access or partner credits.

Christine Gallipeau, a senior loyalty program editor at TPG, says the card’s "fantastic benefits," including its complimentary United Club membership, discounted United awards and up to $150 in annual ride-hailing credits (yearly activation required), "have justified keeping the card in my wallet, especially as a frequent traveler based near United's Washington, D.C., hub."

Against the Quest, the Club costs nearly double, but that gap effectively replaces what would otherwise be a separate United Club membership. Flyers who rarely set foot in a United Club are usually better served sticking with Quest's travel credit and PQP earnings instead. The Club only pulls ahead once lounge access becomes a habit rather than an occasional treat.

Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after you add an employee card to your account in the first three months from account opening.

The packs a surprising amount of value into a moderate $150 annual fee, pairing a travel credit and lounge passes with a PQP boost that can meaningfully nudge business travelers toward Premier status.

It carries the same annual fee as the Explorer (after the first year; the Explorer has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150), but is built for business travelers who can turn everyday business expenses into progress toward Premier status.

Unlike the United Club Card, it offers just two one-time passes a year, which should be enough for someone who only wants occasional lounge access.

That's part of the appeal for Carly Helfand, TPG's director of site content strategy. She says the card works particularly well alongside the United Quest Card: "That card doesn't include any lounge access, so the United Business Card fills a gap with its two United Club one-time passes per year." She also appreciates the 5,000 bonus miles she gets each anniversary for holding both cards: "It's not a ton of miles, but it's a nice reward for keeping a card combo I was going to carry anyway!"

While the Gateway is United's only no-annual-fee card, most United flyers will get more practical value from the Explorer, which offers no annual fee for the first year (then $150). The United Club Business Card is a more compelling option, but its $695 annual fee makes it best suited to business owners who regularly use United Clubs and can maximize the value of its collection of travel and lifestyle credits. For everyone else, the $150 United Business Card offers many of the core United benefits — including two annual Club passes and a free checked bag — at a fraction of the cost.
