#6230. Lufthansa’s First Airbus A350-1000 Has Arrived: 299.5 Seats, Four Cabins, Munich Routes

In 2023, Lufthansa Group placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000 — the order was initially for 10 frames, before being increased to 15 frames the following year. The Lufthansa Group is undergoing a massive long haul fleet modernization at the moment, with both Airbus and Boeing planes on the way.

Along those lines, the first Lufthansa A350-1000 has just joined the carrier’s fleet (in a dazzling livery no less), so let’s cover all the details, including the routes the plane will fly, how the plane is configured, etc.

Between late 2026 and 2030, Lufthansa is taking delivery of 15 Airbus A350-1000s. This is only one of several aircraft types the airline is acquiring, as it’s also taking delivery of Airbus A350-900s, Boeing 787-9s, and (eventually) Boeing 777-9s.

The first A350-1000 has just been delivered today, with three more planes expected to be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of the year. This first plane even features the special 100th anniversary livery, as Lufthansa has seven of these flying, with one representing each fleet type.

The first plane has the registration code D-AIFA, and is named “Deutschland” (since Lufthansa names all of its planes). This is a special plane for another reason, as it’s also the 700th aircraft that Airbus has delivered to Lufthansa Group. How gorgeous is this plane?!?

Here’s how Heiko Reitz, Lufthansa’s Hub Manager for Munich, describes this:

“We are proud that the Airbus A350-1000—Airbus’s most modern long-haul aircraft—is coming to Munich. The introduction of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization in the history of the Lufthansa Group and a key driver on the path to more sustainability. Our new flagship features 40 percent more Business and Premium Economy seats. To put it simply: The A350-1000 strengthens our premium hub in Munich.”

On a slight tangent, over the summer I saw the 100th anniversary Boeing 747-8 in Frankfurt (FRA), and I must say, I think it might be the most breathtaking plane in commercial service. Is it just me?

We’ve known that the Airbus A350-1000s will get the new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris first class and Allegris business class. So, what can we expect in terms of the configuration? The A350-1000 features 300 seats, spread across four cabins, as follows:

As a point of comparison, the A350-900 (the non-stretched version of the plane) features 267 seats, as follows:

So the stretched version has 11 more business class seats, 11 more premium economy seats, and 11 more economy seats (11 more seats across three cabins, what a funny coincidence). The airline is still maintaining only one row of first class, which is kind of “bleh.”

You can find the Lufthansa A350-1000 seat map here.

Lufthansa Airbus A350-1000s will all be stationed in Munich (MUC), which is where Lufthansa bases all of its A350s. The first of these planes is entering long haul commercial service as of early December 2026.

Specifically, as of December 3, 2026, the A350-1000 will fly between Munich and Tokyo Haneda (HND), with the next two destinations being Shanghai (PVG) and Singapore (SIN), and those services expected to launch within weeks, though the schedule hasn’t yet been updated to reflect that.

Note that initially the flights won’t be operated by the A350-1000 daily, so there will be alternating service with the A350-900. It’s interesting that the initial route isn’t to North America, where a single plane could do a same day turn, and continuously stay in service. but I guess there’s enough commonality between the A350-900 and A350-1000, so it’s not a big deal.

As far as US destinations go, it’s expected that Chicago (ORD) and Newark (EWR) will be the first two cities to see the new plane, though there’s no exact timeline for that yet.

In 2023, Lufthansa placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000, and the first of these planes has just been delivered, and will enter service in early December 2026. The plane features 300 seats across four cabins, though still only expect one row of first class seats. The Munich-based plane will initially fly to Tokyo, Shanghai, and Singapore. I must say, Lufthansa knocked it out of the park with its centennial livery, and I can’t wait to see this plane flying.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s Airbus A350-1000 deliveries?

I expect D-AIFA to win this contest by a hair’s breadth — unfortunate, given how AI was always tipped to take delivery of its A350-1000 before Lufthansa, if not for all the seat-installation issues plaguing VT-JRO (which is why JRP is coming first)!

#6228. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

#6227. Airline Interline, Codeshare, Alliance, And Joint Venture Agreements Explained

Airline partnerships are more complex and advanced than ever before, both for better and worse. About 25 years ago the Star Alliance was formed, which was revolutionary at the time. SkyTeam and oneworld quickly joined the scene.

While they all still exist, the global alliances have definitely been deemphasized a bit in recent years. After all, with these alliances having so many members, how much can loosely affiliated airlines really have in common?

Airlines want to work with other airlines that complement them best, and this can come in many different forms. Just to give a few examples of partnerships outside of the traditional alliances:

Airlines have several different levels of cooperation, ranging from interline agreements, to codeshare agreements, to alliance membership, to joint venture agreements. In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the differences between these agreements. Before I do so, let me add two disclaimers:

With that out of the way, let’s take a look at these four kinds of agreements.

Interline agreements are the most basic kinds of agreements you can have between airlines. An interline agreement is simply a commercial agreement between airlines to handle passengers when they’re traveling on multiple airlines on the same itinerary, and it allows an airline to issue a ticket on another airline (though not necessarily on any sort of favorable commercial terms).

This allows passengers to check their bags through to their final destination, get boarding passes all way to their destination, potentially be rebooked on another airline in the event of irregular operations, etc.

This is a basic level of cooperation, so there are airlines that have interline agreements but don’t otherwise have robust partnerships. For example, Etihad doesn’t belong to a major global alliance, but has an interline agreement with dozens of airlines, ranging from American, to Emirates, to JetBlue, to United, to Qatar Airways.

As you can see, this is a level of cooperation we even see between airlines that don’t partner with one another, and that may not even be fond of one another.

It is worth noting that in some cases airlines specifically pull out of interline agreements. For example, many years ago Delta cut its interline agreement with American. Why? At least in part it’s because Delta found that American was rebooking more passengers on Delta during irregular operations than the other way around, so the carrier no longer thought the arrangement was in its best interest.

A codeshare agreement is the next level of cooperation between airlines. This is when two airlines realize there’s value in working together, and they decide they want to place their “codes” on one another’s flights. Typically the main benefit of this is that it drums up business for the airlines that are in a codeshare agreement with one another.

Just to give an example, Alaska Airlines and Icelandair have a codeshare agreement. Icelandair flies to certain gateways in the United States, and then Alaska Airlines provides some of the “feed” for those flights in the form of codeshares.

For example, if you want to fly from Reykjavik to Los Angeles, Icelandair doesn’t operate that route. However, Icelandair flies to Portland, and then you can book a Portland to Los Angeles flight on Alaska Airlines as an Icelandair codeshare.

When you book a codeshare flight, you’ll notice that the flight number is different. So if you booked through Icelandair, your Portland to Los Angeles flight would also have an Icelandair flight number (in this case FI7696). To be clear:

With these codeshare agreements, generally neither airline is getting a huge cut for booking someone on the other airline. Most of the ticket revenue goes to the operating carrier, and often a small amount goes to the airline that sold the flight. However, the biggest advantage of this arrangement is to boost business for both airlines by increasing the number of flights that passengers have access to.

The “big three” alliances — oneworld, SkyTeam, and Star Alliance — have only developed in the past 25 years, though in the meantime many major global carriers belong to one of them. The basic way that alliances work is as follows:

I’d note that different airlines place different levels of emphasis on these alliances, even if they choose to belong to them. For example, Delta is a founding member of SkyTeam, but the airline is heavily focused on joint ventures and airlines it owns a stake in, and cares very little about the airlines it simply shares an alliance with.

If a codeshare agreement is like dating, then a joint venture is like getting married. A joint venture agreement is a massive business decision that typically requires extensive government approval. When airlines form a joint venture they coordinate pricing and schedules, and have a revenue sharing agreement.

Exactly how the revenue sharing works depends on the specific arrangement, but the idea is that two airlines are essentially acting as one under a joint venture.

Note that typically airlines form joint ventures between specific regions, which is why this is different than an outright merger. For example, American has a transatlantic joint venture with British Airways, Finnair, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, while the airline has two transpacific joint ventures, with both Japan Airlines and Qantas (the two are separate arrangements).

From the perspective of a consumer, a joint venture is both good and bad. The good news is that typically it gives you the most flight options in terms of schedules, since the airlines are operating as one. Airlines also often try to make the experience as consistent across brands as possible. The downside is that it’s like a competitor being eliminated in the market, so it could lead to higher fares as it reduces competition.

There are so many different types of agreements in the airline industry nowadays. While the exact terms vary with every partnership, I think the easiest way to sum it up is that an interline agreement is like a friendship, a codeshare agreement is like an engagement, a joint venture is like a marriage, and an alliance is like having a big family, with everyone sort of doing their own thing.

There’s a lot more to all of this, but hopefully the above provides a pretty fair and basic summary. People often misuse these terms, so I figure it’s worth recapping every so often.

#6226. The Most Likely Aircraft To Replace The Airbus A380 On High-Capacity Routes

TheAirbus A380, has been slowly dwindling in number since its maker discontinued production in 2021 as the COVID-19 Pandemic brought the death blow to quadjet manufacturing. In the aftermath of that sad finale for the iconic double-decker’s factory run, at least one airline has made every effort to keep the giants in the air.

That carrier is, of course, Emirates, which has over 100 A380s in its stables: the incredible fleet amassed by the Dubai-based airline accounts for half of the total production run of the A380. Emirates has purchased secondhand superjumbos from carriers that retired theirs due to mounting operating costs, and Dubai International Airport (DXB) even has tailor-made terminals with sky-high jet bridges just for the A380.

Despite clamoring for a renewed A380neo production, Airbus has yet to budge, citing insufficient market demand. So, as these incredible giants of the sky are slowly scrapped, mothballed, and put out to pasture in museums or the boneyard, what will take their place?

The answer is the forthcoming Boeing 777X, which will be the largest twinjet ever made. The gigantic widebody will not seat as many passengers as the A380, nor have its spectacular second deck. Still, it will meet the demands for efficiency that the future requires of the largest commercial planes in service.

The 777X is not set to enter service until 2027, but when it does, the gigantic twin-engine airliner will be a game changer for the commercial aviation industry, specifically, in the long-haul and high-density markets that are served by the A380 and a handful of A340s and Boeing 747s that are still flying. The COVID-19 pandemic brought acute pain to the commercial flying business that exacerbated the already weakening economics of quadjet flying.

That directly caused Airbus to end A380 production in 2021. The world of passenger flying rules the marketplace for commercial jets, with cargo and other niche missions accounting for only a small percentage of total airframe sales. Atlas Air was the last customer to take delivery of the Boeing 747-8F in 2023, buying all three of the final examples to roll off the line.

The A380, meanwhile, failed to become a cargo jet due to the unacceptable costs of refitting it for the mission. As such, if Boeing or Airbus is going to make a big jet, it has to be optimized for passenger service first and foremost. The 777X brings a passenger capacity close to that of the 747-8, and while appreciably less than the A380, it is still close.

That capacity shortfall is more than offset by the dramatically lower operating cost and more flexible deployment options of the 777X. The jet has fewer and less complex maintenance needs, which saves money and increases uptime. It can also fly to more airports thanks to lower airframe weight and quieter engines.

TheBoeing 777X will allow airlines that fly the gigantic A380 to take a minimal hit on capacity per departure while saving significant sums on the cost of flying, plus its modular cabin architecture means that when the demand for premium or economy service shifts, the layout can be swapped. Its improved cabin environment means that first class and economy both enjoy a markedly better experience in flight.

The 777X is designed to seat 400-415 passengers on a typical cabin layout. Compared to the A380, which seats 500-600 in conservative configurations, that number looks small, especially as the A380 is even certified for over 800 seats in an all-economy cabin environment. The problem, however, is that gigantic capacity comes at a steep cost for its operators.

Filling so many seats to satisfy the cost of flying the behemoth just isn’t always profitable, or even possible. The 777X solves that problem by enabling carriers to balance the pendulum between maximum seat count and efficient sustainment. The enormous twinjet will have the largest turbofan engines ever installed on a commercial plane in history.

Its GE9X powerplants are a revolution in commercial aircraft engine technology and make it possible for the 777X to not only haul huge numbers of flyers, but cross incredible distances, move tons of cargo, and do it all while using less fuel. Another important aspect of the future of flying is emissions.

Quadjets like the Airbus A380, A340, and Boeing 747 are prime targets for regulatory bodies and environmental activists due to the high emissions of four-engine aircraft. The 777X not only has just two powerplants, but the GE9X promises to be more efficient and cleaner than the preceding GEnx, as well as more powerful.

Airbus's A380 is equipped with Engine Alliance GP7200 or Rolls-Royce Trent 900 turbofans that put out 70,000 to 81,500 pounds of thrust. The 777X’s GE9X engines, on the other hand, have been recorded at a record-breaking 134,300 pounds of thrust. While the new Boeing may only have two engines, they nearly do the job of all four on the A380.

The A380 is famed for luxurious flying experiences offered by its top operators like Emirates, Etihad, Qatar Airways, and Singapore Airlines. Emirates and Qatar Airways are also two of the topBoeing 777 owners by fleet count and have invested heavily in crafting the most indulgent and pampering premium cabin products on the market.

That outstanding level of service has become a central pillar of the brand identity that many A380-flying airlines will need to sustain as the superjumbos reach the end of their service lives. The 777X provides a large, spacious, and modern cabin environment that forms a strong baseline for unique cabin appointments created by each airline.

In addition to being larger than the legacy 777 cabin by four inches, the lighting is provided by customizable LEDs, and the windows are 17% larger. The windows are also higher on the fuselage and can be optionally installed with electronic dimmer systems instead of physical covers.

The space itself is one thing, but the environmental conditions are also excellent in theBoeing 777X, whose cabin is set at an altitude of 6,000 feet instead of the industry standard 8,000 feet. That is in keeping with the A380’s own pressurization, which is also lower than most jetliners to reduce the fatigue of long-haul flying and jet lag.

Many flights served by the giant jets are transcontinental or transoceanic, which makes this feature invaluable. The 777X will also have cabin humidity that is twice as high as the legacy 777, which will surpass the A380 as well and help to make passengers feel fresher and energetic upon landing, as well as cut down on jet lag effects.

In terms of cabin noise, the 777X’s GE9X engines will be quieter than on previous-generation widebodies. Paired with better cabin insulation, the 777X will have far less engine noise in the cabin. Boeing even went as far as to redesign the air conditioning to bring down the decibel level even more.

A key upgrade that the 777X will give A380 operators is the flexible cabin configuration that is readily changeable depending on the needs of the airline. When market conditions change, customer demand shifts, or new technology becomes available, the 777X is adaptable.

The architecture of the plane is designed to make it possible to reconfigure not only seat rows and premium suites, but also lavatories and galleys. Crew rest areas with bunks can also be installed or removed, depending on the aircraft’s mission. If the demand for air travel falls short on long-haul routes, the cabin can be reappointed with maximum seating capacity to serve high-density destinations.

Vice versa, rows can be removed, and more premium cabin spaces can be set up for long-distance itineraries instead. As the market for premium flying products shrinks or grows, so too can the amount of cabin floor space dedicated to the suites and luxury appointments inside the 777X.

Updating the technology aboard the 777X, like seatback inflight entertainment, will be a breeze as well for airlines that fly the 777X. As premium demand grows, airlines can introduce all-new cabin designs without major overhauls. This open architecture design is crucial for airlines to keep standards high, meet customer demands, adapt to market conditions, and keep up with new trends.

There’s no true replacement for the Airbus A380, which is more than just the biggest airliner to ever take to the skies. It is an icon and a symbol of ingenuity, daring, size, and luxury. The colossal plane will never really be replaced by a smaller twinjet, but it can be retired with the assurance that another great plane is ready to take up the mantle.

Airbus's A380 will go down in history for its sheer size, but also the dizzyingly spectacular offerings of its operators, from lounges and bars in the sky to shower rooms and fully private suites. The 777X cannot hope to achieve the same level of decadent and indulgent air travel as the A380.

However, in a future where the superjumbo simply cannot survive, the new twinjet will fill its place at the top of the food chain. It is a groundbreaking aircraft in its own right and will no doubt be furnished with similarly massive seat capacity and dazzling features by the top airlines around the world.

The best rewards card for your wallet is usually one that rewards you with more of what you really enjoy. For those who love to travel, that might mean earning airline miles or hotel points to help fund the next trip.

But what if what you really love is sports?

The soon-to-be-released Fanatics American Express® Card is being designed specifically around sports fandom, rewarding fans with more of what they already love — from team merch and tickets to collectibles and more.

While the card isn't yet available for applications, we know that the upcoming Fanatics American Express Card will earn rewards in the form of FanCash, Fanatics' loyalty currency.

TPG Tip: You can join the waitlist now to be among the first to get the new Fanatics American Express Card when it is released.

FanCash is simple: $1 in FanCash equals $1 toward eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, from team merch on Fanatics.com to tickets in the Fanatics App and purchases on Topps.com. In eligible states, it can also be redeemed for rewards like bonus bets in Fanatics Sportsbook & Casino.

So whether you want your team's newest jersey, a collectible from a Fanatics auction or tickets to your team's next game, you'll have plenty of ways to put your FanCash to use.

When it comes to earning FanCash, here's what the new Fanatics American Express Card will offer:

And when you use the new card in the Fanatics App, you can stack rewards to earn 8% or more on purchases in the form of FanCash. That FanCash can then go toward things like apparel, tickets, trading cards, collectibles and event experiences, such as the fan favorite Fanatics Fest.

The card will have no annual fee** and will offer new cardmembers $100 in bonus FanCash after spending $1,000 on purchases within the first 90 days.***

Cardmembers can earn another $100 in bonus FanCash after spending at least $500 per month on eligible purchases for 12 consecutive months.†

Earning rewards on your spending is great, but the Fanatics American Express Card is also designed to give cardmembers something even harder for serious sports fans to get: access.

For example, cardmembers will get early presale access to select Topps releases, which could make the difference between getting your hands on something you want and missing out entirely.§

Cardmembers will also receive elevated Fanatics ONE Member Pro status, which includes 50% off ticket fees on eligible ticket purchases in the Fanatics app.‡

And while you'll get Member Pro status simply by having the card, your card can also help you make progress toward even higher Fanatics ONE status levels — and unlock additional perks along the way.

Cardmembers will receive 2,500 tier points and earn an additional 10 tier points for every $50 in card purchases, helping them work toward higher status levels that can unlock additional perks, such as tickets to Fanatics Fest, access to special events, bonus FanCash, a Fanatics ONE concierge and more.‡

With all the perks and rewards it comes with, it shouldn’t be a shocker that the Fanatics American Express Card was going to look cool, too.

And in fact, it’s almost a collectible of sorts on its own. You'll have 500+ card art options to choose from, featuring athletes across the NBA, NFL, WWE and UFC, with a unique Topps-inspired design that lets you rep your fandom every time you pull out your card.

The new Fanatics American Express Card won't just get you access to select drops and earn FanCash. Since the card is powered by the American Express Network, cardmembers will have access to Amex Offers, Amex Experiences™ — with opportunities like ticket presales — and built-in retail protections when you use the card.

There are a lot of ways the new Fanatics American Express Card stands out, but here's a truly unusual card perk.

Fanatics cardmembers will have the chance to participate in what Fanatics calls the Championship Challenge. Correctly predict the champions of the MLB, NBA, NFL and NHL, and you could get up to $100,000 of your annual spending on the Fanatics American Express Card back when the challenge launches.

That means you can put your sports knowledge to the test and have some fun following your picks throughout the year — even if you don't manage to correctly predict all four champions.

But if you do somehow nail all four? Getting up to $100,000 of your annual card spending back would certainly qualify as one of the most exciting credit card perks we've ever seen.

Eligibility requirements apply. Program details, including timing and structure, are subject to change. Terms and conditions apply. Full details to be announced prior to entry.

There are plenty of credit cards that sports fans could use, but very few are designed specifically for sports fandom.

Fanatics set out to create what it calls the “ultimate card for sports fans,” and they have certainly packed in a lot aimed squarely at that large audience.

Between early presale access to Topps releases, the ability to earn FanCash on everyday purchases and a path toward higher levels of Fanatics ONE status — not to mention the fun upcoming Championship Challenge — there are some genuinely unique perks packed into this no-annual-fee card.

If this card has your name (and favorite player) on it, know that it isn’t available quite yet, but it is coming soon.

If you want to be at the front of the line for the new card, you can join the waitlist now to be among the first to know when the Fanatics American Express Card launches.

#6224. Plaza Premium Opening Hong Kong Arrivals Lounge… With Live Music?!

Plaza Premium will be opening an arrivals lounge soon at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG). While these facilities are always useful for a shower and breakfast after an overnight flight, it sounds like there might be a bit more planned for this arrivals lounge? I’m certainly intrigued (thanks to Sel_D for flagging this)…

Plaza Premium is expected to open an arrivals lounge at Hong Kong Airport in late November 2026. The lounge will be located on level three of Terminal 2, in the arrivals portion of the terminal, below the Airport Express platform. That means it’ll be landside.

This actually technically represents the reopening of a lounge, as the global lounge operator had such a facility until 2019. At that point it closed due to an expansion project at the airport. Once open, it will be the only arrivals lounge at the airport. Cathay Pacific used to have an arrivals lounge at its hub, but it closed in 2018, and the airline has no plans to reopen such a facility.

The exact entry requirements of the Plaza Premium arrivals lounge in Hong Kong remain to be seen, but like most Plaza Premium lounges, the expectation is that entry will be possible through select credit cards and Priority Pass, and access can also be purchased directly.

Generally we think of an arrivals lounge in terms of its functional purpose, which is to shower, have breakfast, and get some work done, before heading into the city. Many arrivals lounges are only open in the morning, since that’s when there’s the most value. That’s especially true for people who either plan to head to the office, or who are staying at a hotel, where it’s well before the published check-in time.

While it remains to be seen what exactly Plaza Premium’s facility will be like, it sounds like this will be a rather unconventional arrivals lounge, in a good way. The social media post about the new lounge describes it as “Plaza Premium Lounge – Rhythms.” It will offer a “seamless blend of dining, music, wellness, and refreshment.”

In terms of the range of amenities, we’re being promised live music, wellness experiences, refined dining, and private resting spaces. I’m sorry… live music? Like… someone performing music live? In an arrivals lounge? Fascinatingly, the pictures make it look more like an evening-oriented lounge serving cocktails and wine, for lounging around, rather than your typical arrivals lounge.

A post shared by Plaza Premium Lounge (@plazapremiumlounge)

Suffice it to say that I am very interested in what they come up with here. From a monetization standpoint, this seems kind of smart, since it could drum up more business in the afternoons and evenings, when people might not otherwise consider visiting such a facility. Then again, are people really thinking “I just got off a 15 hour flight, what I could really use is a cocktail before heading to my hotel?” Maybe they are, I suppose!

In the coming weeks, Hong Kong Airport will once again have an arrivals lounge, thanks to the opening of a facility by Plaza Premium. Arrivals lounges are usually pretty basic, and are about showers and breakfast. While we’ll see how much of this is fluff rather than actual substance, Plaza Premium is promising what sounds more like a bar vibe, with live music and cocktails. Bring it on, Plaza Premium, I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of this Plaza Premium concept?

#6223. Delta SkyMiles Gold Card Review: Solid Perks For Occasional Delta Flyers

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card is the mid-range personal credit card in the American Express and Delta co-brand card portfolio, which includes seven cards, covering a variety of annual fee levels, across both personal and business products.

This post is my in-depth review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Amex Card. The card has a reasonable annual fee and is ideal for someone looking for basic benefits that come in handy when flying Delta. However, if you’re a Medallion elite flyer on Delta, another card might be a better option (more on that below).

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card review, here’s a quick look at the card’s main selling points and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Delta Gold Amex welcome bonus and ongoing fees, since these are some of the most important features to consider when opening a new card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex is currently offering new cardholders the following bonus: You may be eligible for as high as 80,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $2,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $880.

This is a solid welcome bonus, though the card recently offered a higher one that included a statement credit along with bonus miles. Everyone has to decide for themselves whether they’d rather wait for a better offer, or apply with this offer so they can take advantage of the perks ASAP.

The welcome offer on the Delta Gold Amex card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past.

You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal versions of the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more) or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the Delta Gold Amex first. That’s because if you do, you’d potentially still be eligible for the Delta Platinum Amex and Delta Reserve Amex. Meanwhile if you apply for one of those cards first, you’d no longer be eligible for the “lesser” card.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score you need to get approved for the Delta Gold Amex. I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been denied, as it’s only one of many factors that determines card eligibility.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees). This is a great opportunity to try the card before you have to “buy” it. The card also has a reasonable annual fee on an ongoing basis, so it’s easy to recoup that fee by taking advantage of the card perks.

You can also add authorized users to the Delta Gold Amex at no extra cost.

If you are going to put spending on the card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees) with the Delta Gold Amex, so you can use the card abroad without paying those high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. Unfortunately the Delta Gold Amex isn’t much to get excited about on that front, but let’s still go over the details.

When it comes to the return on spending, the Delta Gold Card offers:

While it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling. There are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays it’s common to see airlines offer elite status qualification through credit card spending. Delta SkyMiles elite status is based on the concept of Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs), and it’s possible to earn elite status with credit card spending.

The catch is that the Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn any MQDs, so if you want to qualify for status, you’ll have to pick up the Delta Platinum Card or Delta Reserve Card. More on that later.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

As I’ll cover below, having the Delta Gold Amex also gives you access to the TakeOff 15 discount on award tickets, and that can also help you stretch your SkyMiles for travel on Delta.

The real reason you’ll want to keep the Delta Gold Card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which are great for the casual Delta flyer. Truthfully, this is the value proposition of many airline credit cards — it’s largely about the welcome bonus and the perks, so let’s take a closer look at those details for the Delta Gold Amex.

Perhaps one of the biggest incentives to actually spend money on the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is the ability to earn a flight credit. Specifically, if you spend $10,000 on the card in a calendar year, you can receive a $200 Delta eCredit to use toward future travel, which will be deposited right in your SkyMiles account. The credit expires one year after it’s issued.

Getting a $200 Delta eCredit in addition to any miles could be a good incentive to spend $10,000 on the card per year. The credit alone is the equivalent of a 2% return on spending, assuming you consider it to be worth face value.

Just for having the Delta Gold Card you receive up to $100 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $100 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $100, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex, you get a first checked bag free. You can also receive a second checked bag free on eligible domestic Delta flights.

This benefit is limited to the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for your flight with your Delta Amex, though you do need to have your SkyMiles number in the reservation.

With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up. A first checked bag on domestic flights costs $45, and a second costs $55, so even just checking one bag on two roundtrip flights could effectively cancel out the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Gold Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary card member’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation. This benefit is valid for the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation.

If you have the Delta Gold Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible inflight purchases of food and beverages. The statement credit will post within 8-12 weeks of an eligible purchase.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for 1.0 cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the Delta TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta flights booked through delta.com or the Fly Delta app. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card also comes with a rideshare credit. The way it works is that you get up to $10 back as a statement credits each month when you use the card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

You need to enroll in this benefit in order to get the money back, and it doesn’t kick in until after your first card renewal. So while it’s a useful perk if you already pay for rideshares at least once a month, it doesn’t really make or break the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in having as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. Note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card isn’t a card I’d be using for my everyday spending, since there are many more rewarding cards for that. However:

In other words, for someone who flies Delta occasionally, I think this card could make sense, and the benefits can more than offset the annual fee.

Meanwhile if you’re a more frequent Delta flyer, there could be value to having one of the more premium credit cards, which allow you to spend your way to elite status, and earn Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs).

If the Delta Gold Card sounds interesting to you, but you want a business card instead, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card. Learn more about applying for Amex business cards.

The Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (learn more) has a $0 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following benefits:

Beyond that, though, there are limited perks. If you’d get value out of a first checked bag free or priority boarding, then you’re much better off getting one of Delta’s cards with an annual fee. I can’t really see much upside to getting the Delta Blue Card, over the other options in the market.

The Delta Platinum Amex (learn more) has a higher annual fee of $350 (Rates & Fees) and offers more perks than the Delta Gold:

If you want to earn MQDs toward elite status and enjoy more Delta benefits, like an annual companion certificate, the Delta Platinum Amex is the better option between these two cards.

The Delta Reserve Card (learn more) is the most premium option among personal Delta Amex cards, with the highest annual fee: $650 (Rates & Fees)

It also has the most benefits, so it could be worth it if you frequently fly Delta and want the best perks like lounge access:

Those aren’t even all the Delta Reserve card benefits. It also lets you earn MQDs on spending and gets you upgrade priority over other Delta SkyMiles members with your same Medallion tier, product, and fare experience purchased. The annual fee is high, but it’s absolutely worth a look if you want as many Delta perks as possible.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers:

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is a card that can be worth holding onto for the benefits that it offers, like up to $100 in Delta Stays credit, free checked bags, priority boarding, inflight savings, and more.

For the more frequent Delta flyer, consider the Delta Platinum Card, which can offer a larger bonus and additional perks, but also has a higher annual fee. Meanwhile if you’re a true Delta frequent flyer, consider the Delta Reserve Card, which offers some lounge access perks, helps you qualify for status fastest, etc.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Gold Amex Card, follow this link.

These include: Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (Rates & Fees).

#6222. A Look At The Salaries Of US Navy Carrier Air Wing Commanders In 2026

A US Navy Carrier Air Wing Commander (CAG) in 2026 oversees roughly 2,400 personnel, dozens of aircraft, and one of the most complex operational organizations in modern military aviation, but how much does that responsibility actually pay? Following the 3.8% military pay raise implemented under the FY26 NDAA, a Navy Captain (O-6) serving as a CAG can earn well over $200,000 annually once housing allowances, Aviation Incentive Pay, and deployment-related compensation are included.

At a time when commercial airlines continue recruiting experienced military aviators with salaries that can exceed $500,000 per year, CAG compensation has become part of a much larger conversation about retention, naval aviation readiness, and the future of carrier air wings built around the Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet Block III and Lockheed MartinF-35C Lightning II.

Taking into account 2026 DFAS pay tables, Military-Ranks.org compensation data, Glassdoor salary submissions, Navy personnel policies, and official US Navy organizational information, this article breaks down the major factors shaping a Carrier Air Wing Commander’s earnings in 2026. The analysis examines several key areas: base pay and allowances, aviation incentive compensation, how CAG salaries compare with other senior naval aviators and airline pilots, and the operational realities that justify one of the Navy’s most demanding leadership roles.

A Carrier Air Wing Commander holds the rank of Navy Captain, pay grade O-6. According to the Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) 2026 pay tables, O-6 base pay starts at $8,067.90 per month for officers with fewer than two years of service at that grade, but a CAG, by definition, is not a junior captain. Most officers who earn a carrier air wing command have accumulated over 20 years of service, placing them firmly at the upper end of the pay scale.

At 20+ years, O-6 monthly base pay reaches $12,638.40 per month, and at maximum longevity steps it climbs to $14,282.40 per month — though federal law caps O-6 base pay at $15,000.00 per month. That translates to an annual base salary of roughly $151,660 to $171,388 for a typical CAG, before a single dollar of allowances or special pay is added.

The 2026 figure already reflects a 3.8% pay raise that took effect on January 1, 2026, after President Donald Trumpsigned the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26 NDAA) into law on December 18, 2025. That raise, as noted by NavyCS, was mandated by U.S.C. Title 37 and applies uniformly across all active military branches.

For historical perspective, that same O-6 pay grade in 2020 topped out near $12,638 per month; The accumulated raises of the last six years have added well over $1,600 per month to a senior captain's baseline earnings. That upward trajectory has been consistent, partly driven by Congress responding to retention pressures as the commercial airline industry entered one of its largest hiring cycles in history.

Base pay tells only part of the story. Military compensation is deliberately structured as a package, with non-taxable allowances and incentive pay that can add tens of thousands of dollars annually. For a Carrier Air Wing Commander, those components typically include several distinct streams. According to Military-Ranks.org, when the most common allowances are included, total annual compensation for an O-6 Navy Captain in 2026 ranges from $131,113 to as much as $205,687.

The largest single add-on is the Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH), a non-taxable, location-dependent payment designed to offset the cost of off-base housing. The average BAH for an O-6 with dependents sits at $3,075.37 per month ($36,904 per year), though at high-cost duty stations like Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, CA, or the Washington, D.C. area, that figure rises substantially above the national average. Alongside BAH, every commissioned officer also receives a Basic Allowance for Subsistence (BAS) to offset food costs: according to The Military Wallet, the 2026 officer BAS rate is $328.48 per month ($3,941 per year), non-taxable, and uniform regardless of rank or assignment.

Aviation Incentive Pay (AvIP) is a further pillar of aviator compensation: as documented in the Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS), AvIP maxes out at $1,000 per month ($12,000 per year) for aviators with 14 or more years of aviation service, a threshold any Carrier Air Wing Commander has long cleared. Finally, when a CAG's air wing deploys to an active combat zone or operates in an area subject to hostile fire, an additional hazardous duty payment applies: that rate stands at up to $250 per month ($3,000 per year).

Cutting across all of these allowances is a tax advantage that civilian compensation packages simply cannot replicate: BAH and BAS are entirely exempt from federal income tax, meaningfully increasing real take-home value compared to a nominally equivalent civilian salary. As already explained by Simple Flying, compensation for senior naval aviators rises sharply at the command and flag-officer levels, reflecting both operational responsibility and years of specialized aviation service.

To understand why a CAG earns what they earn, the compensation must be weighed against the sheer scope of the role. The "CAG" title dates to World War II, when carrier aviation was organized into "Air Groups" rather than the modern "Air Wings." The formal designation changed in 1963, but the acronym stayed as a small, enduring tribute to the role's lineage.

In 2026, the CAG commands a carrier air wing that typically embeds several squadrons aboard a Nimitz- or Gerald R. Ford-class carrier, operating strike fighter jets, electronic warfare aircraft, early warning platforms, helicopters, and logistics aircraft in an integrated fashion. As reported by LegalClarity.org, "a CAG is a Navy Captain (pay grade O-6) who oversees roughly 2,400 personnel and dozens of aircraft spanning multiple squadron types, making it one of the most demanding leadership positions in naval aviation."

That means a CAG commands more personnel than many Army colonels and manages an air arm more complex than the entire air forces of several NATO nations. As we recently noted, the Super Hornet remains the backbone of current carrier air wings, with the Block III upgrade program ensuring it will remain central to CAG operations well into the 2040s, which also means today's CAG must be conversant in cutting-edge avionics, networked warfare, and the integration of fifth-generation aircraft like the F-35C Lightning II alongside legacy platforms.

According to Glassdoor's March 2026 data, based on 117 salary submissions from active and former O-6 Navy Captains, the estimated average total salary is $203,144 per year, with a range from roughly $159,193 (25th percentile) to $263,446 (75th percentile). These numbers, while self-reported and not official, align well with the computed figures derived from the DFAS pay tables plus standard allowances, and indicate that real-world total compensation for a CAG falls comfortably in the $200,000+ range.

Placing the CAG's salary in context requires a look at both one rank below and one rank above. An O-5 Commander, the rank that typically commands an individual fighter or strike squadron aboard the carrier, earns a base pay of roughly $9,929 per month ($119,148 per year) at the 10-year mark, rising to a maximum of $12,280 per month.

That makes the O-6 CAG's base pay approximately 15–20% higher in dollar terms, but the gap in responsibility is far wider: a CAG runs nine squadrons and 2,400 people, whereas an O-5 squadron commander runs a single unit of roughly 200 to 300 personnel. Above the CAG sits the Rear Admiral (O-7 and O-8) tier, where base pay is no longer capped at $15,000 per month but instead climbs toward the Level II Executive Schedule cap of $18,808.20 per month.

A Rear Admiral Lower Half (O-7) with a carrier strike group command earns between $12,803.70 and $18,458.10 per month in base pay alone, or roughly $153,600 to $221,500 annually, meaningfully above the CAG's ceiling. The trade-off is that the path from CAG to flag officer is intensely competitive: a very small fraction of O-6s earn their first star.

The commercial aviation comparison is, as always, illustrative. According to our previous analysis of USAF pilot salaries, senior airline captains flying major widebody international routes can earn over $550,000 annually in 2026, roughly three times the total compensation of a Navy O-6 with full allowances. The financial gap is simply not closable from a base pay perspective, which is precisely why Aviation Retention Bonuses (AvB) and quality-of-life factors remain critical levers in keeping experienced naval aviators in uniform through the CAG pipeline.

Discover how the growing experience gap is reshaping aviation worldwide.

Every salary figure cited in this article comes with an important context that can shift the real value of compensation significantly. The BAH figure, for example, is highly location-sensitive: an O-6 stationed at Naval Air Station Lemoore (in California's Central Valley) receives a different BAH rate than one based at NAS Oceana in Virginia Beach, VA, or attached to a forward-deployed unit in Japan.

Navy personnel assigned to overseas bases like NAF Atsugi or MCAS Iwakuni receive Overseas Housing Allowance (OHA) instead of BAH, calculated differently and potentially higher. On some overseas assignments, additional Cost of Living Allowances (COLA) can add several hundred dollars per month on top of that.

Deployment also changes the compensation calculus. When a carrier strike group deploys to a combat zone, as multiple carrier strike groups did across the Red Sea, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Indo-Pacific in recent years, service members may qualify for hostile fire pay ($225/month), tax exclusion on base pay earned in a combat zone (a benefit that, for an O-6, can represent a tax saving of $30,000 to $40,000 per year), and in some cases imminent danger pay.

Readers should also note that Aviation Bonus (AvB) figures are not included in the totals above. AvB contracts are negotiated at the end of a service obligation and are not universally offered or accepted at the CAG career point. While some O-6 aviators do receive retention bonuses, these are managed at the Navy Bureau of Personnel (BUPERS) level and vary by community need, timing, and individual agreements. A CAG who is within two to three years of potential retirement may or may not be eligible for or interested in a new AvB contract.

A Carrier Air Wing Commander in 2026 earns a base salary of approximately $151,660 to $171,388 per year. When standard allowances, Aviation Incentive Pay, and broader military benefits are included, total compensation typically rises to between $200,000 and $225,000 annually, with the possibility of climbing even higher during combat deployments.

These are numbers that would make any senior manager in the civilian industry pause, but they also reflect the extraordinary scale of the role itself. A CAG effectively commands the equivalent of a mid-sized air force from the flight deck of a 100,000-ton nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, overseeing roughly 2,400 personnel and dozens of aircraft while operating in some of the world’s most demanding and strategically sensitive environments.

The 3.8% military pay raise implemented on January 1, 2026, represents another attempt by Congress and the Pentagon to narrow the compensation gap between military aviation and the civilian airline industry. Even so, the difference remains significant. Senior airline captains flying the largest commercial widebody aircraft still routinely earn two to three times more than a CAG, a reality that continues to influence Navy retention efforts for highly experienced strike aviators. At the same time, the job itself is becoming increasingly complex.

Ongoing Block III Super Hornet upgrades, the continued integration of the F-35C, and the Navy’s evolving carrier air wing structure are making the CAG position more technically demanding than ever, even as commercial airlines continue competing aggressively for the same pool of elite aviators. The broader context of carrier aviation economics, including the Block III Super Hornet upgrades and the ongoing F-35C integration discussed across Simple Flying's coverage, makes the CAG billet more technically demanding than ever, even as the commercial pull on the talent pipeline remains intense.

#6221. California City Approves Protections for Polyamorous Arrangements

Nobody could have seen this coming, except all the conservatives who said it would happen.

Then-mayor of West Hollywood Chelsea Lee Byers attends the Stonewall Democratic Club’s 50th-anniversary celebration in West Hollywood, Calif., November 15, 2025.

Wilbert Roberts/Getty Images for Connor Treacy

The West Hollywood City Council unanimously approved an ordinance that allows multi-partner relationships (like a so-called throuple) to formally register as a domestic relationship and receive certain legal protections at the local level, such as visitation rights in jail and rental privileges. A “multi-partner relationship,” per the ordinance, requires that the individuals involved share “the common necessities of life,” are over age 18, are competent enough to enter a contract, are all participating consensually, are “responsible for one another’s welfare,” and are not related by blood or a member of an already declared partnership. There is no expressed limit to the number of individuals who may be involved in a recognized multi-partner relationship, and people living outside the city can register their relationship.

The idea of protections for polyamory was brought to Councilmember Chelsea Lee Byers last year by Christina Fialho, an attorney who founded the “Rewrite the BiLine” organization that “reshape[s] cultural norms and drive[s] policy change” through media narratives to “advance health equity, economic opportunity, and civil rights for bi+ people and non-nuclear families.” Fialho told the Los Angeles Times that “this law is just the beginning. . . . I think it makes it possible for people to dream about a future they once thought was out of reach.” According to public records, the city council deemed it “necessary” to recognize “diverse relationship structures,” such as those involving more than two adults, because they are “becoming increasingly common.” The city frames the ordinance as an anti-discrimination measure with symbolic value:

#6220. Lufthansa Takes Delivery of Its First A350-1000

Lufthansa this week took delivery of its first Airbus A350-1000, a type it says will offer a better customer experience while reducing operating costs.

The aircraft was formally handed over to the carrier on Tuesday in the presence of Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr and Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus. Nicknamed “Deutschland,” the jet is Lufthansa’s 700th Airbus airplane, and the seventh in a special commemorative fleet bearing 100th anniversary liveries.

The white and dark blue designs feature an oversized crane, a symbol first used by predecessor Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa Group has ordered a total of 15 A350-1000s. The first 10 will operate for the Lufthansa core brand, and will be based at its Munich hub.

“Deutschland” will fly to Munich on Wednesday, officials said, and operate its inaugural flight, to Tokyo-Haneda, on Dec. 3. The aircraft will also be Lufthansa’s first long-haul airplane equipped with Starlink satellite internet service.

“The fact that, as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus aircraft exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa, and in the year of our 100th anniversary, makes this a very special moment for us,” Spohr said in a statement. “Our partnership is a prime example of what Europe can achieve when it works together.”

Lufthansa’s -1000s will seat 300 passengers in four cabins – First, Business, Premium Economy, and Economy.

#6219. ATMA: Aman’s New Brand, Debuting With A 1,049-Foot Miami Tower

Aman is known for being one of the world’s top luxury hotel groups. Currently Aman Group consists of Aman (the original hotel group) and Janu (intended to be more of a “lifestyle” version of Aman). Aman is now launching a third brand, and it’s yet another departure from the origins of Aman.

Aman Group has announced the launch of ATMA, described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” ATMA means “the spirit” or “the true self” in Sanskrit, and the intent is for the brand to combine wellness, sport, nutrition-led dining, design, and experiential entertainment.

ATMA will “focus on advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities, which have been developed exclusively by ATMA Global Partner Novak Djokovic.”

The first location will be ATMA Miami, and it will include a hotel, branded residence, and a private members club. Specifically, the property will be in the Brickell neighborhood and will have a private marina, with an anticipated opening in 2031.

ATMA Miami is expected to be a standalone 1,049-foot tower, which is as tall as buildings can get in Miami. In terms of height, it’ll be match the new 100-story Waldorf Astoria Miami that’s currently under construction, which will be the tallest building in Florida, once complete.

Details about ATMA Miami are still fairly limited, but we know there will be 480 residential units, in addition to the hotel. Residential units will be between one and six bedrooms, and will be “supported by Aman Group’s service standards.”

There will also be a 120,000 square foot spa and wellness area, set to be the largest of its kind in Miami. Developed in partnership with Djokovic, it will offer performance and recovery experiences alongside indoor padel, tennis and squash courts, a fitness center, group and private training studios, mobility and conditioning labs, a medical wellness center, and dedicated recovery spaces.

So far we’ve only learned about the Miami location, but the claim is that the brand will span urban and remote destinations.

Look, I’ve made my opinions about the Aman brand pretty clear, so I don’t want to sound like some old dude just ranting about the “good old days.” When Aman was founded by hospitality legend Adrian Zecha, it was truly among the most innovative and passion driven hospitality projects we’ve ever seen.

In 2014, Zecha sold the brand to Vladislav Doronin, and since then, the entire philosophy has changed. It’s hard to fault someone for purchasing a brand and trying to cash in and maximize profitability — I mean, that’s kind of how the business world is supposed to work, right?

But of course that doesn’t mean we have to be happy about the evolution. It started with Aman ditching its approach of largely opening hotels in the middle of nowhere, where that was part of the charm. Instead, we saw Aman focus on city hotels. Then Aman became all about opening members clubs. Then we saw the launch of the Janu brand, essentially a higher room count version of Aman, with a more lively spirit.

And now we’re seeing Aman getting into building full-on skyscrapers. Well, or at least partnering on them in terms of branding. Of course some Aman properties already have a residences component, so that’s nothing new, as such. However, the scale of this project couldn’t be more opposite of what Aman initially was. We’re talking about a 100-story building that will have nearly 500 residences, and who knows how many hotel rooms (it hasn’t yet been announced).

Of course in Miami, one of the biggest trends is branded residences, with brands just selling out their name. But if Aman were to just slap its name on a residential project, you’d think it would be something smaller scale than this. This is among the highest unit count developments we’ve ever seen in Miami, at least for a project spanning just one building.

Aman Group has just announced its third brand, and it will be named ATMA. It’s described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” The first location will open in Miami in 2031, and it’ll be a roughly 100-story building with 480 residences, a hotel, and a members club.

Aman as a brand has become unrecognizable compared to what it was 15 years ago. But that’s fair enough, and it’s also what happens when you sell a company to someone looking to maximize their ROI. You can hardly fault someone for that, as much as I don’t personally like it.

#6218. Will Credit Card Interest Rates Be Capped At 10%? Democrats Want To Work With Trump

With the recent midterm elections, the balance of power in Washington is very quickly changing. Given the extent to which things shifted left, Democrats certainly want to be able to show that they can accomplish something in the next two years, to make life better for average Americans.

Along those lines, we’re once again seeing a proposal floated regarding capping credit card interest rates. There’s a lot more support for this than in the past, given the majority that Democrats have, plus the fact that President Trump has also been in support of this concept (or at least claimed to be). Will it actually pass, though?

Senate Democrats are renewing a proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, with Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts specifically bringing this up in a “Face The Nation” interview. Warren is likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee, and could use her position to help advance the proposal.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president. “We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price… pic.twitter.com/0r17PwXPQT

Now, before anyone gets political, keep in mind that this is a concept that Trump actually proposed earlier this year. He claimed that Americans were being ripped off by credit card companies, and that as of January 20, 2026, credit card interest rates should be capped at 10%. However, this just came in the form of a social media post, rather than any actual legislation:

Please be informed that we will no longer let the American Public be “ripped off” by Credit Card Companies that are charging Interest Rates of 20 to 30%, and even more, which festered unimpeded during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration. AFFORDABILITY! Effective January 20, 2026, I, as President of the United States, am calling for a one year cap on Credit Card Interest Rates of 10%. Coincidentally, the January 20th date will coincide with the one year anniversary of the historic and very successful Trump Administration. Thank you for your attention to this matter. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP

Donald J. Trump Truth Social Post 08:10 PM EST 01.09.26 pic.twitter.com/47SQ03yMeo

Unsurprisingly, there was no enforcement mechanism, and this never happened, especially since he got pushback from other Republicans. If he really believed in that proposal, then it sounds like this will be his chance to actually turn it into some sort of a law, with support from Democrats. We’ll have to mark this as “developing” for now.

Just for some context, credit card issuers make money in three primary ways — through interchange fees, through interest charges, and through annual fees. When it comes to interest rates, credit card companies are known for having very high rates, an average of over 20%. These are the charges that apply if you don’t pay your full balance before the payment due date. You don’t pay interest charges if you simply charge your purchase to a credit card, and then pay your balance in full.

On the surface, capping credit card interest rates of course sounds great — some of the rates are really high, and many people view banks as greedy, and think they can afford to give up some of their margins. Obviously for those who are currently financing charges, a cap on interest rates would be positive.

The thing is, a policy change like this wouldn’t come without some other changes. There’s no denying that if interest rates were capped at 10%, lots of consumers with not-great credit would be locked out of getting credit cards, and might even have their accounts closed, because card issuers would find it too risky to loan them money at that rate.

After all, there’s a huge risk to people not making payments, and the economics of that work differently with 10% interest rates rather than 25% interest rates. I would imagine that tens of millions of Americans would have their accounts closed, that we’d see fewer no annual fee cards, etc.

Beyond that, if we did see a long term cap on credit card interest rates, it would likely change the credit card landscape in terms of how rewarding cards are, with everything ranging from welcome bonuses, to rewards on spending, to perks.

Right or wrong, credit card economics are heavily reliant on a cross-subsidized system. That’s the whole reason some of us are able to get such outsized value. Credit card rewards structures nowadays largely more or less rebate back interchange fees to consumers, as it’s easy to earn 2% cash back with cards, or even to earn huge multipliers on spending.

The reality is that the revenue that subsidizes a lot of rewards is the interest charges, since that’s the highest margin revenue stream from many card issuers. So we’re partly earning huge welcome bonuses and 5x points on some transactions because someone else is paying close to 30% interest.

I’m not saying that’s a good system, but I’m just being realistic about how it works. If interest rates are forced to be slashed by more than half in the long run, it will have major implications for rewards. Maybe that’s objectively not a bad thing, but it will happen.

For that matter, it would even have a major impact on airlines — they’re so reliant on credit card revenue nowadays to turn profits, and this would greatly hurt their margins in that area as well.

With Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, there’s a renewed push to cap credit card interest rates at 10%. This is a proposal that Trump made earlier this year, but it didn’t get support from Republicans.

While I totally appreciate that credit card interest rates are often incredibly high, it’s not without reason, given the rate of default on some cards. Approval standards for cards would change, many consumers would have their cards shut down, etc. It would also likely change the economics of the credit card industry, which could even impact airlines.

However, I’m not some lobbyist or apologist for the credit card industry. If the change happens, many people will benefit, and I’m sure the industry will adapt. However, unarguably many people will go from paying 25% interest on their credit card, to potentially paying even higher rates for payday loans, doing business with loan sharks, etc.

What do you make of this proposal to cap credit card interest rates?
