#6215. American First Class Will Get Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights (700-899 Miles)

American Airlines is making a very nice change to first class service on some short haul flights that didn’t previously qualify for a meal service, and it’s something I’m sure passengers will be happy to see.

As things currently stand, American serves meals in first class on flights of at least 900 miles during meal times (900 miles roughly correlates to a little over two hours of flying, on average). In the US, this is basically the industry standard, as Delta and United have the same cutoff of 900 miles for serving meals. On flights shorter than that, airlines only offer drinks and a snack basket in first class.

It looks like American will soon be leading the industry when it comes to service in first class on shorter flights, as it brings back a program it used to offer. JonNYC was first to report that American will be bringing back the “light bites” concept on flights of 700 to 899 miles (700 miles correlates to a little over 90 minutes of flying, on average).

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

As now confirmed by American, this is launching this month on flights between Chicago (ORD) and New York, including Kennedy (JFK) and LaGuardia (LGA). It remains to be seen when it expands to other routes. It must be a decade at this point since American offered this concept.

The expectation is that there will be a rotating selection of options, with two available on each flight, and they won’t be available via pre-order.

Breakfast selections may include smoked salmon, tropical chia overnight oats, prosciutto and melon, fruit and cheese plates, prosciutto and brie, or apple cinnamon chia pudding. Lunch and dinner options may include curry chicken salads, Thai noodle salads, turkey and gouda sandwiches, whipped burrata, poached shrimp with noodle salads, mezze plates, blackened chicken, or grilled vegetable wraps.

It goes without saying that expectations of premium cabin travelers differ massively around the globe. In the Middle East, it’s common to have a 30-minute business class flight with a lie flat bed, cappuccinos, champagne, and a substantial, tasty snack.

In Europe, you’re typically stuck with a pretty underwhelming hard product on short haul flights (just economy with a blocked middle), but regardless of the length of the flight, you’re almost always served something fresh, even if the flight time is well under an hour.

In the United States, we have the benefit of actually having a dedicated first class cabin with larger seats, but the soft product just isn’t great. You can be on a flight of nearly two hours and just be served packaged snacks.

We do have to give credit to Alaska for this, as it’s the only US carrier to serve some sort of fresh food on flights of under 900 miles. On most Alaska flights you’ll get a snack on shorter services, so kudos to the airline for that.

American Airlines will once again serve fresh food in first class on flights of 700-899 miles. This concept will debut on flights between Chicago and New York, and passengers will have the choice of two rotating options. This is really a resumption of something that American offered many years back.

Among the “big three” US carriers, American will be the only one to serve fresh food in first class on flights of under 900 miles, so kudos to the airline for that.

Staying at Walt Disney World on hotel points — within walking distance of two theme parks — might sound like a pixie-dust-fueled dream, but it's actually possible if you stay at the Walt Disney World Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve.

These large, highly visible properties are actually three adjacent but distinct hotels that share access to amenities.

The Dolphin is the 27-story pyramid that opened in 1990 and is visible from just about every Disney World theme park.

The Swan opened in 1990 and is home to two 47-foot swan statues, while the Swan Reserve is the newest of the trio, having just opened in 2021.

These three resorts are clustered together and are all bookable with Marriott Bonvoy points. This is possible because while they each have Walt Disney World in their names and in their location, the Dolphin is actually a Sheraton, the Swan is a Westin and the Swan Reserve is in Marriott's Autograph Collection.

Related: These are the best credit cards for earning Marriott Bonvoy points

That means that the current welcome bonus with the (see rates and fees) that awards three free night awards (valued up to 50,000 Marriott points each; certain hotels have resort fees) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening could cover a three-night stay at one of these properties. And that's especially true if you were willing to top up your awards with up to 25,000 additional Marriott points if the nights you wanted cost a few more points than 50,000. Additionally, new cardholders can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

Generally speaking, the Walt Disney World Dolphin is a large, busy convention hotel with the most on-site restaurants and amenities. The Walt Disney World Swan is comparatively smaller but still a very large, busy hotel that's closest to the Dolphin, with both connected by a covered walkway.

The Swan Reserve is the smallest, most upscale — and most expensive — of the three properties. But combined, these three properties are positively massive with 2,619 rooms, 23 restaurants and lounges, and a host of amenities and facilities.

Due to some wheeling and dealing in the 1980s, the Swan and Dolphin (and later, Swan Reserve) scored some of the best real estate at Walt Disney World.

These resorts are within walking distance of both Epcot and Disney's Hollywood Studios. Or there's a complimentary water taxi that can take you to either of those parks that leaves from the dock between the Dolphin and the Swan.

Only three of Disney's own operated resorts can claim this same feature: Disney's Yacht Club, Disney's Boardwalk and Disney's Beach Club.

All of those are deluxe Disney resorts that regularly start between $600 - $800 per night, where rooms at this trio of properties can start at half that price if you're paying with cash.

Related: How to save hundreds of dollars on a trip to Disney with the Disney Inspire Visa

There are multiple pools at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve, with each property having at least one pool located directly on-site.

But the most expansive pools are situated closest to the Dolphin, including the grotto pool with waterfalls and a waterslide.

There is also a lap pool in case you want to get a water-based workout in. A great thing about the pools — and other amenities — is that it doesn't matter which of these three hotels you are staying at; you can use all the amenities at the other hotels, too.

But it's not just pools you can pick from; there is a very long list of amenities in case the Disney parks leave you with some downtime.

At the Dolphin, you'll find a good-sized arcade and even a small bowling alley.

Between the Swan and Dolphin, there is also sand volleyball, an outdoor playground area for little kids and even swan-themed paddle boats that guests can take out on the water at no additional cost, as rentals are included in the hefty $50 nightly resort fee.

If you wanted to have a resort day outside the theme parks during your Disney World vacation, the odds are high that there is plenty to do at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve to keep you entertained.

Each of the three hotels also has its own fitness area for you to still get your workouts in.

If, after all that activity, you want to rest and enjoy a massage or another treatment, there is a Mandara Spa inside the Dolphin.

Believe it or not, the reason you can enjoy these Marriott hotels, located in the heart of Walt Disney World, dates back to disputes and deals in the 1980s.

The hotels have many Disney perks and an on-property Disney location, but they are not actually Disney-owned and operated hotels. And now they are all hotels where you can earn and use Marriott Bonvoy points to stay in the middle of Mickey's kingdom without paying Mickey's exact price tag.

Guests of the Walt Disney World Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve get to enjoy some really good Disney benefits that are otherwise mostly reserved only for true on-property Disney World guests.

As mentioned, there are complimentary boats to Epcot and Hollywood Studios from these hotels if you don't want to make the 15-20-minute walk.

There are buses that leave from these hotels to Magic Kingdom or Animal Kingdom. The one downside to the buses vs. those at "true" Disney resorts is that the bus to Magic Kingdom takes you to the Ticket and Transportation Center (TTC) instead of to Magic Kingdom itself. From the TTC, you have to take the monorail or ferry boat to the Magic Kingdom.

If that sounds like a hassle to you, it can be a good time to splurge on a Disney-operated Minnie Van you book in the Lyft app to take you directly to the front of the Magic Kingdom with the money you saved by staying at these hotels instead of actual deluxe Disney resorts.

At these hotels, you will find true Disney gift shops, along with Disney park tickets and Disney vacation planning assistance.

If by which hotel is best you mean the nicest, then the answer is likely the Walt Disney World Swan Reserve. It is not only the newest and most expensive of the three hotels, but also the one that falls under the higher-category Marriott Brand, Autograph Collection.

But everyone has different tastes and priorities for their Disney trip, so each of the three hotels has its own fans.

All three of the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve hotels are great choices for families, but if we have to choose, families with young kids may enjoy the Swan and Dolphin a bit more due to more on-site amenities such as the playground and arcade and a slightly shorter walk to the boats or to Epcot and Hollywood Studios.

There are also more on-site food options at the Dolphin and Swan than you'll find at the Swan Reserve.

In part because of conventions and events that do come to these hotels, no single hotel among the three is always the cheapest. The only real way to know for sure on your dates is to run some searches.

However, the Dolphin is the least expensive of the three on average, whether booking on Marriott points or cash, typically followed by the Swan and then the Swan Reserve.

All the rooms at these hotels are nice, especially once the Dolphin finishes its current renovation, but there are differences among them.

Swan Reserve rooms are likely the nicest between the three, with higher-end finishes, two robes available, walk-in showers, a better coffee maker, etc.

The rooms at the Swan are also nice and have been recently renovated. In my experience, they typically offer one robe, and importantly, two queen beds in the rooms with the two bed option.

The rooms at the Dolphin are currently undergoing renovation to make them more similar in appearance to the Swan. However, a significant difference will remain even after the renovations.

The beds at the Dolphin in rooms with two beds are full-sized or double beds, not queen beds. This makes it a tighter fit if you are putting two people in each bed.

There were no robes in our Dolphin room, and the coffee maker is a step down, which makes sense, as this is a Sheraton rather than the higher-tier brands at the other two hotels.

There are more restaurants at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve than it makes sense for me to put in a big list here, but I will mention a few of my personal favorite options.

First, I'm a fan of Rosa Mexicano, especially for an easy, fun arrival-night dinner with margaritas — especially if I have a resort credit to put to good use, as I did recently by booking via Amex's Hotel Collection with my .

Amare, a Mediterranean restaurant at the Swan Reserve, and Todd English's bluezoo, a seafood restaurant in the Walt Disney World Dolphin, are two additional standouts for me, though there are plenty of other great picks, too.

And believe it or not, if you order an entrée at Todd English’s bluezoo, Amare, or Il Mulino New York Trattoria, Rosa Mexicano, Bourbon Steak or Kimonos, your kids ages 5 - 12 can get two free hours at the on-site Camp Dolphin. This supervised childcare includes a take-home craft and a snack.

I also enjoy the grab-and-go options that are available at each of these three hotels for an easy muffin and coffee sort of breakfast in the morning.

If you have Marriott Platinum elite status or higher — which you can get just by having the — you can choose free breakfast as your benefit for the stay, which will get you a daily voucher to use in these shops.

I've stayed at these hotels over a dozen times and there is no doubt in my mind that the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve can absolutely be worth it when deciding between them and Disney-owned resorts.

And don't get me wrong — I really love a good, true Disney resort stay with all of the elaborate themes and locations — but the prices for deluxe resorts owned by Disney are often more than the prices that these three resorts charge. At these hotels, you're often paying a price that is more in the Disney moderate, mid-tier resort range (and sometimes even a value range), but getting closer to deluxe-tier location and amenities.

And you can even use some of your hotel credits from certain Amex or Chase cards and book via programs that give you free breakfast, resort credits and more, like I just did via American Express with my to get $450 in bonus savings and inclusions on a recent stay.

So there are ways you can really bring down your total cost here that typically don't work at true Disney resorts, which don't participate in most of those programs, including even using the simple $100 annual Chase Travel hotel credit from the (see rates and fees).

And that's assuming you're even paying cash — you can also use your Marriott points or free night awards here and save your cash for other parts of the trip.

So yes, I absolutely think it is sometimes worth potentially spending less to stay in the middle of it all at the Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve and still get the overwhelming majority of the perks of being at a true Disney resort.

There are a lot of great places to stay while on a Walt Disney World vacation, but often you have to make trade-offs. You can have a great location, good value, or an upscale stay, but typically not all three at the same time ... except at the Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve, which have the potential to give you the best of all worlds.

While the Swan Reserve is my favorite of the three, I've stayed at all of these hotels multiple times over the years on cash, Marriott points, and even using some of the hotel credits from my various credit cards, and I have every intention of many more stays in the future.

#6212. Not All Property Tax Cuts Are Created Equal

Fiscal conservatives’ aim should be the same as for other taxes: broaden the base, reduce the rate.

An aerial view of a suburban neighborhood in central Florida.

We can at least say this of last Tuesday: It was a great day for homeowners upset over their property taxes. Across five states, voters approved seven ballot measures to directly reduce or otherwise limit local taxes on different kinds of property. Conservatives, instinctively anti-tax in almost every instance, cheered these initiatives.

Yet nuance is needed. Given that taxation is the necessary price of government, conservatives have long accepted that some taxes are better than others. Likewise, some kinds of property taxes are preferable to others, and therefore, not all cuts to property taxes are created equal. Some may even be worse than the status quo.

#6211. How Short Runways Limit Boeing 787-9 Payloads On Hot Days

William Perugini | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

How long it takes a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner to lift its wheels off the ground depends on numerous factors. An aircraft's performance must fall within the manufacturer's defined performance limits. These limitations are usually outlined in the Pilot Operating Handbook (POH) for general aviation aircraft, or a series of publications that cover heavy commercial airliners in collaboration with Dispatch teams:

Consider a flight that is hot, high, and heavy. Higher than standard 59 degrees Fahrenheit (15 degrees Celsius) temperatures contribute to decreased overall performance. A takeoff roll conducted at a high field elevation further reduces a jet's ability to lift off efficiently. Further, a mission that has every seat occupied or near its maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) will further extend a takeoff roll, presenting a challenge to operators in such environments.

Although humidity is a closely related factor when examining hot versus cold days, when comparing the two solely based on temperature, cold days provide increased aerodynamic and engine performance. The terms "hot" and "cold" are relative in aviation. The FAA outlines that temperature effects on aircraft performance are best evaluated using actual temperature values and density altitude calculations, as the resulting performance impacts vary by aircraft type and model. Aircraft performance data published in the POH are specific to each aircraft and are based on defined atmospheric conditions.

Hot temperatures reduce air density by causing air molecules to spread farther apart. According to the FAA's Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (PHAK), this increase in density altitude results in fewer air molecules passing through the engine and over the wings. Consequently, the 787-9's General Electric GEnx -1B variant or Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines produce less power with fewer air molecules available to process. Further, the wings create less lift, leading to longer takeoff distances and reduced climb performance.

However, there is no defined temperature window that is necessarily bad. A 41-degree Fahrenheit (5 degrees Celsius) day with high humidity may be unpleasant for a pilot operating in such conditions, but that same 5-degree day with low humidity would likely result in decent overall performance when looking at temperature and humidity alone. But in general, the colder it is at the airport, the performance curve increases.

However, temperature is only one piece of the puzzle. Atmospheric pressure can produce similar performance penalties even when temperatures are relatively mild. As pressure decreases, the air becomes less dense, reducing the amount of air flowing through the engines and over the wings. This is why aircraft performance calculations rely on pressure altitude rather than field elevation alone. Two airports at the same physical elevation can produce different takeoff performance results if the atmospheric pressure differs on a given day.

For a Boeing 787-9, pressure variations are incorporated into dispatch and performance software before every departure. Lower pressure conditions effectively make the aircraft behave as though it is operating from a higher airport. Less dense air reduces engine thrust output and aerodynamic efficiency, requiring higher true airspeeds to generate the same amount of lift. While day-to-day pressure changes are generally less dramatic than large temperature swings, they can still materially affect takeoff distances when combined with hot temperatures, heavy payloads, or high-elevation airports.

Standard Pressure (29.92 inches of mercury, 76 cm)

The challenge for operators is that pressure rarely changes in isolation. As AOPA notes, while pressure rarely matches from one location to another, atmospheric pressure is relatively uniform across geographical areas. A low-pressure weather system often arrives with other unfavorable conditions, raising the question of how elevation itself changes aircraft performance before temperature and weight are even considered.

Some routes are long, and some push aircraft to the limit. United Airlines has pushed its 777-300ER so much that on this route, fuel stops are likely.

That question becomes particularly important at airports located thousands of feet above sea level. Even under standard atmospheric conditions, higher-elevation airports contain less dense air than airports at sea level. In practice, this means a Boeing 787-9 departing from Denver International Airport (DEN) will require more runway and achieve lower climb performance than the same aircraft departing with the same weight from a coastal airport.

The difference can be substantial. Denver sits at approximately 5,434 feet above sea level, while airports such as San Francisco International Airport (SFO) operate essentially at sea level. Although both airports routinely accommodate long-haul widebody aircraft, the thinner air at Denver requires airlines to pay closer attention to payload restrictions, fuel planning, and runway performance calculations. A 787-9 departing Denver on an ultra-long-haul mission may face limitations that would not exist from a lower-altitude airport using the exact same aircraft; United Airlines operates more long-haul flights from SFO for this very reason.

Altitude alone does not necessarily prevent a successful departure. The real challenge emerges when altitude combines with high temperatures, creating density altitude values that can dramatically exceed an airport's actual elevation. This brings the discussion to perhaps the most controllable factor of all: aircraft weight.

Unlike temperature, pressure, or field elevation, aircraft weight is one factor airlines can directly influence. Every additional passenger, checked bag, cargo container, and pound of fuel increases the amount of lift required to become airborne. As a result, heavier aircraft require higher takeoff speeds and longer runway distances to lift off safely.

For the 787-9, the maximum certified takeoff weight varies depending on the specific configuration and option package selected by the airline, but it exceeds 500,000 pounds in every configuration. At these weights, performance planning becomes a balancing act between payload and fuel. Airlines may occasionally choose to leave cargo behind, block seats, or schedule a fuel stop if environmental conditions prevent a fully loaded aircraft from departing safely within performance limits.

The consequences of excess weight become most apparent on demanding routes. When high temperatures, high elevations, and near-maximum takeoff weights occur simultaneously, airlines may be forced to find creative solutions that maintain both safety and profitability. In United's case, many international routes served by the Chicago-based carrier are simply not possible from Denver; the required fuel weight could exceed the maximum allowable fuel weight for a takeoff from Denver on a hot day, preventing the jet from reaching its destination.

The phenomenon is a consequence of the aircraft's design.

Airlines have several tools available when performance calculations indicate a 787-9 cannot safely depart at its desired takeoff weight. The simplest solution is reducing aircraft weight. This may involve limiting cargo loads, carrying fewer passengers, reducing fuel, or planning an intermediate refueling stop. While these decisions can affect profitability, they allow airlines to continue serving challenging destinations without compromising safety.

A real-world example can be found at United Airlines' Denver hub. While Denver supports an extensive network of long-haul international flying, its combination of high elevation and summer temperatures can present operational challenges. Routes with extremely long stage lengths, such as a hypothetical nonstop Denver-Manila service, would require significantly more fuel than many existing transpacific flights. SFO-MNL is significantly easier to plan and dispatch as a result, not to mention a slightly shorter trip distance as well.

Even these solutions have limits. As aircraft missions become longer and passenger demand grows, airlines must decide whether operational workarounds are enough or whether different aircraft are fundamentally better suited for certain environments. Boliviana de Aviaciónand Aeromexico struggle with this, as their primary hubs of Vicecomodoro Angel D. La Paz Aragonés Airport (LPB) and Mexico City International Airport (MEX), respectively, are situated at high altitudes. With generally warm temperatures at field elevation to supplement the challenge, both carriers can be somewhat limited in range and aircraft weight.

The 787-9 was designed to maximize long-haul efficiency, but aircraft such as the Boeing 757-200and Boeing 737-700 became known for their strong runway performance and ability to operate from airports where environmental conditions limit larger aircraft. The 757, in particular, remains one of the most respected performers ever produced by Boeing. Equipped with powerful Rolls-Royce RB211 or Pratt & Whitney PW2000 engines and a relatively modest wing loading for its size, the aircraft developed a reputation for operating from hot-and-high airports while still carrying meaningful payloads over long distances.

The smaller 737-700 similarly benefits from a favorable thrust-to-weight ratio and lower overall weight compared to larger members of the Boeing 737 family. For airlines serving airports with runway constraints, altitude challenges, or frequent high-temperature operations, these characteristics can often matter more than maximum passenger capacity.

The challenge facing airlines today is that there is no true modern replacement for the niche the 757 occupied. While aircraft such as the Boeing 787-9 can fly substantially farther and carry more passengers, they cannot always replicate the same combination of field performance and operational flexibility.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6210. Aer Lingus Pilots Threatened With Criminal Charges Over Bomb Threat Diversion

Last week, I covered how dozens of flights across Europe were faced with bomb threats. It was clearly a hoax, but these have to be taken seriously, and we saw all kinds of diversions, flight cancelations, and more.

Europe’s largest union representing pilots is now sharing the details of an incident that happened with one of these diversions, whereby an Aer Lingus flight was forced by fighter jets to divert to a French military base. When the pilots weren’t comfortable doing so, they were reportedly threatened with criminal charges.

This incident happened on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and involves Aer Lingus flight EI402, scheduled to operate from Dublin (DUB) to Rome (FCO). The Airbus A320 with the registration code EI-DEH took off at 6:40AM local time, and made its way southeast toward Rome.

The A320 flew for around an hour, and made it just past Paris, when the plane changed heading and prepared to divert. French fighter jets had been deployed to escort the aircraft, and demanded that it divert to a French military base. Specifically, the plane diverted to Évreux-Fauville Air Base (EVX), located in Normandy.

The plane touched down there at 10:05AM local time, 2hr25min after it first departed (there was a one hour time change). Coincidentally, that’s basically the same flight time as it would’ve been to Rome, as the aircraft had to hold for an extended period of time.

The plane ended up returning to Dublin later in the day, departing at 4:59PM local time, and landing in Dublin at 5:20PM local time, after a flight time of 1hr21min. So passengers spent nearly 12 hours on the plane, only to end up back where they started. Man, that’s rough, especially when you consider these A320s don’t have power ports, Wi-Fi, etc.

Here’s where the story gets really interesting, as explained by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), which represents over 44,000 pilots across Europe, including pilots at Aer Lingus. The union is expressing serious concerns about how this incident was handled.

What happened is that the Aer Lingus pilots didn’t want to divert to Évreux-Fauville Air Base, because they didn’t have the necessary operational information and aeronautical charts to land there. They requested a landing at another airport, but were rejected. According to the pilots, they were even threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert to the airport as requested.

That’s the point on which the union is sounding the alarm. Let me just quote the union on this:

As representatives of the pilot profession, ECA, IALPA and SNPL fully recognise and appreciate the assistance provided by authorities in responding to these threats and supporting flight crews in bringing their passengers and aircraft to safety.

However, reports indicate that, in certain circumstances, military aircraft have intercepted civilian airliners and directed aircraft commanders to land at specific airports without adequately considering aircrafts’ operational and safety requirements.

According to information received by IALPA, in one recent incident involving an Aer Lingus aircraft, military fighter aircraft directed the flight crew to divert to a military airfield for which they did not have the necessary aeronautical charts and operational information to safely conduct a landing. Despite the flight crew seeking an alternative and more suitable diversion airport, their request was refused.

ECA, IALPA and SNPL are also alarmed by subsequent reports that the pilots were apparently faced by the prospect of possible criminal prosecution for actions that were, at all times, aimed at protecting their passengers, crew and aircraft.

The union emphasizes that the captain of a flight should have the ultimate responsibility for the safety of passengers, crew, and the aircraft, and that the captain is uniquely positioned to assess the operational circumstances and determine the safest course of action, taking account of all relevant factors, including aircraft performance, available aeronautical information, airport suitability, operational limitations, and the availability of emergency assistance on the ground.

The union points out how the prospect of criminal prosecution against pilots exercising their professional judgment in such circumstances risks undermining aviation safety, and the effective cooperation between flight crews and authorities.

An Aer Lingus A320 was recently forced to divert to a military base in France, after the aircraft faced a bomb threat (which also impacted dozens of other flights). Fighter jets reportedly demanded the plane divert to this airport despite objections from the pilots, who felt they didn’t have sufficient operational information and aeronautical charts to land there.

The union representing pilots claims that the pilots were threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert there, which the union believes undermines the responsibility that pilots should have over the safety of their aircraft.

I fully side with the pilots and union here. It’s silly to me that a bomb threat that’s an obvious hoax puts pilots in a situation where they don’t feel comfortable landing at, with no alternatives offered.

What do you make of this Aer Lingus pilot situation?

#6209. End Of An Era: Hong Kong’s Iconic “Symphony Of Lights” Show Ending

Hong Kong is one of my favorite cities in the world. When I think of Hong Kong, the beautiful waterfront and skyline on both sides of Victoria Harbour come to mind. Along those lines, a nightly staple of the waterfront is coming to an end, and I’m sad about it…

Since 2004, Hong Kong has had the “Symphony of Lights” show every single night at 8PM, lasting for around 10 minutes. It holds the Guinness World Record for being the world’s largest permanent light and sound show, as it involves dozens of buildings.

It’s one of the things that contributes to Hong Kong’s electric energy, as you have a sea of people lining up on the waterfront (typically on the Tsim Sha Tsui side, though sometimes also on the Central side) every night to watch it.

Well, after 22 years, the Symphony of Lights will be coming to an end. The last show is expected to take place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. To mark the end of the era, the final show will feature special pyrotechnics and fireworks.

Why has Hong Kong decided to end the nightly Symphony of Lights show? Officially, it’s a strategic shift in the city’s tourism and event strategy, described as being driven by shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions. We’re told that we can expect “something new” in the future, but it doesn’t sound like it’ll be a full replacement for the Symphony of Lights.

I must admit, I’m sad to see this change in Hong Kong. No matter how often I visited Hong Kong, I always made a point of watching the Symphony of Lights, and always found it to be so enjoyable. Hong Kong has one of the world’s most gorgeous skylines, and the nightly show just took that to the next level.

I am curious what the backstory here is. Was the cost of operating this really so high, in the scheme of things? While I can in theory appreciate the concept of diminishing appeal, the nightly show always had a crowd in the thousands waiting to enjoy it — that was true 20 years ago when I first visited Hong Kong, and it was also true when I visited earlier this year.

Hong Kongers will soon have to bid farewell to the Symphony of Lights, the iconic nightly show that has been lighting up the city’s skyline since 2004. Officially, this change is described as being due to shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions.

I’ve enjoyed this show every time I visited Hong Kong, so I’m sad to see this development. The skyline is still incredible and leaves me in awe every time, but there’s no denying that the nightly show added just a little bit of extra sparkle.

What do you make of Hong Kong’s nightly Symphony of Lights ending?

#6208. Aeromexico Adds New U.S. Routes, Flights

Aeromexico is again expanding its footprint in the U.S. with assistance from longtime partner Delta.

The carrier announced Monday that it will connect Mexico City with Nashville, Tennessee, New Orleans, and San Juan, Puerto Rico. None of the three cities currently has nonstop service to the Mexican capital.

All three connections will operate four times weekly. Service to Nashville will launch first, on June 13, 2027, followed by New Orleans on June 17 and San Juan on June 24.

Flights to Nashville and New Orleans will use Embraer E190 aircraft with 99 seats. For the route to San Juan, the airline will operate Boeing 737 MAX 8s with 166 seats.

Aeromexico will also launch a second daily service between Mexico City and Austin, Texas, on June 3.

“The addition of Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan to our network will allow us to provide more connectivity options, bringing our customers closer to destinations known for their unique identity and remarkable attractions,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeromexico, said in a news release. “Together with Delta, we continue to open markets and create more opportunities that strengthen tourism and ties between Mexico and the United States.”

Last month, the partners announced new routes from Mexico City to Orange County, California, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Portland, Oregon.

#6207. Alaska, Hawaiian Pilot MECs Approve Tentative Joint Contract

Pilots at Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines are one step closer to a deal that will bring both work groups together under a single labor contract.

ALPA announced Wednesday that its Alaska and Hawaiian master executive councils unanimously approved a tentative agreement on a joint collective bargaining compact. The two councils had been negotiating since February 2025.

The proposed agreement will now go before the combined membership for a ratification vote.

Details of the agreement were not immediately available to the public.

Union officials said they worked to address the priorities of both work groups and have established a “contractual foundation for their future as a combined workforce.”

“This TA is the result of more than 600 days of challenging negotiations, countless hours of work by our volunteers, and an unwavering commitment to the pilots we represent,” Drew Coyle, the Alaska MEC chair, said in a statement. “Our Joint Negotiating Committee remained focused on the priorities of both pilot groups while working through some of the most complex issues facing our combined membership. Nothing about this process was easy. Now it’s our pilots’ turn to review the agreement, ask the tough questions, and decide whether it meets their expectations.”

Ratification voting starts Dec. 1 and closes Dec. 22.

Alaska and Hawaiian merged in 2024 and received a single operating certificate from the FAA in 2025. This effectively transformed Hawaiian from an independent airline to a brand under Alaska Air Group. Alaska has pledged to maintain Hawaiian’s brand identity, and Hawaiian retains a separate corporate leadership based in Honolulu.

The two brands have continued to integrate however, with Alaska now making use of long-haul aircraft originally owned by Hawaiian. Earlier this year, Alaska implemented a single passenger service system.

#6206. Buy Wyndham Rewards Points With Best-Ever 100% Bonus (0.65 Cents Each): Worth It?

Wyndham Rewards has launched its latest promotion on purchased points, which is potentially in line with the best-ever offers that we’ve seen from the program. This could be a great value for unlocking discounted award stays, as the program is offering up to a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.65 cents each.

Link: Buy Wyndham Rewards points with a bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM on December 31, 2026, Wyndham Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. The best offer appears to be for up to a 100% bonus, though you’ll have to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for.

With this offer, you can unlock the highest bonus if you purchase at least 3,000 points in one transaction. If you purchase 1,000 or 2,000 points, you don’t receive any bonus. If you purchase points, they’ll post to your account within 72 hours, and purchases are non-refundable. Purchased points don’t count toward Wyndham Rewards elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy Wyndham Rewards points for 1.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses, and that includes all taxes and fees.

If you maxed out the promotion and were eligible for a 100% bonus, you could purchase 400,000 points (including 200,000 bonus points) for $2,600, which is a rate of 0.65 cents per point.

This is the best bonus offer I ever recall seeing from Wyndham Rewards, so if there has ever been a time to buy points, this is it.

Wyndham Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 100,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been doubled, to 200,000 points.

When Wyndham offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s most commonly an 80-100% bonus. So this 100% bonus is at the very top end of that scale. However, personally I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Wyndham Rewards on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Wyndham Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

Generally speaking, I only recommend buying points when you have a specific, short-term use in mind. In the case of Wyndham Rewards points:

More generally, there are definitely some properties where there’s value in outright buying points for the purposes of a redemption. Let me actually give a direct example, as I recently purchased some Wyndham points for a hotel stay, rather than booking with cash. I needed to be in Colorado Springs, and I booked The Mining Exchange Hotel, part of Wyndham Registry Collection (the hotel even has a Michelin key!)

The cash rate for a base room at the hotel would’ve been $307.57, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Meanwhile the hotel was charging just 30,000 points. At a rate of 0.65 cents per point, that’s like paying $195 for the stay, inclusive of taxes & fees. Not bad, eh?

Well, it gets better than that. Wyndham Rewards often lets you book premium rooms at no extra cost when redeeming points, so I was able to book a club room for the same 30,000 points.

If paying cash, that would’ve cost $438.54, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Now, the club rooms absolutely aren’t worth it, since you just get access to a pantry with some packaged snacks. But hey, if the cost is the same, I’ll take it. 😉

Wyndham Rewards has a four tier award chart, so free night redemptions will cost one of the following amounts:

While I wouldn’t say there’s widespread appeal to buying Wyndham Rewards points for these kinds of redemptions, there are some situations where the numbers will work out. Perhaps the best value would come in situations where you just need to buy a few thousand points to have enough for an award stay.

Wyndham Rewards has more than 9,000 hotels across 20 brands in 80+ countries. Some of the most popular Wyndham Rewards brands include Registry Collection, Wyndham Grand, Dolce, Wyndham, La Quinta, Wingate, Wyndham Garden, Ramada, Days Inn, Super 8, Howard Johnson, and Travelodge.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Wyndham Rewards points to be worth 0.6 cents each. Admittedly that’s a very conservative valuation, and there should be opportunities to get way more value than that.

Wyndham Rewards has one of the most complicated points expiration policies of any hotel loyalty program:

Wyndham Rewards partners with a variety of transferable points currencies, including Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou. The catch is that transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, so I wouldn’t at all consider that to be a good redemption value.

That’s because you could be getting way more value from your transferable points than moving them to a program where points can be purchased for well under a penny each.

Wyndham Rewards also has a portfolio of credit cards issued in the United States, which are potentially quite lucrative if you frequent the brand.

Wyndham Rewards is offering up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.65 cents each. While I most definitely wouldn’t speculatively buy Wyndham Rewards points at this cost, there are some situations where the math works out, so everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves.

To those who are Wyndham Rewards fans, are there any properties you can get outsized value at with this promotion?

#6205. British Airways Unveils 8 New Boeing 787 Heathrow Routes: See Full List Now

Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

British Airways is one of only a tiny number of operators to fly all three variants of the Boeing 787. Ch-aviation shows that the oneworld member has 44 Dreamliners, which is the Boeing moniker. It has 18 787-9s (215 and 216 seats), 14 787-10s (256 seats), and 12 787-8s (204 seats).

The subfleet is entirely deployed from London Heathrow. However, BA eventually plans to replace its so-called Gatwick-configured 777-200ERs at the UK's second-busiest airport, which have fewer premium seats and higher overall capacity, with the 787-10. In time, Gatwick's widebodies will be all-Dreamliner.

OAG data was used to examine BA's 787 network from Heathrow. This looked at the routes available between January and September 2026, and then compared that to what's scheduled to operate from October 2026 through next year. This reflects what is known as of November 12 and certainly may change. Recent analysis shows that BA has pulled the 787 from six routes.

Start Date For 787 Flights (October 2026+)

% Of Flights On The 787 (Until October 2027)

Up to daily through the end of March 2027 (replaces the A380)

Up to five weekly (route switched from Gatwick, on which the 777-200ER was deployed)

Up to daily (route switched from Gatwick, on which the 777-200ER was deployed)

Daily (replaces the 777-200ER; route currently suspended)

Some of the routes are highly intriguing. This includes service to San José, the capital of Costa Rica and an increasingly important gateway for higher-end nature tourism. While the long route to Central America was flown by BA from Gatwick for the past decade, it is the first time that Heathrow has had flights there. The switch will help achieve higher yields and, somewhat paradoxically, a greater focus on connecting traffic.

On October 28, 2026, BA reintroduced the 787 on the short hop from Heathrow to Madrid, which links two critical IAG hubs. BA has flown widebody aircraft to Barajas for a long time. Iberia has too, and continues to do so on the A330 and A350 (I have flown the A350 on this route). The primary reason is to provide additional belly hold freight capacity to South America.

BA deployed the 767-300ER to Madrid for years, followed by the 777-200ER and the 787. The A380 appeared for crew familiarization and training. The so-called Dreamliner was used to Spain between 2017 and 2022, so the return after four years was notable. The type more or less replaced the Triple Seven, although that type is still going to appear occasionally this winter. The 777-200ER will replace the 787 next summer.

The 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 are all scheduled to operate this route. This might reflect the lack of aircraft availability and 'slotting in' variants based on their availability. It is one of only six routes in the current month to see all three variants, although it's usually the case that one of the variants has very few flights, but they do exist.

Another route will also stop seeing the type. Find out more here!

Some seek out specific aircraft types or variants when choosing where or when to fly, and I do this when I can. As such, the following table summarizes the dates on which each piece of equipment is due to fly between Heathrow and Madrid. Occasionally, BA will switch the 787 for the A320 (or other narrowbody aircraft), which is the risk of it. However, Flightradar24 data shows that the 787 has appeared as scheduled so far.

#6204. American Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Period in Years

American Airlines expects to fly over 8 million people in the days leading up to and following Thanksgiving.

The carrier said Monday that it will operate around 85,000 flights between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1. During that time, an American flight will depart every 13 seconds, officials said.

American said it will operate 7,021 flights on the Sunday after Thanksgiving, Nov. 29, making it the airline’s largest operating day since the COVID-19 pandemic.

At 11 a.m. Central Time on Nov. 20, 29, and 30, the carrier will have 1,130 flights operating simultaneously.

“Our team is ready for one of the busiest travel periods of the year, and we’re focused on delivering a safe, reliable operation so our customers can spend less time thinking about holiday travel and more time enjoying the holiday,” American Chief Operating Officer David Seymour said in a news release.

According to TSA data, the Sunday following Thanksgiving is often the busiest day of the year for air travel. The Tuesday and Wednesday preceding Thanksgiving also rank high, as do certain weekends in June and July.

A deadly flash flood swept through Grand Canyon National Park in northern Arizona over the weekend. An active search-and-rescue operation is underway along the Colorado River, and parts of the inner canyon and South Rim are closed at this time.

Due to extreme damage and flash flooding in the Grand Canyon this past weekend, the National Park Service announced immediate closures of the following areas until further notice: Phantom Ranch, Phantom Ranch cabins and canteen and Bright Angel Campground. The entire North Kaibab Trail — from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch — is also closed until further notice. The Silver and Black footbridges crossing the river have been affected as well.

For the latest trail and closure information, visit the park's Key Hiking Messages webpage.

A threat of severe weather still remains, and visitors are urged to exercise caution. Videos posted online by the Associated Press showed the destruction caused by the flooding. This devastating flash flood comes just a year after the Dragon Bravo wildfire forced the evacuation and closure of the North Rim in July 2025.

The closure of the inner canyon will allow the National Park Service and the Arizona Department of Public Safety to continue search-and-rescue operations. There are still visitors unaccounted for, and the NPS Investigative Services Branch is seeking the public’s assistance.

The flash flood significantly affected infrastructure in the canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, and, as a result, the visitor facilities at the South Rim are also affected.

Yes, it is safe to travel to portions of Grand Canyon National Park, but there are some restrictions that visitors should be aware of. We suggest bookmarking the park's main page, which lists updates and links to advisories.

The Places To Go page is full of helpful visitor information and maps.

The National Park Service has issued a closure notice for Monday, Aug. 31, at noon local time for the South Rim hotels located within Grand Canyon National Park due to damage to the Transcanyon Waterline. All water at the South Rim is delivered via the waterline, and additional reserves are running low. Only dry camping will be permitted at the South Rim.

It’s important to note that the park will remain open for day use, and food-and-beverage services at the South Rim will remain open (though some may reduce hours of operation).

As we’ve previously reported, the Transcanyon Waterline dates back to the 1960s, and the park has already invested $208 million in a multiyear rehabilitation project that isn't expected to be completed until 2027. The most recent update provided by Grand Canyon Lodges lists the hotels at the South Rim as projected to reopen on November 20, 2026.

Tusayan is the gateway to the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park at the Route 64 entrance, and its hotels and restaurants remain fully operational and unaffected, as it's located outside the national park.

Until further notice, the Colorado River is closed to river traffic due to metal structures and debris entering the river, according to a notice from the National Park Service. River operations rangers are coordinating with visitors already in the canyon, and the Grand Canyon River Alert system is also sending advisories. If you have an upcoming river trip scheduled, you should contact the commercial outfitter that you booked with or the NPS River Permits office for trip-specific information.

#6202. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM ET on November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that).

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Do you plan on buying IHG points with a bonus?

#6201. Avelo Brings First Commercial Flights to McKinney

Avelo operated its inaugural flight from McKinney National Airport in McKinney, Texas, on Wednesday.

Avelo Flight 1848, operated with a Boeing 737-800, was the first commercial airliner service from the airport to Fort Myers, Florida.

“We target the secondary airports of very large metropolitan areas where we can offer a different experience to the customers,” Avelo founder and CEO Andrew Levy said in an interview with AirlineGeeks.

McKinney is the third airport in the Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex to offer commercial service, with Dallas Love Field and Dallas/Forth Worth International Airport being the other two.

“For a lot of folks we’re going to be closer and a more convenient drive. And hopefully they’ll take advantage of that,” said McKinney airport director Ken Carley.

Carley said the airline has been wanting to be in the market since 2018. McKinney is the first new airport in Texas in 20 years to be certified for commercial air service.

“We had to build all this infrastructure because it did not exist. There was nothing on this side of the airport. So it’s not just this building, it’s the ramp and the taxi lane and all of that stuff, the taxiway that connects to the runway system. So it was a building, all the infrastructure, and meeting all those requirements,” Carley said.

McKinney is about 30 miles northeast of Dallas in Collin County. Levy said the area is growing like crazy.

“What we’re going to offer people who live close to this airport is a very different experience than getting on the highways and driving all the way to DFW or going down to Love Field,” he said.

The Texas-based airline will serve 11 destinations from McKinney: Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Fort Myers, Sarasota/Bradenton, Nashville, West Palm Beach, New Orleans, Denver, Atlanta, and Fort Lauderdale.

“I think it’s phenomenal that Avelo has announced additional routes before they’ve even started service. That’s a testament, I think, to what they’re seeing in the response they’re getting from for bookings. So they think it’s a strong market,” Carley said.

Levy said the approach was to offer a lot of selections and get a better sense of the market.

“All the markets we’re serving have massive proven demand from this area. And so of course, the trick for us is just to get people to know we’re here and then give us a try,” Levy said.

McKinney is a crew base for Avelo, its fifth, with pilots, flight attendants, airport operations personnel, and aircraft technicians, about 150 people behind the operation, Levy said.

“The demand will dictate how we grow, if we grow, and how fast we grow. This is going to be based on, do customers like the service? Does it resonate with them? Are we serving a need that exists every other place we’ve been? We don’t have any trouble filling up airplanes. I think this market is just going to do great, but time will tell, and the consumer will let us know,” Levy said.

“Our focus is on building a business that’s sustainable for the long term,” he added. “And that means everything we do has to work. It’s got to work well.”

Avelo currently offers service from DFW to New Haven, Connecticut. Levy said that service will continue but could move to McKinney at some point.

#6200. Etihad Slashes Flights, Pulls Airbus A380 Off Two Routes (Including Toronto)

Etihad Airways has just filed a major schedule update for early 2027, impacting a couple of dozen routes. In isolation, you might not think much of this, as the first several weeks of the year have weaker demand in many markets. However, in light of what’s going on in Etihad’s commercial division, I can’t help but be curious if there’s a bit more to this, and wonder how things will evolve.

AeroRoutes reports on how Abu Dhabi-based Etihad has filed a schedule change for the first quarter of 2027, with most of the changes taking place for flights as of January 11, 2027. For the most part, the reductions are for around a couple of months, through March 2027. There are two ways to look at this:

The frequency reductions we’re seeing are pretty significant. Just to look at service to North America:

Specific to the A380, it seems that Etihad is taking the jet off the Toronto and Singapore (SIN) routes over that period, and it doesn’t seem like the super jumbo will be flying any other routes in place of that, at least based on current schedule filings. During that period, Etihad will only be flying the A380 to four destinations — Bangkok (BKK), London (LHR), Paris (CDG), and Tokyo Narita (NRT).

It’s a fascinating time for Etihad. Obviously Gulf carriers are having a rather difficult time with everything going on in the region at the moment, and it comes at a unique time for Etihad, as the carrier has been going through a massive expansion.

Now, I’ve been a bit skeptical about the claimed economics of this expansion, but Etihad management has insisted everything couldn’t be better… until Etihad Chief Commercial Officer Arik De recently “departed” the airline.

The can of worms that this departure opened is truly unlike anything I’ve seen at any airline before… and I’ve been following this industry for a long time. Seriously, check out the 520+ comments on my post about his departure, because employees have a lot to say. It’s so salacious that it has gotten OMAAT blocked in the UAE.

The point is, if even a quarter of the things are to be believed — and I’ve had some very interesting conversations with some formerly very high up people at the airline — then the carrier’s entire commercial strategy has been a bit questionable, to put it politely, and more about serving a certain someone’s LinkedIn profile ego, rather than actually developing a commercial strategy.

So with him no longer there, I’m curious to see how this all evolves. Let me emphasize that this is of course in no way a knock on all the hardworking employees at Etihad who have had to endure this “leadership” for too long. It seems like they now have quite the web to untangle, especially given the toxic people who are reportedly still there.

Etihad Airways has just filed a pretty big schedule change for early 2027, whereby a couple of dozen routes are seeing significant capacity reductions. Most notably, the Airbus A380 is being taken off of both the Toronto and Singapore routes.

In isolation, you might not think much of this, as demand is often a little lighter earlier in the year. But what I find interesting is that this follows a period of very rapid expansion, along with the carrier’s head of commercial strategy getting the boot.

Based on what I’ve heard from a countless number of current and former Etihad management employees, the strategy of the past couple of years hasn’t been as sound as a certain someone has tried to make it appear. We’ll see how this all unravels.

What do you make of this Etihad schedule change, and how do you see things playing out?

#6199. The Rise of the Rosé States

A rosé state’s political disposition is recognizably Republican, but that disposition is conditional on a normie GOP.

Karno Muji Saputra/Getty Images, NR Illustration

When Ted Cruz was up for reelection in Texas in 2024 (and Trump hadn’t yet been swept back into power), I had a conversation with a political operative who had just gotten back from running a mock debate with him. We talked about Cruz and John Cornyn and what kind of Republican each was, and how they would fare in a world where Trump completed his comeback.

I spitballed an idea that had been kicking around in my head for a time: that Texas wasn’t as red as everybody thought, or at least not as uniformly MAGA; that it was still much closer to the state George W. Bush took over from outgoing Governor Ann Richards in 1995; and that election results had largely masked an underlying political disposition that was a quite light shade of red. Given that reality, I said, Cornyn was a better indication of where Texas voters were than Cruz.

Karno Muji Saputra/Getty Images, NR Illustration

#6198. United Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights For Customers

In the first such move by a U.S. airline, United will ban third-party AI from parts of its digital platforms and adjust its policies to prevent access via travel agencies and aggregators.

“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” the airline said in a statement.

The carrier also said AI actions could violate FAA and Department of Transportation regulations. As an example, it cited the requirement that passengers confirm in person that their bags do not contain banned items, such as explosives.

“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access, directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the statement continued. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.”

United said its stance is in line with companies in the banking and retail sectors. It is now “encourag[ing] others” to consider measures “that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.”

The airline said it will update its Digital Trust Center to clarify the new restrictions.

#6196. Cathay Pacific Orders 41 Airbus A330-900neos, As New Regional Workhorse

In August 2024, Cathay Pacific placed an order for 30 Airbus A330neos. There’s now an update, as the airline has just bumped this order by 11 more planes, meaning that there are now a total of 41 of these aircraft on order. Let’s take a look at all the details, and discuss what this means for fleet modernization at the Hong Kong based oneworld carrier.

Cathay Pacific now has a firm order for 41 Airbus A330-900neo aircraft, which are expected to be delivered between 2028 and 2035.

This follows an evaluation of the carrier’s mid-size wide body fleet renewal program, and it will enable Cathay Pacific to modernize its earlier generation A330-300 fleet, and expand its operations on high capacity regional routes. However, the airline is leaving plans for this plane open, and also emphasizes how the jet offers the flexibility to serve longer range destinations.

For those not familiar, the A330neo is the updated version of the A330, featuring improved range and fuel efficiency. The A330-900neo is the larger of the two new variants (with the other being the A330-800neo). The plane has a range of 7,200 nautical miles, plus a capacity for 287 passengers in a standard three cabin configuration.

I think it’s safe to assume that at least most of these A330neos will be equipped with the new Aria Studio business class product, which is expected to be retrofitted on select existing A330s in the coming months. This will finally see the carrier introduce a dedicated regional product with flat beds, which is exciting, though it’s not quite to the level of the long haul Aria Suite business class.

Here’s how Cathay Pacific CEO Ronald Lam described how the A330neo fits into the carrier’s fleet, back when the first 30 frames were ordered:

“The A330 is an aircraft type that has been serving Cathay Pacific well for nearly 30 years. These new aircraft will principally serve our regional destinations in Asia, while also providing the flexibility to serve longer-haul destinations as required. The improved fuel efficiency of these A330neos, together with their high standards of comfort, will enable us to further elevate the experience we provide for our customers while also contributing towards our goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.”

Cathay Pacific refreshing its short and medium haul fleet with the Airbus A330-900neo makes perfect sense, and is just about the safest, most expected aircraft order that Cathay Pacific could place. For context on Cathay Pacific’s fleet, the airline has:

Now Cathay Pacific’s fleet renewal plans are becoming a bit clearer, as the airline has:

So a decade down the road, you can expect that Cathay Pacific will primarily be flying A321neos, A330-900neos, A350s (-900s and -1000s), and 777-9s. That seems like a pretty logical fleet development plan to me.

Cathay Pacific now has an order for 41 Airbus A330-900neos, which the airline will primarily use to modernize and grow its regional fleet. The carrier already flies A330-300s, some of which are nearly 25 years old, so it’s logical that the airline would slowly be looking to replace these jets.

Cathay Pacific now has a pretty impressive (but not overly ambitious) order book, with A321neos, A330-900neos, and 777-9s, used for fleet renewal.

What do you make of Cathay Pacific’s Airbus A330-900neo order?
