There is no shortage of ways to redeem your points and miles for travel to Europe. With most flights being overnight, booking a lie-flat seat is an excellent way to ensure you arrive rested and refreshed on the continent.

Points and miles enthusiasts usually need to choose between paying high redemption rates or high surcharges. Programs like Delta SkyMiles charge just $5.60 in taxes and fees for business-class flights to Europe but expect up to 500,000 miles per person for flights as short as seven hours on peak dates.

Many European programs have much lower redemption rates, such as British Airways Club, which charges just 88,000 Avios for a one-way, off-peak flight to London from the Northeast. The trade-off is you will need to stump up almost $500 in taxes, fees and surcharges to BA.

The Scandinavian Airlines EuroBonus program charges just 60,000 EuroBonus points for a one-way, SAS-operated Business Bonus award between North America and Europe. The cherry on top? You'll need to pay just $5.60 in taxes and fees. Although this loyalty currency has traditionally been difficult to earn, thanks to the new Rove transfer option, you can fly to Europe for less than the price of a cup of coffee in taxes and fees by redeeming miles.

Related: Earning 28 miles per dollar: How a 2-night New York City hotel stay earned me enough miles to fly to Europe using Rove

Here's how to do it and what my experience was like.

SAS doesn't add carrier-imposed surcharges to awards on flights it operates, making SAS EuroBonus one of the best-value Rove transfer partners for business-class travel to Europe.

SAS flies nonstop to Copenhagen Airport (CPH) from the following U.S. gateways, although some routes are seasonal:

SAS also flies nonstop from Newark to Oslo Airport (OSL) and Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN).

Related: SAS has brought back European Business class on short-haul flights

Business Bonus seats at the fixed 60,000-point rate were strictly limited and were not available on every route or date I searched. When they were unavailable, SAS displayed regular fares that could be paid with points at a much higher rate, so flexible dates helped a lot.

Rove miles transfer to EuroBonus points at a 1:1 ratio, with a 2,000-mile minimum and transfers in increments of 100 miles. My transfer posted instantly, though Rove says transfers usually complete within one day.

Transfers can't be reversed, so the golden rule applies here: Find award space you're happy with before you move a single mile.

SAS award flights booked on the website must currently be reserved at least three days before departure. The SAS app allows closer-in bookings, but for reservations made within three days of departure, the EuroBonus member must be traveling.

Taxes and fees were higher on the way back. When I checked, a SAS business-class award from Copenhagen to the U.S. required about $95 one-way.

Related: A game of thrones: Flying business class on Scandinavian Airlines' A321LR from Copenhagen to Washington

EuroBonus isn't the only option to redeem your Rove miles to fly to Europe. Other transfer partners can be used, but the combination of redemption rates plus taxes, fees and surcharges is not as attractive as EuroBonus:

Related: How to avoid paying fuel surcharges when redeeming points and miles

My journey to Europe began by purchasing a tall latte from Starbucks at ATL for $6.16, including Georgia sales tax, more than the taxes and fees I paid for my business-class flight.

I then used the Sky Priority check-in for my flight to Copenhagen, which allowed me to check two bags, each up to 70 pounds.

SAS business-class tickets to Europe include access to Delta Sky Club lounges. SAS departs from Concourse F, one of the two international concourses at Atlanta Airport, so I headed to the Sky Club in this concourse.

Related: A posh Delta One lounge is coming to Atlanta

It featured an outdoor terrace, which was a great place for planespotting and soaking up the Georgia sunshine.

A kindly staff member who noticed my photo-taking gave me a tip that there was a newer and more luxurious Sky Club in Concourse D I could access on the same ticket. Since I still had several hours before my flight, I headed over there.

It was a big, bright room with floor-to-ceiling windows on both sides looking out over the airfield, and the green and teal decor was a nod to Atlanta's "City in a Forest" nickname.

Based on my visit, I would recommend heading to Concourse D if you have time; I preferred its newer, larger space.

Related: Inside Delta's brand-new Sky Club in Atlanta, its nicest one yet

There were plenty of hot and cold food options available, which is ideal for anyone heading to Europe and wanting to maximize their rest on their flight.

Despite being busy during the late afternoon and early evening, the bartenders happily served up sparkling wine, beers and soft drinks and well as whipping up cocktails and chatting to guests about their travel plans.

After taking advantage of priority boarding for business passengers, I boarded the SAS Airbus A350-900, which had 40 business-class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, so every passenger had direct aisle access.

The cabin had a calm, understated palette of charcoal gray seat shells with brushed silver trim and blue-flecked gray fabric, with a tan, leather-look panel lining each side console to warm it up.

The bedding was already at my seat when I boarded, wrapped in plastic. It came from Dux, the Swedish bedmaker that was SAS's official comfort partner at the time, and included a gray and white pinstriped duvet and two pillows.

The amenity kit was a limited-edition one for SAS’s 80th anniversary. It came in a navy zip pouch with the airline’s 80 logo on the front. Inside was a matching navy eye mask, earplugs and a dental kit, plus lip balm and hand cream from Swedish skincare brand Muro Scents.

A pair of SAS-branded over-ear headphones hung on a hook in the side console. There was a universal power outlet and a USB port right next to it, and the seat itself was controlled from a touchscreen panel, including lumbar support.

I was more interested in sleep than cinema on my flight to Denmark, but the 18.5-inch touchscreen had a solid selection of recent releases, including "The Devil Wears Prada 2."

The drinks list was where SAS leans hardest into its Scandinavian roots.

Alongside Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve Champagne, there was a hazy IPA brewed by Danish brewery Mikkeller in collaboration with SAS; two SAS-exclusive spirits, Herno Old Tom Gin and High Coast whisky from Sweden; and a cocktail menu that included the SASmopolitan.

For my Atlanta departure, the menu had a definite Georgia flavor. The starter options were grilled peaches wrapped in prosciutto with mozzarella and balsamic pearls or seared ahi tuna. Main courses included smoked beef short rib with stone-ground grits from Georgia's Riverview Farms, a hot honey-glazed chicken thigh and goat cheese and apple ravioli.

I chose the ahi tuna, which was a light and fresh start to the meal, with a hearty slice of sourdough bread on the side.

For the main course, I went for the beef short rib, an indulgent and delicious option with super-tender beef and creamy grits.

With a fairly short flight time and a full stomach, I skipped dessert, reclined my seat fully flat and settled in for the night.

The crew set up a snack bar for business-class passengers who got hungry during the flight, but most focused on getting a good night's rest.

I slept right through breakfast (the crew had asked at dinner whether I wanted to be woken) and arrived refreshed and ready to explore the charming city of Copenhagen.

After years of having to choose between high redemption rates and high surcharges, booking through SAS EuroBonus could be the ultimate sweet spot to Europe.

I've flown plenty of business-class products across the Atlantic, and SAS offered a very respectable experience on the A350 with friendly staff, direct aisle access, comfortable bedding and some fun Scandic touches.

Joining Rove costs nothing, and you can earn 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link. As an added bonus, new users can earn an additional 5,000 miles after making their first hotel booking of $500 or more with code "BRIANKELLY500".

I'd much rather pay $5.60 for a lie-flat seat to Europe than a cup of coffee. How about you?

#6194. Delta Platinum Amex Card Review: Big Benefits & Strong Welcome Offer

The Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card is the second most premium personal credit card in the Delta SkyMiles and Amex co-brand card portfolio.

If you fly Delta several times a year and want perks like a companion certificate and the ability to spend toward elite status qualification, the Delta Platinum Amex is worth a look, and can easily be worth more than the fee. This post is my in-depth Delta Platinum Card review, so let’s get into all the details.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card

Before we get too deep into my Delta Platinum Amex review, let me give a quick overview of the card’s main features and fees:

I also put together my top pros and cons for the Delta Platinum SkyMiles Card:

Let’s cover the welcome bonus, eligibility details, and fees, of the Delta Platinum Card. After all, these are major factors that people consider when applying for cards.

The Delta Platinum Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 90,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $3,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $990. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome offer on the Delta Platinum Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal version of the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the less premium cards first, and then work your way up. That way you’re potentially eligible for the welcome offers on each of the cards. Meanwhile if you start with the most premium card, you wouldn’t be eligible for the offers on the less premium cards.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Platinum Delta Amex has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees). You can add additional users to the card at no extra cost (Rates & Fees). As mentioned above, this is the second highest annual fee personal card in the Delta and Amex portfolio.

If you are going to put spending on the Delta Platinum Amex, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use the card abroad without paying high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. How does the Delta Platinum Card do on that front? Well, among airline cards, I’d say it’s pretty competitive, so let’s cover those details.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers the following miles earning opportunities for spending:

Since I value Delta miles at 1.1 cents, I think this card offers a 3.3% return on its 3x miles categories (purchases made directly with Delta and directly with hotels), a 2.2% return on its 2x miles categories (restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets), and a 1.1% return on non-bonus spending.

The card has solid bonus categories for a co-branded airline card, but purely in terms of rewards for spending, I think there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, hotel purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Platinum Amex can help you earn status:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

If you’re serious about earning elite status with credit card spending, you’ll want to consider the more premium Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more) instead, since it earns MQDs twice as fast — you earn $1 MQD per $10 of eligible purchases, rather than $1 MQD per $20 of eligible purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on airlines like LATAM and WestJet, which aren’t part of SkyTeam.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Platinum Delta Credit Card has a nice welcome offer. In general, I’d say it could be worth putting spending on the card if you’re trying to earn Medallion elite status with Delta SkyMiles. For most people, the reason you’ll want to keep this card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which for many people will more than offset the annual fee. Let’s go over some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of your Delta Platinum Card, you can receive a Delta Main roundtrip companion certificate. You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. This is a great deal that can be worth significantly more than the annual fee in and of itself.

If redeeming the certificate there are some things to be aware of:

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you can receive up to $150 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you can receive $150 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $150, if you wanted to. If used right, there’s real value here.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers. This is super easy to unlock, though admittedly the increments as such are quite small.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases with U.S. Resy restaurants.

Just for having the Platinum Delta Card you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up.

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a single trip could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Platinum Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you’ll need to ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation (though there’s no need to actually pay for the flight with the card).

This benefit is valid for a total of up to nine people traveling on the same reservation with the primary cardmember.

If you have the Delta Platinum Card, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

The Platinum Delta Amex offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years for the application fee for TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This can save you time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible. (Enrollment required)

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible Delta Amex card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta (the discount doesn’t apply to taxes and fees). Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. (Enrollment required)

The Delta Platinum Card gets you complimentary Hertz Five Star status. Enrollment is required, and you receive the following benefits with the rental car company:

The Delta Platinum Amex comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Platinum Credit Card isn’t necessarily the best card for the casual Delta flyer, and it’s also not a card I’d recommend putting much spending on, unless you value the MQDs that you can earn with the card. Even if you value MQDs, you’re better off with the more premium card, since you can earn them twice as fast.

However, this card has solid perks, ranging from a companion certificate, to free checked bags, to priority boarding, to savings on award flights, to access to exclusive award redemption opportunities, to valuable statement credits, and more.

Bigger picture, is the Delta Platinum Card worth it, though? There are a few things to consider.

If the Delta Platinum Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. The main earning difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on transit, at U.S. shipping providers, and on single eligible purchases of $5,000 or more (on up to $100,000 of combined eligible purchases per year), while the personal card offers 2x miles at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets (both cards offer 3x miles on Delta purchases and hotel purchases).

The business version of the card also offers an annual Delta Stays credit of up to $200, rather than one of up to $150, so it’s arguably more lucrative.

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) is a good card for occasional Delta flyers who want basic airline perks. It has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees) and a smaller list of perks, including:

The Delta Gold Card offers the same discounts you get with the Delta Platinum Card, as well as the rideshare credit, but in this case it only kicks in after your first renewal. The Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn MQDs toward status, so that’s another potential downside to keep in mind.

For the very frequent Delta flyer, there’s the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more), which has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). What differentiates this card?

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. These points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50K per calendar year, and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25K per calendar year, and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at amextravel.com

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers solid perks for those who fly Delta frequently, especially Medallion members. For many, the annual companion certificate will more than justify the annual fee in and of itself, without even accounting for all of the other perks. Some will also get value from the 2,500 MQDs that are offered annually just for having the card.

The annual fee on this card is potentially quite easy to justify, thanks to all the credits you can earn with rideshares, Resy, and even Delta Stays.

#6193. American Airlines Plans To Bring Back First Class Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights—Starting With New York–Chicago

This is a very good change. A flight can take up much of your afternoon without crossing American’s 900-mile meal threshold, especially when you include getting to the airport, boarding, and a connection. A small meal makes first class more worthwhile.

JonNYC reports that American Airlines is bringing back light bites and mini-meals on 700–899-mile domestic first class flights, starting on NYC/ORD.

American used to have a service between a basket of packaged snacks and a full meal. Before the pandemic, shorter flights could get something plated that would tide you over.

In 2016 I reported plans for plated morning items, including yogurt and breakfast cake. And my 2018 menu coverage included Lite Bites cheeses with cracked black pepper cheddar, cave-aged cheddar, Appalachian Tomme, and smoked Gouda.

American’s mainline standard is a snack basket on 500–899-mile flights during meal times, with meals starting in the 900-mile range.

United actually raised its meal threshold from 800 to 900 miles in January 2024. American would be moving in the other direction, offering something more substantial on flights where Delta and United generally hand out snacks.

Alaska is still the standard to beat. They already feed passengers on shorter flights, and I’ve found their domestic first class food better than competitors’.

New York–Chicago is an obvious place to start. New York LaGuardia–O’Hare is about 730 miles, and New York JFK–O’Hare about 740. An expansion might include:

American also used to have meal “exception markets”: shorter routes that got meals for competitive reasons. My January 2020 service guide listed Chicago–Dallas, Chicago–Boston, Chicago–New York, Los Angeles–Denver, and LaGuardia–Atlanta, among others.

I like a broad 700–899-mile rule better than making customers depend on whether their particular city pair merits an exception, though the exception markets got real meals and some were even shorter like Chicago–Washington National at just 612 miles which still wouldn’ qualify for a lite bite under this distance band.

This does mean more work for flight attendants. Individual food service means preparation, distribution, and clearing, with less time to do it on a shorter flight. American is also adding first class seats to some of its aircraft.

The airline’s product turnaround has been surprising, and surprisingly fast. They’ve introduced new business class suites, improved regional cabins and internet, upgraded coffee, and put money into lounges. They’re also reversing years of bad product decisions, including plans to bring back seatback screens and add more extra legroom coach seats.

Their returning coach food reservation program, announced with an initial Dallas–Fort Worth–Los Angeles test, should help passengers get the item they actually want. Mostly, though, I like that American seems to be loading enough food that there’s still something left when the cart reaches my aisle.

American has now announced the return of lite bites, with options including:

There will be two options onboard a given flight, with choices rotating “throughout the year.”

#6192. Muscle Memory: Heathrow Tail Strike Wrote Off 33-Year-Old Airbus A300 After Aborted Landing

Just over a year ago, an Airbus A300-600F cargo aircraft operated by European Air Transport Leipzig as part of Deutsche Post's DHL-branded airfreight operations experienced a dramatic tail strike upon landing at London Heathrow Airport (LHR). The jet subsequently went around and landed at the second time of asking, but the damage had been done, and it only flew once more before being written off.

Now, a bulletin issued by the Air Accidents Investigation Branch of the United Kingdom has explored the finer details of the incident, ultimately finding that muscle memory had resulted in reverse thrust being selected despite the decision to go around. While the aircraft was able to be repaired temporarily so that it could be flown into storage, the cost of fully bringing it back up to speed was just too high.

As detailed by the AAIB bulletin, the incident occurred on October 12, 2025, with the A300 in question bearing the registration D-AEAG. According to Planespotters.net, this aircraft was 33 years old at the time, having first flown passengers in Japan in 1992. Its conversion to a cargo jet took place in 2011. Data from Flightradar24 shows that the flight in question was QY2212 from Leipzig Halle Airport (LEJ).

The aircraft had two pilots on board, and was cleared to land at 5:12 PM local time (4:12 PM UTC), having left Leipzig around an hour and a half earlier. As seen in the video embedded above, the aircraft's first landing attempt was captured on a livestream, with the jet bouncing as it touched down. This prompted the pilot to initiate a go-around, but, as the jet climbed away, it suffered a tail strike. The AAIB explains:

"The commander increased the aircraft’s pitch, which, combined with the continued extension of the ground spoilers and their associated pitch-up effect, resulted in a tailstrike."

Now, more than a year later, the AAIB's bulletin reveals the finer details that contributed to the tail strike and the subsequent aircraft write-off. The AAIB's findings show that muscle memory seemingly kicked in, with the pilot having selected reverse thrust. While this is a key component of a standard landing, they did so without conscious acknowledgement, meaning that their co-pilot was unable to correct them.

As such, this complicated the go-around procedure, with the engines being slower to respond once the pilot opted to go-around and selected takeoff/go-around thrust. This resulted in a drop in speed, and, while the jet did eventually take off again, it took several seconds to do so, compounding the tail strike caused by the pitch-up effect that came about as a result of the aforementioned ground spoilers.

The aircraft subsequently landed safely at the second time of asking, but the damage had been done, with the tail strike causing "damage to the lower tail section at frame 77." This, the AAIB says, "included buckling of the skin inwards at the frame, the rivets joining the skin to the frame having separated from the skin, and the tail skid having sustained abrasion damage." It ultimately proved too costly to repair.

Following its dramatic arrival in London, D-AEAG remained on the ground at Heathrow Airport for more than three months. While the resulting damage was too expensive to repair to the standard that would allow the jet to re-enter commercial service, it was patched up for one final flight, as seen above. This occurred on January 31, as D-AEAG flew from London to Lleida (ILD) for storage and scrapping.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The nature of the temporary repairs meant that the aircraft could only cruise at an altitude of 10,000 feet. This is often the case for post-repair ferry flights where pressurization may be an issue. It took off from London at 8:53 AM and landed in Lleida at 12:14 PM on January 31, just over two hours later. This brought an early end to its flying career, which ended, as many do, at a Spanish aircraft storage facility.

#6191. Korean Air Adds Newark Flights From Incheon, Joining United & Air Premia

Korean Air has just quietly added a new long haul route, as the airline will be adding service to Newark, New Jersey. What’s interesting is just how competitive this market has become, but it’s logical in the context of what’s going on at the airline (thanks to S_LEE for flagging this).

As of May 22, 2027, Korean Air plans to launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Newark. The flight will operate with the following schedule:

KE97 Seoul Incheon to Newark departing 10:00PM arriving 11:00PMKE98 Newark to Seoul Incheon departing 1:00AM arriving 5:15AM (+1 day)

The 6,896-mile flight is blocked at 14hr to the United States, and 15hr15min to South Korea. Korean Air will use a Boeing 777-300ER for the route, featuring 277 seats, including eight first class seats, 42 business class seats, and 227 economy seats.

This technically marks a service resumption, as Korean Air last served Newark through September 2001, but then suspended flights after the 9/11 terror attacks, and never resumed the flights. This new service will complement Korean Air’s existing service to New York Kennedy (JFK), which typically operates twice daily.

On top of that, Korean Air’s destinations in the United States include Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Chicago (ORD), Dallas (DFW), Honolulu (HNL), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), San Francisco (SFO), Seattle (SEA), and Washington Dulles (IAD).

Interestingly, Korean Air faces quite a bit of competition in the market between Incheon and Newark. Going back several years, it’s a route that no airline served.

However, that has changed in recent times. In May 2023, South Korean budget carrier Air Premia launched service in the market using a Boeing 787. Then in September 2026, United Airlines launched flights in the market, also using a Boeing 787. Korean Air’s timing is very similar to Air Premia’s in both directions, which isn’t too surprising.

Some people might be surprised to see Korean Air adding flights to Newark in addition to existing service to Kennedy (with no plans to reduce that service), but this actually seems pretty straightforward to me.

Keep in mind that Korean Air and Asiana have merged, and in the coming weeks, the two airlines will even take on the same brand. Historically these carriers were huge competitors, so of course in some markets they’ll be reducing capacity. In other words, the combined Korean Air won’t have quite as many frequencies to places like Los Angeles, New York, and San Francisco, as the two airlines did separately.

That of course opens up the opportunity to serve more new markets, and clearly Newark was identified as one of those opportunities. Also keep in mind that Korean Air operates as part of a transpacific joint venture with Delta, so the airlines can coordinate fares and schedules, and it’s all about the combined depth and breadth of service.

If you’re looking at this from a Manhattan centric perspective, you might be surprised that the airline is bothering to serve both airports. However, service to Newark goes way beyond that, and the idea is that this flight is useful for serving parts of New Jersey, Pennsylvania, etc. Admittedly those flyers likely aren’t loyal to SkyTeam, but from a Korea point of sale perspective (especially with the number of people studying in the region), it makes sense.

As of May 2027, Korean Air will be launching daily flights from Seoul Incheon to Newark, complementing existing service to Kennedy. This means we’ll see three daily flights between Incheon and Newark on three different airlines… that’s quite the step up from the zero daily flights we saw several years back!

With Korean Air’s takeover of Asiana complete, it’s logical that the South Korean mega carrier would be looking at adding some new markets, given the increased connectivity and scale of the operation.

What do you make of Korean Air launching Newark flights?

#6190. Where Does the U.S.-Israel Relationship Go from Here?

Opposition to Israel now has a toehold in both parties.

Israeli and American flags are flown at the March for Israel rally on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., November 14, 2023.

In the days since the midterms, it has become clear that the U.S.-Israel relationship is under assault in both parties. On the left, a group of DSA-linked Democrats has been elected to Congress. Like their precursor Zohran Mamdani in New York City and led by Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, these new members place opposition to Israel at the center of their politics. It isn’t one concern among many but the defining issue of their candidacies. El-Sayed used his graceless and vengeful victory speech to attack Israel in barely disguised language: “Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here for schools here and health care here and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”

For the first time, both the Senate and the House will have — among the majority side — dedicated opponents of all aid to Israel, including even the sale of defensive weapons. They will see moves like an end to military assistance as weak half-measures, when much more must be demanded.

Israeli and American flags are flown at the March for Israel rally on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., November 14, 2023.

‘Tis the season … when frequent flyers scramble for eleventh-hour ways to qualify for airline elite status they haven’t quite reached yet.

If Southwest is your airline of choice, the end of 2026 is particularly important to hit status milestones, as Southwest’s Rapid Rewards program is about to change in major ways in early 2027.

With fewer international flight options and no premium cabins for upgrades, chasing Southwest status might not seem as necessary as it does with larger competitors like United Airlines or Delta Air Lines.

But if you fly Southwest a lot and are close to hitting a status goal, it’s wise to explore easy and inexpensive ways to get over that hump.

What you need to do to earn status depends on what part of Southwest’s program you are targeting. Southwest technically has two official status tiers in 2026. Plus, members who fly (or spend) the most can unlock its popular Companion Pass.

Coming next year: Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes

You can check how close you are to status by logging into your Rapid Rewards account where there are easy-to-read status bars for each goal.

There are very different methods for earning the Companion Pass than there are for earning A-List and A-List Preferred status. If the Companion Pass is your only goal, you need to act quickly. The “easy” way to do that with credit card bonuses effectively ends forever no later than Dec. 2, 2026.

This year also marks the last that many partner points count towards Companion Pass, from credit card refer-a-friend bonuses to completing hotel stays booked on the Southwest Hotels portal.

More: Last chance to earn a Southwest Companion Pass the easy way with card bonuses as high as 90,000 points

If traditional A-List or A-List Preferred status is your goal, however, here are 5 ways you can get the flights or points you might still need.

Note that beginning in 2027, Southwest will rename those tiers as part of a broader overhaul (more on that below), but that will not affect how you qualify in 2026 for 2027.

If you are only a few flights away from qualifying for Southwest status, one of the easiest ways to get to the finish line is by taking a trip or two before year’s end.

The amount of money spent doesn’t matter at all if you qualify purely by counting up the number of one-way flights flown, so book and fly the cheapest nonstop Basic fares you can find.

Use Southwest’s Low Fare Calendar to search quickly for the least expensive days to fly to various destinations. The best deals are usually midweek. Early and mid-December (between peak Thanksgiving and Christmas holiday travel) will likely offer lower prices and reduced chances of travel disruptions.

If you can’t hit a status goal by counting one-way flights and need to earn status via tier qualifying points instead, you should take the opposite approach. Instead of booking inexpensive Basic fares, book and fly Southwest’s most expensive fare option: Choice Extra.

This fare earns a whopping 14 TQPs per dollar spent in 2026. If you spend $500 on Choice Extra fares for a November or December mileage run, for example, you will add a quick 7000 TQPs to your Rapid Rewards account balance—one fifth of the way to A-List status.

Those same points are also worth about $90 when redeemed for award travel, so consider the rebate in your cost-benefit calculation.

If actually flying the airline before the year is up isn’t a realistic option, another way to earn tier qualifying points is by spending on a Southwest credit card.

The different cobranded cards earn TQPs differently in 2026. Holders of the lower annual fee (see rates and fees) are out of luck; that card doesn’t earn TQPs at all.

The higher fee cards each earn incrementally higher TQPs, as follows:

(Note, however, that all cards earn Companion Pass qualifying points at a different rate—1 point per $1 spent.)

One critical detail: TQPs earned from credit card spending only count towards 2026 status if the points post to your account before year’s end. That means it is essential to complete all spending before the closing date of your December credit card statement, meaning many travelers may only have a few weeks left.

A reminder, though: Credit card spending will count differently beginning next year for customers trying to qualify for status for 2028.

*The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you have a card (see rates and fees) and already spend heavily on it, there is a quick and easy shortcut to Southwest A-List status (but not A-List Preferred). If you spend $75,000 on that card annually, you'll be rewarded with complimentary A-List status for the remainder of the year and the following year (activation required).

You'll also earn a $500 annual credit towards booking Southwest flights in the Chase Ultimate Rewards portal. That same spending level unlocks other perks from a variety of travel brands like Hyatt and IHG, so there are more benefits than just the Southwest ones to consider.

This method doesn’t require fussing with flight counts or TQPs or even hopping on an airplane before 2026 is up, but it’s only a viable option for a smaller subset of Southwest customers who carry the card and are capable of meeting a significant spending minimum.

Like many airlines, Southwest offers a status match promotion and challenge where you can leverage your elite status on another airline into temporary status on Southwest. If you hold status elsewhere, consider taking advantage.

The current promotion is open for registration through Dec. 30, 2026. As soon as you register, Southwest confers automatic status for a 120-day trial period. You can extend this status for another 12 months if you complete additional flights or earn additional TQPs in the promotion period.

If you plan to fly several trips on Southwest at the end of 2026 or in early 2027, this promotion might make sense. The requirements to meet the status challenge extension are substantially lower than the ones for achieving status the standard way.

Just be aware that only flights booked after registering for the status match count. If you have future Southwest travel already booked, you’ll need to cancel and rebook, potentially at higher prices.

Before committing to any of these strategies, be certain that you understand how Southwest counts Rapid Rewards points in 2026.

Southwest currently counts points three different ways. There are points redeemable only for award travel, and there are two other types that count towards status. Only tier qualifying points, earned primarily through flying or credit card spending, count towards A-List and A-List Preferred Status.

A broader collection of companion pass qualifying points (including credit card welcome bonuses) still count towards earning the Companion Pass for 2026 only.

A lot will soon change when the calendar page turns to 2027.

A-List members will become Silver, and A-List Preferred members will become Gold. Members who have earned a Companion Pass due to points activity in 2026 will continue to be able to use those benefits until the end of 2027.

If you want to earn a Companion Pass anew in 2027 or later, however, you’ll have to aim for a new status tier: Platinum. And if you want to achieve Silver or Gold in subsequent years, be aware that that benchmarks will change. The way TQPs are calculated for several Southwest fare types and for credit card spending will be different as well.

#6188. United Airlines Plans Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins For Aging Boeing 757-300s—Retirement Can Wait

United Airlines is planning a major cabin upgrade for its 21 Boeing 757-300s, bringing seatback entertainment, larger overhead bins and refreshed interiors to planes that average roughly 24 years old. American Airlines retired its last 757s early in the pandemic. United apparently sees enough flying left in these stretched jets to spend money on them. According to aviation watchdog JonNYC, the work will bring the aircraft into the airline’s United Next cabin program. That’s a strong indication they’re sticking around for years, even as United replaces a different part of its 757 fleet with new Airbus aircraft. Jon reports that the 757-300 modification includes: Boeing Space Bins, providing more overhead storage. Panasonic on-demand entertainment at every seat. A full cabin in-seat power system. New cabin dividers, headers and United branding. Refreshed seats and cabin fixtures throughout the aircraft. JonNYC’s report on United’s Boeing 757-300 cabin upgrades — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 10, 2026 He says the delay involved getting larger bins certified for this particular version of the 757. Going through that work for the 21 airplanes is a substantial commitment. The current 757-300 cabin relies on entertainment streamed to your own device. The planes already have power. Screens and larger bins are big improvements. The Specific 757-300 Plan Is New United’s broad promise to upgrade its domestic cabins goes back to the original United Next announcement in June 2021. Back then, they said the retrofit would be 99% complete by summer 2025. That… didn’t happen. When United placed their huge 2021 aircraft order, Andrew Nocella said it wasn’t intended to replace the 757-300s. What’s been missing is a concrete upgrade plan for a small fleet that kept flying with a noticeably older product while hundreds of other aircraft received new interiors. Now we know the plan, and why it took so long. United’s Two 757 Fleets Have Different Futures The 757-300 is the long, high-capacity domestic aircraft. The shorter 757-200 is the one associated with United’s thin transatlantic routes and premium transcontinental flying. United Aircraft Fleet Current Seats Plan Boeing 757-300 21 234, including 24 domestic first class United Next cabin upgrade reported by JonNYC Boeing 757-200 40 176, including 16 lie-flat business class Replacement flying by Airbus A321XLRs and A321neo Coastliners United’s last annual report put the average age of the -300s at 23.3 years at the end of 2025, versus 28.9 years for the -200s. United also owns all 21 of the stretched planes. In March, United laid out that premium Airbus narrowbodies would replace the flying of 40 Boeing 757-200s. United’s first A321XLR entered domestic service in September. I’ve covered how the A321XLR changes the economics of those thinner international routes. United’s have 150 seats, including 20 business class and 12 premium economy seats. American accelerated its 757 retirement in 2020, eliminating an aircraft type and the associated training and maintenance costs. American never operated the -300. How The 757 Became So Hard To Replace The 757 entered service in 1983 as a more efficient replacement for the Boeing 727. It combined two engines, a two-pilot cockpit and a new wing with the ability to operate from demanding airports. Boeing developed it alongside the 767, with closely related cockpits allowing pilots to qualify on both. It became useful for far more than its original domestic role: busy trunk routes, transcontinental flights, Hawaii, leisure flying and eventually thinner routes across the Atlantic. The combination of payload, range and strong performance on shorter runways and at hot or high-altitude airports gave airlines options that weren’t available from smaller narrowbodies. Approvals for extended overwater flying helped open transatlantic routes. Continental used the 757-200 to connect Newark with European cities that couldn’t support a bigger airplane. Winter headwinds meant that United was said to operate focus cities at Goose Bay and Gander. But selling enough seats to support a 757 was easier than filling a widebody. The -300 entered service in 1999 with Condor, adding 23 feet, 4 inches of fuselage to carry more passengers, with less range than the -200. Only 55 were built. Continental took its first 757-300 in December 2001, initially deploying it on domestic routes from Newark. Familiar routes include Chicago–San Francisco, Chicago–Los Angeles and Washington Dulles–Los Angeles. It’s an unusually long airplane with just one aisle. United’s regular domestic A321neo carries 200 passengers. Its 757-300 carries 234, including four more first class seats. That’s 34 additional customers on one departure. An A321 can be configured much more densely, but United couldn’t simply swap in its current domestic Airbus cabin and preserve that capacity. The Airbus A321XLR comes closest to replacing the 757’s longer missions. And its advertised range of up to 4,700 nautical miles exceeds the 757’s. The missing airplane is one that combines all the desired capacity, runway performance, payload and operating economics. I recently wrote about Scott Kirby complaining that he’s been asking for a 757 replacement for more than 20 years. Boeing studied a new middle-of-the-market airplane, often called the “797,” but never launched it. Boeing ended 757 production in 2004 and delivered the last aircraft in 2005. United Next Is Still A Work In Progress The cabin program has made substantial progress since I covered the first Airbus retrofit in early 2023, but the original summer 2025 finish slipped badly. United reported more than 530 new and retrofitted aircraft with its signature interior at the end of 2025. In March 2026, they said 70% of the narrowbody retrofit plan was complete. The most recent broader measure is from last week: more than 181,000 seatback screens, covering about 85% of the mainline fleet. That includes aircraft with older entertainment systems, so it isn’t an 85% completion figure for United Next. On the October 21 earnings call, Nocella said United expects to finish installing its signature cabins, including screens, larger bins and new lighting, by the end of 2027. Starlink Is Coming To The 757s, But None Are Equipped Yet United’s official Starlink tracker, updated November 11, shows: 691 aircraft equipped: 352 regional jets, 332 mainline narrowbodies and seven widebodies. 54% of daily flights operating with Starlink. The tracker shows 46% completion of its aircraft installation program. All 61 Boeing 757s listed as “coming soon.” None is shown with Starlink installed. That includes the 21 757-300s. So they’re in the plan. I’ve covered United’s accelerated Starlink installation plans. Their latest targets are coverage of 61% of departures by the end of this year, 87% by June 1, 2027, and completion of the fleet rollout by the end of 2027. For now, a United 757 still means the older internet. United’s tracker lets you check a specific flight within three days of departure. According to aviation watchdog JonNYC, the work will bring the aircraft into the airline’s United Next cabin program. That’s a strong indication they’re sticking around for years, even as United replaces a different part of its 757 fleet with new Airbus aircraft.

Jon reports that the 757-300 modification includes:

JonNYC’s report on United’s Boeing 757-300 cabin upgrades — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 10, 2026

He says the delay involved getting larger bins certified for this particular version of the 757. Going through that work for the 21 airplanes is a substantial commitment.

The current 757-300 cabin relies on entertainment streamed to your own device. The planes already have power. Screens and larger bins are big improvements.

no, Andy, I have repeatedly said that Scotty Kirby has a severe case of FOMO which is why he holds onto every airplane so UA DOES keep growing everything but its bottom line.

#6187. JetBlue’s New First Class Is Missing A Cabin Divider… But Why?!?

In the coming weeks, JetBlue will be introducing a domestic first class product for the first time, which will be known as BlueFirst. This is an exciting and long overdue development, and I trust it will help JetBlue’s revenue performance, especially given how efficiently planes are being reconfigured (by reducing legroom in economy).

The first aircraft has now been retrofitted with the new cabins, and it appears that JetBlue had a media day today for this showing off both the new hard and soft product. We already largely knew what to expect, but what stands out to me is the one thing that’s missing, which I really can’t make sense of.

I don’t want to bury the lede here, so let me get right to it — on planes with BlueFirst, JetBlue won’t have any sort of a cabin divider between first class and the rest of the cabin. It’s not just that there isn’t a curtain, but there’s not even a divider hanging from the overhead bins.

JetBlue unveiled its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country’s carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.Read more: https://t.co/5o3k2Ru5R9 pic.twitter.com/1BTcLVOr7s

I guess this also explains the very creative angles of the renderings that have been released up until now, which clearly try to avoid highlighting this reality.

I really can’t make sense of this decision. I know we no longer live in an era where there are real, full bulkheads between cabins, since that’s not efficient. But just installing a small, flimsy divider, along with a curtain, costs very little, doesn’t weigh a lot, etc.

To be clear, this isn’t about “oh, I don’t want to be seen by anyone.” Instead, it’s about managing traffic to and from the forward lavatory. At US airlines, the most common policy is that on domestic flights, you can use any lavatory onboard the aircraft, even in a different cabin. There are some exceptions, including for JetBlue Mint, but that’s also easier to enforce thanks to how the A321 is configured, with a lavatory behind Mint, in front of economy.

I’m not sure if JetBlue intends to reserve the forward lavatory for BlueFirst passengers, but either way, you can expect there will be a steady stream of passengers lining up to use the forward lavatory. So it’s not even about potentially not having a dedicated lavatory, but instead it’s about just constantly having people standing in the aisle right by your seat. This will also make the life of the first class flight attendant more difficult.

Take Aer Lingus AerSpace, for example, which is Aer Lingus’ premium product on short haul flights in Europe. It’s simply the first row of seats with blocked middles, and no divider between that and the rest of the plane. The problem is that if you’re seated in the aisle in AerSpace, you basically just have someone’s butt in your face the entire flight. You’re almost better off not booking the product, just to avoid that.

Anyway, I can’t really make sense of this decision, so I’d be fascinated to know what the logic was. There’s not another US airline with first class that has no separation between first class and economy. Spirit’s “Big Front Seat” didn’t have any divider, but that also wasn’t first class — it was just an, ummm, big front seat.

Similarly, Breeze Airways’ “Nicest” product also doesn’t have a divider, but it’s also not a separate cabin.

CNBC’s Phil Le Beau was onboard JetBlue’s first BlueFirst A320 with CEO Joanna Geraghty. I like Le Beau, but this interview is also the perfect example of why I just don’t really value interviewing airline executives in a traditional sense.

Le Beau asked Geraghty a good question — “did you wait too long to add a first class?” If we are being honest, there’s only one correct answer, which is OF COURSE. Like, unarguably, JetBlue was at least years late, if not a decade late, to introducing first class. That’s not even Geraghty’s fault, it’s that previous CEO Robin Hayes was perhaps one of the least focused CEOs the US airline industry has ever seen.

Geraghty’s answer, though, was “I don’t think we’ve waited too long, we’ve had Mint for a very long time, it just takes time with some of these products to roll them out.” I get it — nobody wants to be, like “we screwed up and waited too long, but I mainly blame the guy before me.”

Seriously, though, if she really doesn’t think JetBlue waited too long to commit to introducing first class, then I’d question how observant the executive team has been of the industry. I mean, Frontier announced it would introduce first class before JetBlue, which should tell you all you need to know. Oh, and Frontier will even have divider, even if it doesn’t have recline, food, or drinks!

Also, the below screen grab from the interview gave me a chuckle…

JetBlue’s BlueFirst class is entering service soon, which is exciting. I’m a huge fan of JetBlue, and I think historically they’ve done a great job with both their hard and soft product, and have great attention to detail. So I’m just a bit puzzled as to how they came to the conclusion that there was no need to introduce a cabin divider between first class and economy.

JetBlue will be the first airline in the US with first class to not have any sort of a cabin divider, and I can’t make sense of that.

What do you make of JetBlue’s odd cabin divider decision?

This is petty, but I still think they should’ve gone with “Junior Mint” (though the resulting IP lawsuit probably wouldn’t have been worth it, financially.)

I wouldn't be surprised if this was due to a FAA certification issue

#6186. United Airlines Bans “AI Agents,” Claims It’s To “Protect Customers”

United Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this). That’s an interesting stance for United, easily the country’s most tech savvy airline, to take. So what’s actually going on here?

United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket. In the section about prohibited practices at the airline, the carrier added the following:

The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.

The “AI Agents” term is defined by United as follows:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual. AI Agents include but are not limited to: (i) AI assistants built into social media, messaging, search or other consumer platforms; (ii) AI-enabled browsers and standalone AI agents; and (iii) any third-party AI assistant that accesses United through a tool, application or connection provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

United even put out a press release about this change, claiming that it’s making the change to “protect” customers. Here’s part of the explanation:

Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles. Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations – as an example, flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

United claims it’s taking steps to restrict this kind of access, both directly within its digital platforms, and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third party personal AI agents or assistants.

It goes without saying that use of AI is becoming exponentially more popular in recent times, and is a force to be reckoned with. It’s anyone’s guess just how far it goes, in terms of how much the average person uses it in their everyday life.

There are certainly aspects of AI that are incredibly annoying, whether you look at it as an individual or a business. Admittedly I’m biased, but I’m so tired of feeling like half of what I’m reading online (whether on social media or websites) is written by a computer and not a human. It even extends to things like TripAdvisor reviews.

It’s also frustrating how many people write 30 paragraph emails nowadays, which are clearly 90% AI. I don’t really understand how that makes anyone’s life better. As far as I’m concerned, just give me the bullet points you fed your AI buddy, and we’ll all be better off for it. Anyway, rant over, back to United…

I suspect United’s real motive here is that it doesn’t want AI automatically being able to track and reprice flights (and then issue vouchers for passengers), or being able to too closely compare overall value on different airlines. For that matter, it probably just doesn’t want a third party getting that much data on the airline, not to mention that all of this can take a considerable toll on servers, if this scales.

But here’s what I find most interesting — the way this rule is written strikes me as being incredibly broad, no? Not to repeat the quote again, but this is the part I’m referencing, in particular:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual.

Any software that automatically “discovers” or searches for any product or service offered by United would include all award search tools (along with all kinds of other businesses), no? Is that actually the intent here, or does United just plan to selectively enforce rules? We did see Air Canada engage in a battle over this a few years back, so is United planning something similar?

United Airlines has today updated its rules to ban “AI Agents,” and the airline even put out a press release about it. The company claims it’s making this change to protect customers and their accounts, as AI bots could have unintended consequences.

Many people are understandably skeptical of that explanation, as I imagine the airline also wants to ban these kinds of things to help people reprice tickets, get better fares, etc. For that matter, based on how broadly the definition is written, it seems that even things like award search engines would be banned.

AI agents would have a terrible look to book ratio, which will drive up costs for the airline. This has been around for travel agents for years. If we shop too much but book to little, we'll get reprimanded. Since that can't be done with bots, they have to be stopped somehow from shopping around too much. A human can perform only a limited number of searches at a time, whereas bots theoretically could search indefinitely. That would bring server and CRS costs go through the roof.

This seems pretty clear to stop an AI agent that would auto rebook the flight as it gets cheaper.

Horse has bolted. UA might as well get used to the flood and find a way to integrate such searches into its business. we are quickly heading to a future where your personal bot will be shopping from the merchants' bots.

There seems to be little discussion of when an airline's website makes the mistake. For a long period, BA Avios award searches for AA flights always reverted to the prior day rather than the date selected. I assumed this had to do with the time difference but whatever. I can clearly state that BA took no responsibility for any bookings based on their website error. The actual penalty was diminimus so i and I assumed others let it pass.

People seem to think there is this gray area if a bot or AI makes a mistake on your behalf. If a bot books the wrong date, destination, class or number of checked bags, that is all on you. You will be the one stuck with the consequences.

#6185. Bank Of America’s No Annual Fee Card Pays 6% In Year One — Here’s The Best Way To Use It

The Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards credit card pays 6% back in a category you choose during your first year, with no annual fee. That can include online shopping, phone and internet bills, or home repairs. Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards‘ initial bonus offer is a $200 online cash rewards bonus after you make at least $1,000 in purchases in the first 90 days of account opening. I like finding worthwhile cards outside the familiar bank discussions. More competition is good, and a card can deserve some of your spending without replacing everything else in your wallet. What The Card Currently Offers The standard consumer card has: No annual fee. A $200 initial bonus after $1,000 in purchases within 90 days of account opening. 6% in your selected category during the first year: the normal 3% plus a temporary extra 3%. 2% at grocery stores and wholesale clubs. 1% on other purchases. The higher rates all share a $2,500 quarterly spending allowance; once you’ve used it, those purchases earn 1% too. Banking relationship bonuses can increase earning. For the choice earning category, you can select among gas and electric vehicle charging; online shopping, including cable, internet, phone plans and streaming; dining; travel; drug stores and pharmacies; or home improvement and furnishings. You can change your category once each calendar month for future purchases. Leave it alone and your selection carries forward. It starts out as gas and charging, so someone getting the card for online shopping needs to change that setting. Earning scales withBofA RewardsTM based on qualifying funds with the bank: Relationship Tier And Qualifying Balance Choice Category, First Year Choice Category, Afterward Groceries And Wholesale Clubs Other Spending / After Cap Not enrolled 6% 3% 2% 1% Member: no minimum balance 6.3% 3.3% 2.2% 1.1% Preferred Plus: $30,000+ 6.75% 3.75% 2.5% 1.25% Preferred Honors: $100,000+ 7.5% 4.5% 3% 1.5% Premier: $1 million+ 8.25% 5.25% 3.5% 1.75% The first three rewards columns remain subject to the shared quarterly spending limit. The banking program requires enrollment and an eligible personal checking account. Higher tiers generally use your combined qualifying average balances over three months. The relationship bonuses are 10%, 25%, 50% and 75%. They apply to the normal earnings, while the extra 3% first-year bonus isn’t multiplied. (At the highest tier the calculation is 3% × 1.75 + 3% = 8.25%, not 10.5%). Qualifying Merrill investments, including eligible retirement accounts, count toward the balance requirement. You don’t have to leave $100,000 sitting in a checking account. Online Shopping And Home Improvement Are My Preferred Categories For someone who already has good travel cards, I’d look first at purchases those cards don’t bonus. Online shopping would be my default selection. Bank of America’s category definitions include purchases through websites and apps, plus cable, internet, phone plans and streaming. Merchant examples include Amazon, Walmart, Etsy and Ticketmaster. That covers purchases across different merchants with one selection, and you can combine eligible shopping portal rewards with the cash back from paying by card. Online shopping has exclusions: taxes, insurance, medical bills, tuition, utilities and various non-retail services don’t become bonus purchases by paying on the website. Home improvement and furnishings. The bank includes qualifying contractors such as plumbers and electricians, alongside furniture and hardware stores. I’d keep online shopping selected most of the time and switch before paying for a repair or furniture purchase. Travel is useful, especially in the first year. The bank includes airlines and hotels, but also cruises, vacation rentals, attractions, transit and parking. You can book directly rather than going through a bank’s travel portal. That makes it worth considering for a domestic vacation rental or cruise payment. I earn well with other cards on airfare and hotels, but bonusing short-term rentals and cruises can fill a gap. How I’d Fit It Into A Travel Rewards Wallet I’d rate this 4 out of 5 as a spending category specialist for someone who can use the first-year offer or who qualifies for elevated banking rewards. It’s best for someone with online purchases or home improvement bills that otherwise earn an ordinary return. The standard card charges a 3% foreign transaction fee. This is for domestic purchases. And even the highest relationship tier pays just 1.75% on ordinary spending and after the cap, less than a straightforward 2% card. You can redeem cash back for statement credits without a minimum, or deposit it into eligible Bank of America or Merrill accounts. Checks, qualifying Merrill 529 contributions and automatic redemptions have $25 minimums. Rewards don’t expire while the account remains open. I’d take the cash. It can pay award ticket taxes, a hotel outside a chain, or anything else.
