#6184. Here's How The Airbus A350 Stacks Up Against Boeing's 777X For The Next Decade Of Long-Haul Flying

The two powerhouses of aerospace that divide the global industry of jetliner building are locked in a years-long struggle for domination of the next-generation widebody airliner market. Boeing has promised to revolutionize the size and scale of twinjets with its 777X, which integrates the legacy 'triple seven' airframe with 787 Dreamliner technology and industry-first folding wingtips. Meanwhile, Airbus has already delivered many A350 jets and is now working on an ultra-long-range variant.

The problem for Boeing is the fact that all three variants of this 777X remain uncertified for full-scale production. Seven years after the original launch date, it still has just a handful of examples sitting on the flight line in Washington; there are no jets ready to be delivered. Airbus may not have handed over many of its largest A350 variants, but the airframe has proven itself in revenue service and remains in full-rate production with continued orders coming in.

The A350 represents a lightweight, highly optimized, all-composite platform built for flexible point-to-point networks, while the 777X is a massive, metal-composite hybrid giant designed to unlock maximum passenger and cargo volume on high-density trunk routes. Boeing aims to have the 777-8 and 777-9 certified next year, but Airbus will already be moving on to deliver Qantas' A350-1000ULR for the unique 'Project Sunrise' that will pressure any new era of ultra-long-haul flying.

The next decade of long-haul flying will be defined by how airlines choose to route their passengers. Airbus has optimized the A350 family for a fragmented market, betting that travelers prefer direct, point-to-point flights between mid-tier cities. Because the A350 is inherently lighter due to its carbon-fiber fuselage, it does not suffer a massive financial penalty if a flight is only 70% full, giving the carrier 'right-sized' versatility to open new, experimental long-range routes.

On paper, the 777X’s massive engines, the largest commercial turbofans in the world, achieve a 10% reduction in fuel burn per seat compared to older legacy aircraft, closely rivaling the A350-1000's efficiency. Thanks to its revolutionary wing design, the 777X can fit into gates where the 747 and A380 could not, yet it maintains a worse fuel efficiency baseline than the A350. The A350-1000 does not suffer from this scaling penalty.

The 777X wing is so wide that Boeing had to engineer a revolutionary folding wingtip mechanism that retracts 11.5 feet (3.5 meters) on each side upon landing. Boeing also had to design that wing to support a staggering maximum takeoff weight of 716,000 lb (325,000 kg) and General Electric GE9X engines delivering 105,000 lb of thrust (467 kN) each. Because the 777X is significantly heavier than the A350, its advantages only begin when it is full.

The A350 relies on a lighter, all-composite fuselage to cut fuel burn, and Airbus limited its wingspan to 212 feet (64.7 meters). While this shorter span yields a slightly less optimized ratio than the 777X, Airbus offsets the deficit by constructing 53% of the entire airframe, including the fuselage, out of carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic.

Airbus also integrated bifunctional winglet technology that actively twists and morphs the trailing edges of the wing during flight via the fly-by-wire system. This continuous, automated optimization reduces drag in real time as fuel burns off. Such granular engineering ensures the A350 remains efficient across various mission profiles, whereas the 777X requires specific capacity thresholds to justify its heavier airframe.

The commercial aviation industry has definitively entered a post-quadjet era, leaving the 777X to claim an uncontested monopoly as the absolute largest passenger aircraft in production. By designing the 777X to seat up to 450 passengers, Boeing is betting that mega-hub congestion will compel airlines to buy the massive twinjets. Airbus, conversely, has intentionally conceded the capacity crown, positioning the A350-1000 as the "right-sized flagship designed to align perfectly with the average demand of a point-to-point market.

The 777-9 was specifically designed by Boeing to be a direct replacement for the 747. The 777-9 fills the void left by the retirement of the double-deck jumbo aircraft, aiming for an astounding 33% lower operational cost per seat than the legendary 747-400. Additionally, because of its folding wingtips, it may enter regular Code E gates instead of just Code F gates designed for the A380, increasing destination alternatives and lowering operating costs.

Qatar Airways, British Airways, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, Riyadh Air, Philippine Airlines, Air Canada, China Airlines, Japan Airlines, Etihad Airways, Virgin Atlantic, Air France, Ethiopian Airlines

Atlas Air, Air France-KLM, Etihad Airways, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Cargo, Air China Cargo

Emirates, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Etihad Airways, British Airways, All Nippon Airways, Air India

Qatar Airways Cargo, Cargolux, Korean Air Cargo, Lufthansa Cargo, All Nippon Airways Cargo, Ethiopian Airlines

In the meantime, Airbus built the A350-1000 with the idea that networks with scattered city pairings, rather than expansive hub-to-hub airways, are the way of the future for long-haul aviation. Rather than squeezing 450 people onto a single mega-twinjet, Airbus scaled down the A350-1000 to a more modest 350 to 410 seats. Outside of specific mega-hubs, the A350's smaller size offers less risk and more flexibility, allowing airlines to operate varying long-haul routes even during off-peak seasons.

Hub-centric airlines that rely on maximum volume to conquer slot constraints remain entrenched in the 777X concept. Emirates alone anchors the program with a massive backlog of 270 units to preserve its mass-transit business model. However, with the vast majority of international carriers expanding their networks, Airbus’ biggest twinjet is sweeping the market. Recently, airlines like Riyadh Air firmed up their orders to 31 A350-1000s, Philippine Airlines doubled its commitment to 18, and Air Canada finalized a fleet pivot to eight of the type.

The aircraft has exceptional ultra-long-range capabilities.

Airbus enjoys an absolute, uncontested monopoly on the extreme frontiers of commercial aviation, in large part thanks to the A350-1000ULR being chosen for Qantas’s upcoming 'Project Sunrise' nonstop flights connecting Sydney to London and New York. As the first completed example progresses through its flight testing campaigns ahead of its April 2027 delivery to Qantas, Airbus is reinforcing a halo status for the entire A350 program.

By capturing the contract for the most demanding mission of the decade, Airbus has proven that its jet can adapt to any point on the globe. Thanks to an ultra-light 53% composite airframe with a heavily stripped-down, low-density cabin, Airbus had the extra payload margin to permanently mount a 35,274-lb (16,000 kg) Rear Center Tank. That pushes the plane’s range to an unparalleled 9,700 nautical miles (17,900 km).

Its composite airframe gives the A350-1000 a massive 'weight budget' advantage, but Airbus is swapping the weight of 170 passengers for the RCT, which makes the ULR variant possible. Even with a carbon-fiber airframe, flying 10,000 nautical miles (18,520 km) requires further weight sacrifices, which is why Qantas’s Project Sunrise configuration is strictly limited to a low-density layout of just 238 seats. Meanwhile, the 777X is incapable of playing this low-density weight game because it is trapped by its own size.

When Boeing unveiled the 777X program, the aerospace industry took note.

The 777X's conventional widebody cross-section is positioned to dominate the lower-yield freight markets of the upcoming ten years, even while passenger capacity takes center stage. The 777X specifically increases its capacity for large, containerized cargo, which enables airlines to make money on long-haul flights even when passenger cabins are only partially filled. A 777-9 can transport up to 40 standard LD3 cargo containers on profitable freight corridors around the Pacific, surpassing the A350-1000's 44 lower-volume position limit.

The 777X can transport enormous, tall, and oddly shaped cargo pallets that fit in the A350's hold thanks to its 10% volumetric advantage. For airlines like Cathay Pacific or Singapore Airlines, this under-floor freight capability represents the thin margin between a profitable flight and a loss-making one when passenger load factors dip. The Airbus A350 utilizes a unique ovoid, or egg-shaped, fuselage cross-section designed primarily to maximize passenger shoulder space in the main cabin.

Mothballed giants are coming back online.

The sharp differences in delivery schedules are the most obvious division in this ten-year contest. With more than 600 aircraft now in active service, the Airbus A350 is a well-established, fully approved program that enables airlines like Delta and Lufthansa to regularly plan fleet renewals. On the other hand, Boeing's current goal of having the 777-9 enter service in 2027 comes after a startling seven-year delay from its initial 2020 launch schedule.

The 737 MAX disaster and the Federal Aviation Administration audit that followed, which took away a large portion of Boeing's previously granted compliance power, are directly responsible for this bottleneck. The FAA now enforces an unprecedented level of independent verification. Compounding this regulatory inertia, GE Aerospace has faced rigorous scrutiny over a durability flaw regarding an engine seal in the massive GE9X powerplants, demanding extensive engineering fixes.

The visible consequence of this certification bottleneck is vividly on display across storage airfields in Everett and Moses Lake, Washington, where more than 30 fully assembled Boeing 777-9 jets sit parked in limbo. Boeing currently faces a significant mechanical challenge in the form of change incorporation as a result of its decision to maintain low-rate manufacture of 'at-risk' airframes before completing the drawn-out certification procedure.

Even ardent, traditionally exclusive Boeing operators are carefully hedging their long-haul bets in the interim. By methodically taking advantage of Boeing's structural weakness, Airbus has made the fully developed and certified A350 program the standard long-haul architecture for the late 2020s. Airbus' overall firm order book for the A350 family has increased to 1,628 total orders, whereas Boeing has written off nearly $15 billion in pre-tax charges because of development failures and client compensation.

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

If you fly United Airlines regularly, the (see rates and fees) can be a powerful way to earn more miles and reduce your out-of-pocket travel costs.

As someone who frequently flies United, I've found that the Quest hits a practical middle ground. It offers meaningful airline perks, including a $200 annual United TravelBank credit, two free checked bags and discounts on award flights, without the hefty annual fee of a premium airline card.

But with a $350 annual fee, the Quest isn't necessarily right for everyone.

Here's who I think can get the most value from the card and who might be better off with another option.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

New United Quest cardholders can currently earn 500 PQP after their first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, you can earn another 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg United miles at 1.2 cents apiece, the full 90,000-mile bonus is worth $1,080. That's not including the additional value of the 500 PQP, which can help you get closer to United Premier status.

While not the strongest offer we've seen in the card's history, it's still a great time to apply if you've already been considering the Quest, particularly if you have upcoming United travel planned.

There's a lot to love about the . Here's who will benefit most from having the card.

If you fly United several times per year, you'll want to take a closer look at the Quest.

That’s because many of the card’s most valuable perks are tied directly to flying United. Cardholders receive:

One of the card's strongest perks is its earning structure. The United Quest earns a strong 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights as a United MileagePlus member — that's a whopping 12% return, according to TPG's valuations (mileage earning may differ for basic economy and base option tickets).

As someone who holds Premier Silver status, I can earn a total of 12 miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights when using my Quest, which is an even better return.

But what I find especially valuable are the discounts United cardholders now receive when booking award flights. Eligible United cardholders without Premier status save at least 10% on qualifying United-operated award flights, while cardholders with Premier status save at least 15%.

I take advantage of these discounts pretty regularly. Recently, I booked two tickets from Washington, D.C.'s Dulles International Airport (IAD) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for a mother-daughter trip to Europe. Thanks to my cardholder discount, each ticket cost just 34,000 miles plus $11.20 in taxes and fees, rather than 45,000 miles plus taxes and fees.

That's a savings of 11,000 miles per ticket, or 22,000 miles total, worth $264 according to TPG's valuations.

The Quest also offers two additional award flight discounts: 10,000 miles beginning with your first card anniversary and another 10,000 miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

I recently used my 10,000-mile award flight discount toward a transatlantic flight from Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) to IAD. The flight would have cost 34,000 miles, but the credit brought it down to just 24,000 miles plus $112.83 in taxes and fees.

That's another $120 worth of miles saved, based on TPG's valuations.

Between the cardholder award pricing discounts and the annual award flight credits, the Quest gives me several ways to stretch my United miles further, which is why it's a card I plan to keep in my wallet long-term.

Related: United unveils huge MileagePlus shake-up, rewarding cardholders with higher earn rates

This is one of the most underrated — and potentially most valuable — perks of the United Quest Card.

The card includes two free checked bags for you and a companion on the same reservation. On domestic economy flights, United typically charges $50 ($45 if prepaid) for the first checked bag and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second bag.

That means you could pay up to $110 per person each way if you check two bags without a card benefit.

If you and a companion each check two bags round-trip on just one domestic flight, that could cost up to $440 total. That alone covers the Quest Card’s $350 annual fee.

Personally, I frequently fly United and regularly check two bags free thanks to my Quest Card. For travelers who often travel with a companion, don’t pack light, take longer trips or occasionally travel with bulkier items like skis or golf clubs, this benefit alone can justify holding the card year after year.

Related: These 27 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight

Each account anniversary, the Quest Card provides $200 in United TravelBank cash. This credit can be used toward United-operated flights and is automatically deposited into your TravelBank account.

I recently used my $200 TravelBank credit to offset the cost of a round-trip flight from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to IAD to visit family. The ticket originally cost $560, but my TravelBank credit brought my out-of-pocket cost down to $360.

And the TravelBank credit isn't the only statement credit available with the Quest.

Cardholders can also receive other statement credits, including:

I wouldn't go out of my way to use a credit just to justify the card's annual fee, but if you're already spending money with these merchants, they can provide some additional savings.

For me, the TravelBank credit is the easiest to use. When you subtract its $200 value from the Quest's $350 annual fee, that leaves an effective cost of $150 — assuming you can use the credit in full — before factoring in free checked bags, award flight discounts and other benefits.

If you're working toward United Premier status, the Quest Card can also help you get there.

Cardholders can earn 1 PQP for every $20 spent on purchases with the card, up to 18,000 PQP per calendar year.

Those PQP count toward United Premier status qualification, potentially helping you close the gap to your next status tier.

Plus, beginning in 2027, eligible United cardholders will receive a head start on status qualification. United will deposit PQP equivalent to 5% of the amount required for their current Premier status tier into their accounts at the start of the year. That means Premier Silver members, for example, will receive a 300-PQP boost.

I earned United Premier Silver status for the first time last year, and I've already secured it again for next year, thanks in part to the PQP boost I received at the beginning of the year and the PQP I've earned through flying and spending on my Quest.

I generally don't put much spending on the card outside of United purchases, since I have other cards that earn more flexible rewards on everyday expenses. However, I did intentionally increase my Quest spending over the past few months to earn the additional PQP I needed to secure Silver for another year.

For me, that was worth it because I regularly fly United and appreciate the benefits that come with Premier status.

Of course, I wouldn't recommend putting unnecessary purchases on a card just to earn PQP. But if you're already close to qualifying for status, the Quest can give you another way to get there.

The United Quest Card is a strong step up from the (see rates and fees) — especially for travelers who fly United more than once or twice per year.

The Explorer is a great entry-level option, with a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150) and useful perks like a free checked bag and two one-time United Club passes each year. For occasional United flyers, that may be all you need.

But if you’re booking multiple United flights annually and check bags or redeem miles, the Quest’s incremental perks can quickly outweigh the difference in annual fees and deliver stronger long-term value.

In short, the Explorer fits the occasional flyer. The Quest is designed for frequent United travelers who can maximize its recurring value.

While the is packed with benefits for United fans and frequent travelers, there are a few reasons why the card might not be the right fit. Let's take a deeper look at who the card isn't the right fit for.

While the United Quest Card has many travel-related benefits, it does not come with any lounge privileges, and you don’t get any guest passes.

If lounge access is a priority, the (see rates and fees) may be a better fit. It includes a United Club membership as part of its annual fee, which grants access for the primary cardholder and eligible guests.

And for those who don't want to pay the United Club's steep $695 annual fee, remember that the offers two guest passes annually for a much more approachable fee ($0 introductory; $150 after the first year).

That said, not everyone needs airline-specific lounge access. For example, I personally get lounge access through the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so I don’t need the Quest Card to provide that benefit.

While the number of Capital One lounges is limited, the Venture X also includes a Priority Pass lounge membership (at participating lounges), so I rarely feel short on options.

If you also already have lounge access through another premium travel card, the lack of United Club access here may not matter.

Related: Is the United Club Card annual fee worth it?

The United Quest Card is subject to Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you’ve opened five or more personal credit cards across all issuers in the past 24 months, you’re unlikely to be approved.

If you’re currently over 5/24, you may need to wait — or consider a card from another issuer.

Related: Chase's 5/24 rule: Everything you need to know

The United Quest Card earns United MileagePlus miles. If you don’t regularly fly United — or you prefer more flexibility in how you redeem your rewards — a transferable points or miles card could be a better option.

Flexible points and miles can typically be transferred to multiple airline and hotel partners or redeemed in other ways, giving you more options.

Two strong alternatives with significantly lower annual fees include:

If you value flexibility over airline-specific perks, one of those cards may be a better long-term fit.

If you fly United multiple times per year, check bags regularly and can easily use the $200 annual TravelBank credit, the United Quest Card’s ongoing perks can quickly offset much of its $350 annual fee.

However, if you prioritize lounge access, prefer flexible points or miles over airline-specific miles or only fly United occasionally, another card — either within United’s lineup or outside of it — may be a better fit.

Ultimately, the Quest Card shines for travelers who are loyal enough to United to benefit from its airline perks but don’t need the full premium treatment of a club membership.

#6182. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby Bans AI Agents From Booking Tickets, Doesn’t Want “Another Middleman”

“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.”

I get that they want to negotiate the terms before a new company gets between United and its customers. But United can’t just decide that customers will have to do the work themselves and expect that all customers will go ahead and do the work to buy tickets from United when it becomes easier just to buy from someone else. And writing a ban into a contract doesn’t mean United can actually identify an AI booking that comes through Expedia.

United’s November 11 contract of carriage revision adds AI agents to its prohibited ticketing practices. Rule 6.J.6 bans: The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product. The definition includes assistants accessing United through a travel agency or another intermediary. Human supervision or approval doesn’t circumvent that. And its Rule 5.H gives United the right to cancel reservations made, modified or serviced by these agents. The Wall Street Journal says agents can still present United flights and prices. AI research, followed by the customer making a purchase on their own, doesn’t run afoul of United’s rules. United Wouldn’t Know If An AI Agent Bought Through Expedia? Expedia already has a ChatGPT integration. It returns flight and hotel options with prices and availability. Expedia’s current instructions then send the customer to Expedia to complete the purchase. It’s not an autonomous purchase inside ChatGPT, but if an agent completes the purchase on Expedia United just sees an Expedia booking not how the booking was made. United says its systems can identify booking sources. Sure, but that is a non-sequitur. A contractual ban isn’t a technical one. United may push intermediaries to enforce the restriction, but there are lots of intermediaries out there. But we’ve seen airlines go to war with online travel agencies before, cutting off their own sales. The Strongest Case For United Is About Bargaining Power United may want to limit access to its sysems: The next middleman could become expensive. An assistant that decides which flights customers see can eventually demand referral fees, sell placement or favor suppliers that agree to its terms. Sam Altman says that if an AI does this, no one will trust it, and the stakes are too high to compromise trust for a travel commission. Someone has to own the mistakes. An agent can buy the wrong dates, misunderstand a fare restriction or cancel a ticket the customer wanted to keep. Agencies have commercial arrangements for ticketing and servicing. An AI assistant operating a browser may not bring the same accountability. And the law is evolving here. I’ve covered Delta’s own AI canceling a return flight it said it would preserve. Delta acknowledged a bug and restored the itinerary. Shopping consumes resources even when nobody buys. An agent can compare far more combinations than a human. The International Air Transport Association has examined the cost of growing search volumes. But United isn’t banning search, just completing the transaction. United can do this now, but it won’t last. The airline says agent bookings are still rare. That makes this a relatively inexpensive time to withhold permission. Every customer who gets used to buying another airline through an assistant becomes harder to win back. And the same customers most likely to use an AI assistant are the ones most likely to come over to United for Starlink. United has a hub in San Francisco. It’s ultimately not going to work for Scott Kirby to stand athwart history yelling “stop!” Customers Have A Reason To Hire The Bot United’s safety argument is weak. The federal hazardous-materials rule requires passenger notices, including at ticket purchase where practical and at check-in, and passenger acknowledgment in self-service transactions. It doesn’t require the customer to manually complete every other step of a booking. An assistant can stop and ask the passenger to review a disclosure or give a required confirmation. United’s definition still covers an agent whose actions the customer supervises and approves. Nor does accepting an agent have to mean giving unfamiliar software unrestricted use of a MileagePlus password. Visa is developing ways for merchants to recognize approved agents and connect their actions with customer and payment information. The customer’s time is part of the cost of buying a flight. If I can tell an assistant my dates, preferred airports, seat requirements and budget, there’s value in having it compare the choices and handle the purchase. Sometimes United’s schedule will be good enough that consumers will do the extra work. Sometimes another airline will offer a comparable trip and let an assistant finish it. We’ve already seen an airline overestimate its ability to make customers use its preferred distribution channels. American backed away from its plan to deny mileage earning on certain travel agency bookings. Customers didn’t all abandon the agencies and processes they preferred just because American wanted them to. There’s also an obvious reason airlines might dislike an assistant that works well for the passenger. It can compare the total price, recognize benefits the customer already gets from status or a credit card, and decline add-ons that aren’t worth buying. United has the worst value prop of any U.S. airline for basic economy! I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but customers get better tools too. Sam Altman says that if an AI does this, no one will trust it, and the stakes are too high to compromise trust for a travel commission. Someone has to own the mistakes. An agent can buy the wrong dates, misunderstand a fare restriction or cancel a ticket the customer wanted to keep. Agencies have commercial arrangements for ticketing and servicing. An AI assistant operating a browser may not bring the same accountability. And the law is evolving here. I’ve covered Delta’s own AI canceling a return flight it said it would preserve. Delta acknowledged a bug and restored the itinerary. Shopping consumes resources even when nobody buys. An agent can compare far more combinations than a human. The International Air Transport Association has examined the cost of growing search volumes. But United isn’t banning search, just completing the transaction. United can do this now, but it won’t last. The airline says agent bookings are still rare. That makes this a relatively inexpensive time to withhold permission. Every customer who gets used to buying another airline through an assistant becomes harder to win back. And the same customers most likely to use an AI assistant are the ones most likely to come over to United for Starlink. United has a hub in San Francisco. It’s ultimately not going to work for Scott Kirby to stand athwart history yelling “stop!” Customers Have A Reason To Hire The Bot United’s safety argument is weak. The federal hazardous-materials rule requires passenger notices, including at ticket purchase where practical and at check-in, and passenger acknowledgment in self-service transactions. It doesn’t require the customer to manually complete every other step of a booking. An assistant can stop and ask the passenger to review a disclosure or give a required confirmation. United’s definition still covers an agent whose actions the customer supervises and approves. Nor does accepting an agent have to mean giving unfamiliar software unrestricted use of a MileagePlus password. Visa is developing ways for merchants to recognize approved agents and connect their actions with customer and payment information. The customer’s time is part of the cost of buying a flight. If I can tell an assistant my dates, preferred airports, seat requirements and budget, there’s value in having it compare the choices and handle the purchase. Sometimes United’s schedule will be good enough that consumers will do the extra work. Sometimes another airline will offer a comparable trip and let an assistant finish it. We’ve already seen an airline overestimate its ability to make customers use its preferred distribution channels. American backed away from its plan to deny mileage earning on certain travel agency bookings. Customers didn’t all abandon the agencies and processes they preferred just because American wanted them to. There’s also an obvious reason airlines might dislike an assistant that works well for the passenger. It can compare the total price, recognize benefits the customer already gets from status or a credit card, and decline add-ons that aren’t worth buying. United has the worst value prop of any U.S. airline for basic economy! I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but customers get better tools too. #6181. Singapore Airlines Reconsiders New Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-new cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change…

On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the new business class seat design.

In response to this, he reportedly said “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin said this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the new design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”

To state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a new business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

Is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a new business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#6180. Binoche Triumphs over Feminism

The great French actress Juliette Binoche can look at the world around her so naturally that no matter what character she’s playing (whether in Rendezvous, Flight of the Red Balloon, Summer Hours, Certified Cop, Camille Claudel 1915, Let the Sunshine In, Winter Boy, The Taste of Things, or in her Oscar-winning role in The English Patient), she presents a woman in a mode of inquiry.

In Queen at Sea, Binoche portrays middle-aged Amanda, a Frenchwoman living in England who is juggling a marital separation, a teenage daughter, a professorship, and her aged and senile mother, for whom she is responsible. Each aspect of troubled conscience contributes to Amanda/Binoche’s natural beauty. Binoche is a French version of the intelligence and sophistication associated with Irene Dunne in such films as The Awful Truth, Theodora Goes Wild, and Unfinished Business.

The considerable dramatic conflicts in Queen at Sea would be chaotic without Binoche to guide us through. As devised and directed by American filmmaker Lance Hammer, Queen at Sea catches the obstacles faced by Amanda and those closest to her. Starting with Amanda’s shock when she checks in on her senescent mother Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall) and stepfather Martin (Tom Courtenay), only to discover the seniors in flagrante delicto, Hammer’s method is both confrontational and complexly personal. Amanda reacts politically, calling in the state apparatus to resolve unexpected domestic issues. She’s alarmed by consensual sexuality that doesn’t meet her preference. “If we don’t get some help, it will overwhelm us,” she tells her stepfather, whose most eloquent response is to look at her with surprise, then steely anger.

Amanda interferes like the most aggravating Karen in contemporary cinema. But that’s precisely Hammer’s point and Binoche’s artistic venture. Queen at Sea brings to light the imperiousness of feminism that has seized contemporary Western life. Acting out of her own uncertainty, Amanda would be a dislikable pedant, except that she is steadfast and loving in her intentions toward her mother, her stepfather, and her daughter Sara (Florence Hunt) who, in Hammer’s balanced narrative contrast, is just beginning to discover her own sexual nature.

Queen at Sea is a schematic exercise from the first shot of the elderly Leslie and Martin slowly climbing up a public staircase. Everything is a negotiation with progress. That was also the problem with Hammer’s previous film, Ballast (2008), the condescending racial drama set in the American South. Since then, Hammer has been on an artistic sabbatical, teaching in academia until he made this second feature. Like Binoche, Hammer is also in a mode of inquiry, which comes through when Amanda, in professor-speak, belittles Martin’s intimacy with Leslie: “This disinhibition is a consequence of the disease eroding the areas of the brain used to keep the primal instincts in check.”

Martin responds rationally: “Why are you so keen to deprive her of something that gives her comfort, pleasure at a time in her life when she needs them most?” This is a genuinely difficult dilemma, such as few contemporary films have dared. Hammer achieves a level of respectable compassion, yet one can’t help longing for Mike Leigh to step in and rescue it all.

Queen at Sea raises an essential question: Must movies be variations on social issues, or personal experience? Hammer’s art-minded condescension was transparent in Ballast, but it’s more effective here in compositions that depict the emotional friction between Amanda and Sara through Mondrian squares and distance — the space observed on the retirement-home surveillance monitors that capture Leslie’s sexual abuse. Montages of Sara and her wild-haired friends exploring their sexuality pay homage to Brady Corbet’s The Brutalist. (The teens express their “fear of the sublime” while literally searching the world’s structure to find responsibility or freedom.) Through Amanda’s frustration, Lesley’s quiet, and Sara’s naïveté, Hammer probes the sexual intimacy that most feminist filmmakers don’t articulate. (Martin and the male experience are sidelined.)

That the politicization of cinema has been ruinous is apparent in how Queen at Sea improves on such age-themed films as of Away from Her, 45 Years, and Under the Skin. The empathic Hammer rejects the nihilism of Michael Haneke’s Amour, which Americans mistook for a geriatric love story. Inspired by an actress from the French tradition of sexual candor, an empath like Hammer can only provide a heroine who thinks her way past this era’s political clichés.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6179. Air India Cancels 8 Major International Routes: See Full List Now

Since the beginning of 2026, Air India, which is India's largest international airline, has made several changes to its international network. The carrier has added new destinations but has also withdrawn from several long-haul markets such as Chicago, citing high jet fuel prices.

In addition, the Star Alliance member has been transferring several international routes to its low-cost subsidiary, Air India Express. It has particularly been doing so from airports outside its main hubs.

Three of the cuts are to Europe. Perhaps the most notable is its service between Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) and Birmingham Airport (BHX), which ended earlier this month. According to Sabre Market Intelligence data cited by Aviation Week, approximately 207,300 passengers traveled between Birmingham and India in 2025, representing an 8.3% decline from the previous year.

Delhi was the second-largest market, accounting for around 53,600 passengers, behind Amritsar. Another destination the Indian flag carrier has withdrawn from is Vienna International Airport (VIE), which had also served as a stopover for some of its North American flights. This has left the Austrian capital without a nonstop connection to India.

No more direct Delhi flights from Birmingham

Replaced by Air India Express (4x weekly from December)

Replaced by Air India Express (5x weekly)

Replaced by Air India Express (up to 2x daily)

In terms of the numbers, Delhi was Vienna's largest Indian market in 2025, accounting for approximately 68,400 of the 173,500 passengers who traveled between Vienna and Indian cities that year. Elsewhere in Europe, the Star Alliance member has also discontinued its service to Copenhagen, Denmark.

Furthermore, Air India has also completely withdrawn from the international market at Chennai International Airport (MAA). Last year, the airline ended its daily flights to Bandaranaike International Airport (CMB) in Colombo, Sri Lanka. In March, it discontinued its daily service to Dubai International Airport (DXB), followed by its Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) route in May.

The latter had operated twice daily until April but was reduced to a daily service in May. However, Chennai has not lost its nonstop connection to Singapore. The route has been transferred to Air India Express. The low-cost subsidiary resumed twice-daily flights between the two cities on October 25, using its Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft. It had previously served the route until July 2025.

The Dubai route was also transferred to Air India Express, but the carrier operated it only briefly. According to scheduling data from aviation analytics company Cirium, the budget airline operated just seven flights on the route in March, and no nonstop services are currently scheduled between Chennai and Dubai.

Three of these are international long haul routes.

2026 has been a difficult year for airlines worldwide due to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and rising jet fuel prices. For Air India, the situation has been further complicated by Pakistan's airspace closure, which has been in place for Indian airlines since April 2025. These restrictions have particularly affected its long-haul flights from Delhi to Europe and North America.

The airline now has to take lengthy detours over the Arabian Sea, adding up to four hours to flight times and increasing operating costs. As a result, the Star Alliance member has suspended some routes and reduced frequencies to several US destinations.

It has also reported substantial financial losses; it recorded a consolidated net loss of around $2.4 billion (₹22,238 crore) in the 2025–26 financial year. Air India reportedly lost a further $1.12 billion (₹10,500 crore to ₹10,800 crore) between April and September 2026.

The airline is now looking to make changes to its long-haul network. As reported by Eastern Eye, speaking at the Aviation India and South Asia 2026 conference in New Delhi, CEO and Managing Director Tewolde Gebremariam said Air India plans to shift some of its long-haul operations from Delhi to Mumbai as part of a wider network rebalancing. Bengaluru is also being considered as another hub.

#6178. ICE Checked 7 White Men’s IDs At The Airport—Then Arrested A State Trooper

Two ICE agents spent nearly an hour at the Madison, Wisconsin airport looking for a state trooper. Before finding him, they approached at least seven other white men and checked their IDs. Then they handcuffed the 21-year old officer, who had federal permission to work through 2030 and was flying to visit his parents. Newly released surveillance footage shows how the November 5 arrest unfolded. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe was released the following evening after a Republican congressman contacted the Homeland Security secretary. He still faces immigration proceedings. They Went Looking For White People! In Wisconson! The two immigration agents wore baseball caps and hoodies, with no obvious identification on their clothing. They carried manila folders and consulted papers while looking for someone matching Van Der Merwe’s description. The agents approached seven white men visible in the recording, plus another person outside the camera’s view. The men generally looked young, wore everything from sweatpants to business casual, and mostly carried backpacks. They produced ID and were allowed to continue. Two uniformed deputies waited with the agents. Once their target arrived, he handed over identification, spoke with the agents and walked with them to the airport’s entrance doors. An agent handcuffed him there. Van Der Merwe explained that he had a work permit and a pending asylum application, and the agents said they “did not care.” The Government Had Authorized Him To Work Van Der Merwe’s parents brought him from South Africa in March 2019, when he was 14. His original admission permitted a six month stay. His attorney says the family applied for asylum and has spent seven years waiting for an interview. He’s included in his father’s application and holds federal employment authorization through 2030. According to his attorney, he wanted to join the military but couldn’t because of his immigration status. He earned a criminal justice degree at New Mexico Military Institute and went into law enforcement instead. He’s been with the Wisconsin State Patrol since July 13, 2025 He was work-authorized by the federal government but that’s also consistent with a visa overstay, as I explained when ICE arrested Southwest Airlines flight attendant Lorenzo Thompson at Nashville airport. A person can have an unresolved asylum claim, hold a valid employment authorization document, and still face removal proceedings. That’s a pretty upside down world, since the government said he could work here and should allow him to stay pending resolution of asylum – which he’s been waiting for the government to address for years. Homeland Security says Van Der Merwe overstayed his original admission. His lawyer says he’s followed the legal process and has been waiting for the government to decide his case. Federal law allows detention while a removal case is pending. Prior to the Trump administration, a work-authorized individual with a pending asylum claim was essentially considered to be in valid status, and ICE hasn’t alleged any separate crime. The government knows where he lives and works, in a role promoting public safety, so it’s not clear what benefit there is to taking him off a family trip and putting him in jail while his asylum claim remains unresolved. The President now says his approach to immigration has been too harsh. Q: You think your deportation policy went too far? Trump: I think it might be too tough. https://t.co/NKhFjZKxnd — Clash Report (@clashreport) November 8, 2026 Airports Make People Easy To Find TSA likely alerted ICE when he bought his ticket. A May 2025 agreement obtained by American Oversight formalized information sharing between TSA and ICE, including storage of information by ICE. As I wrote in July, passenger information collected for aviation security is being used to locate immigration targets. Homeland Security says it considers people unlawfully present “can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” An airline reservation tells the government where someone plans to be and when. That makes an airport a convenient place to arrest them. But using TSA this way becomes a distraction from its security focus. We’ve already seen a U.S. citizen handcuffed while boarding Delta after being mistaken for a British man, and plainclothes agents abandon an attempted arrest at Las Vegas airport, leaving a traveler with a handcuff attached. Van Der Merwe went to jail and was released November 6 without posting bond after Representative Derrick Van Orden contacted Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Homeland Security says it considers people unlawfully present “can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” An airline reservation tells the government where someone plans to be and when. That makes an airport a convenient place to arrest them. But using TSA this way becomes a distraction from its security focus. We’ve already seen a U.S. citizen handcuffed while boarding Delta after being mistaken for a British man, and plainclothes agents abandon an attempted arrest at Las Vegas airport, leaving a traveler with a handcuff attached. Van Der Merwe went to jail and was released November 6 without posting bond after Representative Derrick Van Orden contacted Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. In Wisconson! The two immigration agents wore baseball caps and hoodies, with no obvious identification on their clothing. They carried manila folders and consulted papers while looking for someone matching Van Der Merwe’s description.

The agents approached seven white men visible in the recording, plus another person outside the camera’s view. The men generally looked young, wore everything from sweatpants to business casual, and mostly carried backpacks. They produced ID and were allowed to continue.

Two uniformed deputies waited with the agents. Once their target arrived, he handed over identification, spoke with the agents and walked with them to the airport’s entrance doors. An agent handcuffed him there.

Van Der Merwe explained that he had a work permit and a pending asylum application, and the agents said they “did not care.”

Van Der Merwe’s parents brought him from South Africa in March 2019, when he was 14. His original admission permitted a six month stay. His attorney says the family applied for asylum and has spent seven years waiting for an interview. He’s included in his father’s application and holds federal employment authorization through 2030. According to his attorney, he wanted to join the military but couldn’t because of his immigration status. He earned a criminal justice degree at New Mexico Military Institute and went into law enforcement instead. He’s been with the Wisconsin State Patrol since July 13, 2025 He was work-authorized by the federal government but that’s also consistent with a visa overstay, as I explained when ICE arrested Southwest Airlines flight attendant Lorenzo Thompson at Nashville airport. A person can have an unresolved asylum claim, hold a valid employment authorization document, and still face removal proceedings. That’s a pretty upside down world, since the government said he could work here and should allow him to stay pending resolution of asylum – which he’s been waiting for the government to address for years. Homeland Security says Van Der Merwe overstayed his original admission. His lawyer says he’s followed the legal process and has been waiting for the government to decide his case. Federal law allows detention while a removal case is pending. Prior to the Trump administration, a work-authorized individual with a pending asylum claim was essentially considered to be in valid status, and ICE hasn’t alleged any separate crime. The government knows where he lives and works, in a role promoting public safety, so it’s not clear what benefit there is to taking him off a family trip and putting him in jail while his asylum claim remains unresolved. #6177. Amex Business Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 300K Points Welcome Offer

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express is one of the most perks-rich business cards out there, and is useful if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 300,000 points are worth a staggering $5,100. As I see it, that’s basically the best welcome offer you’ll find on any card.

Let me emphasize that Amex uses a variety of factors when deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Platinum Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible Amex Business Platinum bonus through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there.

That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method. However, it can always be worth checking back every so often, because the promotions people are targeted for can change over time.

The Amex Business Platinum bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to nearly $6,700 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners. Also keep in mind that having this card lets you unlock the full value of Amex Pay With Points, potentially allowing you to get up to 1.54 cents of value per point toward the cost of airfare on a designated airline (this comes in the form of a 35% Pay with Points rebate, up to one million points per year). You could then use that redemption rate for all your linked Amex Membership Rewards cards.

Just to give a couple of examples of how much value those 300,000 Membership Rewards points could get you:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find the Amex Business Platinum to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Platinum, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). While this isn’t the most rewarding card in terms of the return on spending, it does have a huge number of valuable perks, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the Amex Business Platinum annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

Just to give a sense of the immense value, below is a basic rundown of the Amex Business Platinum credits, which should for many people help offset the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

Of particular note is that the card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits, in the form of a $300 credit semi-annually, and largely helps with offsetting the annual fee. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

When it comes to the Amex Business Platinum rewards structure, the card offers:

There’s another incentive to put at least $250,000 in eligible purchases on the card each calendar year, as that unlocks the following credits, which can be worth up to $3,600:

Read a full review of the Amex Business Platinum Card here.

There’s currently an excellent Amex Business Platinum Card bonus, which is as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points upon completing minimum spending. While the spending requirement is significant, so is the number of points you can earn, so this is worth it if you’re eligible, and can swing it.

This card offers all kinds of great perks that can help offset the annual fee, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status, and more. You can even see what offer you’re eligible for on the card without a hard credit pull, so it’s worth seeing if you qualify, in my opinion.

Do you plan on picking up the Amex Business Platinum Card? What kind of a welcome offer are you eligible for?

The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

It's a question we've been diving deep into at The Points Guy this month (and something we've been debating for years now). Not only has it been harder to get upgrades and more expensive to earn status, but redemptions have gotten more expensive and watered-down benefits have made pursuing status less appealing for many of us at The Points Guy.

But not me. Despite my complaints, I'm still a fan of top-tier status and can't quit the hamster wheel, though I'm not trying for quite so many these days.

I've already requalified for World of Hyatt Globalist status this year, and I'll be able to requalify for top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status. But I will also hold lower-tier status with United MileagePlus, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program and Delta SkyMiles.

In 2027, I'll continue to hold Platinum Elite status in IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy, as well as Hilton Honors Diamond status and Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, just for carrying credit cards.

I even have top-tier status with Starbucks Rewards.

Here's the full breakdown of my elite-status plans for 2027, the credit cards I use to fast-track them, plus some tips to help you achieve your own status goals before the end of the year.

I've held top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage Executive Platinum status on and off for years now. I'm already getting closer to requalifying for 2027, and since the qualification year runs through Feb. 28, I have a few more months to work toward my goal.

So far, I've earned 148,538 Loyalty Points — the metric that AAdvantage members must accrue to earn elite status — toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required to qualify for the Executive Platinum tier. Once I hit that threshold, I'll requalify for perks like a 120% mileage bonus, Group 1 boarding, complimentary food and drinks when traveling in the main cabin and more.

Related: 5 ways to earn more American Airlines Loyalty Points before February ends

Thanks to the airline's Loyalty Point Rewards milestones, I can also hit a few more reward tiers along the way to Executive Platinum status. For example, once I hit 175,000 Loyalty Points, I can choose from a menu of valuable benefits, including two systemwide upgrade certificates.

I'm likely to choose systemwide upgrades again, but the 25,000 bonus miles and the trip credits are probably the best alternate options.

I've already used two systemwide upgrades from coach to business class on AA's transcontinental flight from San Francisco to New York and back. I also just confirmed two more upgrades for upcoming international trips, including a flight to Paris from New York and another from London back to New York.

Holding the (see rates and fees) makes it easier to rack up Loyalty Points. This card helps me reach my status goal by netting me up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per elite status qualification year (10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points).

Related: How I booked Japan Airlines first class for just 80K American Airlines AAdvantage miles

Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards is now the only major U.S. airline loyalty program that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles. That means you don't have to spend an outrageous amount of money to earn top-tier status (though you can choose to earn status via spending). Alaska Atmos Rewards members can now also earn points on award redemptions, which has driven my status earnings this year.

I've spent my Atmos Rewards points on award tickets flying Cathay Pacific within Asia and a flight from Seattle to Hong Kong in business class, a Hawaiian Airlines first-class flight from Honolulu to New York and an American Airlines flight from New York to Prague.

So far, I've earned the 40,000 status points required for Gold status this year through a combination of reward flights and spending on my . In addition to earning 1 status point for every $2 spent, with no spending cap, I also earn 10,000 status points each year on my account anniversary and 3 points per $1 on all foreign transactions with this card. This makes it worth the $395 annual fee, to me.

(Cardholders with the $95 annual fee earn 1 status point per $3 spent, also with no spending cap.)

While Alaska's partnership with American Airlines means I can fly Alaska flights with my top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status, I'm considering pursuing an even higher Alaska status in 2027. One of the main reasons is that Alaska upgrades its top-tier Titanium members (and a companion) to business class on international flights on the day of departure. Those with status are also now eligible for complimentary upgrades on Hawaiian Airlines flights. I've gotten upgraded on Hawaiian a few times with my status.

I'm also putting a ton of spending on my Summit card now, since Atmos Rewards has a partnership with Bilt that gets you 3 Atmos Rewards points for every dollar of rent you put on the card.

All that spending could help get me a good chunk of the way toward top-tier Titanium status, which requires 135,000 status points. I need to make a decision soon about my 2027 focus, but I haven't been able to cut the cord with American Airlines and fully commit to Alaska... at least not yet.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Alaska Atmos Rewards elite status

Over the past few years, my status with Delta has been on a steep decline. I enjoyed several years as a Delta Diamond, but it's just become too expensive (28,000 Medallion Qualification Dollars, to be exact) to earn top-tier status.

I only qualified for entry-level Silver last year, which requires 5,000 MQDs. A friend threw me a bone and gifted me second-tier Gold status, which typically requires 10,000 MQDs, but I'm not on track to re-earn it for 2027.

So far, my total spending this year is just 7,338 MQDs. This includes 5,000 MQDs just for holding the and the .

The $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) for the Delta Reserve is steep, but it's often worth it for those chasing status. It's just not enough of a boost to get me even to Gold status.

The Reserve card does give 1 MQD for every $10 you spend on the card. Technically, you could spend your way to status, but there's no way I can put that much spending on my Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card. While I still like the card for all its perks, I'm no longer putting much spending on it.

While I am likely to drop down to Silver for 2027, I'll still fly Delta occasionally.

I've made great use of SkyMiles over the years. Last year, I lucked out with an award from Mexico City International Airport (MEX) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and then to Brisbane Airport (BNE) in Delta One. There was a brief moment when the flight was available for just 73,000 SkyMiles one-way. I jumped at the opportunity to fly in Delta One on the more-than-14-hour flight to Australia.

Despite being what I'd consider the least valuable airline currency, SkyMiles remain appealing, and I'll keep my Reserve and Platinum cards for the long term. I've gotten a lot of use out of the statement credits that come with holding the cards.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

I added another airline elite status to my collection in 2026: Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, which I received simply for signing up for the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and carrying the card. This would typically require earning 25,000 Status Qualifying Credits through the airline.

Unfortunately, I haven't had many opportunities to actually fly with Air Canada, and I've even let some of my valuable eUpgrade credits expire unused.

Still, I've become increasingly interested in the Air Canada Aeroplan program, especially because of its extensive network of airline partners and the ability to book some excellent business-class award flights through them.

One of my favorite redemptions using my welcome bonus on that card was booking a business-class flight on Emirates from Rio de Janeiro to Buenos Aires for just 56,000 Aeroplan points. It's a fascinating fifth-freedom route, and I was especially excited about the opportunity to finally experience Emirates.

I was also able to book Swiss Airlines business class from Cairo to Zurich and then on to New York for just 85,000 Aeroplan points.

Looking ahead, I'm particularly intrigued by Aeroplan's generous stopover rules. The program allows travelers to add a stopover of more than 24 hours on eligible international one-way award itineraries for just 5,000 additional points. That's an incredible opportunity to visit two destinations on a single award ticket.

Even though I haven't gotten much use out of my Air Canada elite status, Aeroplan remains one of the most interesting airline loyalty programs in my points-and-miles arsenal. I'm hoping to put more of those points — and perhaps some of those elite benefits — to work in the year ahead.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

Another new status for me is United Airlines MileagePlus Premier Silver. I actually did a status challenge with United late last year, and enjoyed a few months of top-tier United Premier 1K status, but I wasn't able to complete the challenge to unlock it for a full year.

Still, I've really enjoyed flying United more. It's easier to get to their hub at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) from my New York City apartment, and I ended up flying and earning enough this year to earn the entry-level United Silver status, which requires at least 6,000 Premier qualifying points or 15 Premier Qualifying Flights and 5,000 PQPs. (In 2027, United is ditching PQFs, making status eligible only through PQPs.)

Silver status allows me to get priority boarding, extra-legroom seats at check-in 24 hours before flying and standby for earlier flights.

During the brief window I had 1K status, I really enjoyed boarding ahead of Group 1.

Related: 5 last-minute ways to earn United elite status this year

More importantly, during my challenge I signed up for the (see rates and fees), which got me a good stash of United miles that I've used effectively.

I was able to spend just 85,000 United miles for a one-way business-class flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark this year, and I've just booked another business-class flight from Sydney, Australia, back to New York for 85,000 United miles.

I've earned a total of 8,640 PQPs toward status this year, but I'm unlikely to earn the more than 3,000 more I'd need for Premier Gold before the end of the year. I think Silver status is just fine for me for now.

I've loved having top-tier World of Hyatt Globalist status again this year. I've been able to use suite upgrades at several stand-out properties this year, including the Grand Hyatt Kauai Resort & Spa in Hawaii, the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro in Brazil and the Hyatt Regency Cairo West in Egypt.

Globalist benefits include guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, free breakfast and better upgrade odds.

This year, I've earned top-tier status organically with stays all over the world. I especially loved finally getting to check out the newly renovated Park Hyatt Tokyo and to stay at the Park Hyatts in Shanghai and Beijing.

While earning Globalist status requires 60 nights at Hyatt hotels per year, I've already stayed 79 nights this year. I may try to hit 90 nights in 2026, so I can earn another Milestone Rewards choice.

I also plan on keeping both my (see rates and fees) and my (see rates and fees) to help me get more elite nights toward status each year.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

I've also been putting Hyatt stays on my World of Hyatt Credit Card to earn 4 points per dollar spent at Hyatt hotels and resorts. You also earn two elite nights for every $5,000 you put on the personal card.

To me, World of Hyatt is the most valuable hotel loyalty program because I often get upgraded and never have to fight for late checkout. Hyatt points also stretch very far, especially compared with Hilton and Marriott. I already have trips on the books next year for Alila Villas Uluwatu in Indonesia, Park Hyatt Milan and Hyatt Paris Madeleine.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

Hilton Honors elite status is one of the easiest achievements to reach. Although I stayed at a Hilton hotel only a few times this year, I maintained Diamond status. How did I manage that? It's a perk of holding .

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Hilton Honors elite status

The card comes with Hilton Diamond status for as long as you hold it. Despite a $550 annual card fee (see rates and fees), the card is still worth keeping.

There are other valuable inclusions, such as up to $400 to spend at Hilton resorts every year (up to $200 in statement credits from January to June and another up to $200 in statement credits from July to December), up to $200 in statement credits for eligible flight purchases (up to $50 per quarter) and a free night when you open the account and reach your annual card anniversary.

Last year, I used my free night at the chic Conrad Tokyo on a room that would have been more than $1,100. This year, I used it at the Hilton Tokyo in a room that went for more than $650 a night.

I used one of my $200 stay statement credits last year at the Hilton Tangier Al Houara Resort & Spa in Morocco, and the other at Resorts World Las Vegas. In past years, I've also used it at Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort and Hilton Hawaiian Village Waikiki Beach Resort in Hawaii.

I also use the airline fee credits regularly. When using the Aspire card to pay, you get up to $50 in statement credits for eligible airline purchases each quarter.

Thanks to this card, I've had Hilton Diamond status since 2020.

Related: No suite upgrade but charm aplenty: What it's like staying at one of Hilton's SLH properties as a top-tier elite

While I have had some nice stays at Hilton properties — including the stunning Conrad Bora Bora Nui — over the years, I've rarely been upgraded despite my Diamond status. Still, the statement credits alone justify keeping the Aspire card and my Diamond status for 2027, even if I don't have as much luck getting upgrades with Hilton as I do with Hyatt.

I will earn Platinum Elite status with Marriott again this year just for holding a credit card.

In the past, I've been content with the Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status I receive courtesy of the ; it gives status in several hotel programs, including Marriott Bonvoy (enrollment required).

Related: Guide to Marriott and Hilton elite status with the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum

Then in 2022, American Express surprised everyone by announcing that holders of the would get Platinum Elite status for as long as they hold the card. I jumped at the chance to apply for it. As a result, I've held Platinum Elite status since then.

I've spent more than two dozen nights at Marriott properties this year and having Platinum Elite status certainly enhanced my trips with benefits like guaranteed late checkout, lounge access and complimentary breakfast. I even got an upgrade at the Ritz-Carlton in Hong Kong.

I used the annual free night that comes with the Brilliant card two years in a row at the lakefront Hotel President Wilson in Geneva, Switzerland. Last year, I used it for London's Bankside Hotel.

Related: 30 best Marriott hotels in the world that you can book with points

So far, I've booked 46 Marriott nights this year. I won't try to get the higher Titanium status — which requires 75 nights — though the idea of opening the is intriguing. Each year you hold the card, you receive 15 elite night credits toward the next level of Marriott Bonvoy elite status.

At least for now, though, I'll keep the personal Brilliant card open and enjoy Platinum Elite status without worrying about how many nights I need to stay.

Related: Last-minute strategies to earn Marriott Bonvoy elite status

Like my other hotel statuses, I have Platinum Elite status with IHG One Rewards by virtue of holding its hotel-branded card.

Last year, I stayed at several memorable IHG properties, including the Kimpton Fitzroy in London, the InterContinental Porto in Portugal, the Kimpton Overland Hotel in Atlanta and the InterContinental Ljubljana in Slovenia. This year, I've checked into the Hotel InterContinental Bordeaux Le Grand and WM Hotel in Sai Kung (a Vignette property) near Hong Kong.

Despite staying only seven nights at IHG hotels in 2026, I will maintain IHG Platinum Elite status simply by holding the IHG One Rewards Select Credit Card (no longer open to new applicants). In addition to elite status, my favorite perk of this card is its free night award worth up to 40,000 points, which I've used at the Kimpton Armory Hotel in Bozeman, Montana, and the aforementioned InterContinental in Portugal.

The information for the IHG One Rewards Select card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The new version of the card is the (see rates and fees), which also provides Platinum Elite status. It also comes with a fourth night free on award stays and the ability to add points to your 60,000-point anniversary free night certificate (these perks aren't available on the Select card). The annual fee is $350.

I'll keep my IHG card for status (and a free night) again next year. I'm also sitting on a nice stash of points, so odds are I'll enjoy some great redemptions in the not-too-distant future — though I don't have any IHG stays planned so far in 2027.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning IHG One Rewards elite status

The last status I'll mention is with Starbucks, since I'm a regular at the cafe near my apartment.

That regularity earned me top-tier Reserve status in the Starbucks Rewards program, which was overhauled earlier this year.

Reserve status earns 0.7 Stars more per dollar spent than entry-level Green status (for a total of 1.7 Stars per dollar) and requires earning an eye-watering 2,500 Stars over a rolling 12-month period to reach. That's 2,000 more Stars than necessary for the next-lowest tier, Gold.

It may not be the most rewarding program in the world — especially if you have a lower status tier — but the savings I get through the program add up and have me just as hooked on it as I am on my preferred hotel and airline programs.

Related: Why I got top-tier status with Starbucks and enjoy it — despite the reduced earnings for some

I've thought about going fully free agent and stopping my pursuit of status. But the truth is, I have fun on the hamster wheel, and the perks really make the game worth playing.

I'll have top-tier status with American, Hyatt and Hilton again next year. I'm excited to use more of my perks in 2027, and I will report back on my 2028 plans next year.

If you're considering going for status, you should really do the math to see if the extra costs are worth the benefits you get. It's harder to earn status these days, and the benefits keep getting whittled down. Don't do it unless you know you will use the perks and that you can do it without spending a small fortune.

It can be more cost-effective to get a credit card that automatically gives you some status perks, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

At least think about it. I'm not sure I'm the best at following my own advice.
