#6175. Updated: Frontier Airlines Flight Declares Mayday After Lavatory Floods The Cabin — “We’re Worried About Electronics”

A bathroom sink sprang a leak on Frontier Airlines flight 3566, spraying so much water into the cabin that the pilot declared “Mayday, Mayday, Mayday” and requested a diversion. It was so bad he told air traffic control, “We’re worried about electronics.” The Denver – Detroit flight landed safely in Chicago. This may be the most Frontier Airlines story ever that doesn’t involve a passenger fight. The November 11 flight was operated by an Airbus A321neo N688FR. “Our forward lav sink has sprung a leak and it’s spraying so much water, it’s flooding, uh, the cabin area in the back. We’re worried about electronics. We’d like to divert to Chicago O’Hare.” Frontier flight 3566 declares an emergency over a flooding lavatory — November 11, 2026 The pilot reads back a clearance directly to O’Hare, asks to begin descending while the crew prepares for the arrival, and then reads back an instruction to descend to 24,000 feet. The just begs for potty jokes, but the leak was spraying water, not a passenger clogging the toilet. And there wasn’t apparently sewage flowing through the aircraft. Is this covered under warranty from Airbus? https://t.co/PPIcibQN9Y — Thenewarea51 (@thenewarea51) November 11, 2026 The reason to get the aircraft on the ground before water finds its way into the avionics is well-established. The NTSB concluded that a Delta Boeing 767 investigation faced freezing flight control components as a result of leaking water that froze, limiting control over the aircraft’s ailerons. Here, the Frontier aircraft landed safely. I covered a Delta flight in June where passengers were told to hold their bags in their laps for landing as water spread through the cabin approaching San Francisco. And the closest comparison is an Alaska Airlines flight from Honolulu to Anchorage that turned around after a sink overflow. Passengers reported two to four inches of standing water. Flight attendants tried to soak it up with paper towels. And some of you still walk into airplane lavatories barefoot. The Denver – Detroit flight landed safely in Chicago. This may be the most Frontier Airlines story ever that doesn’t involve a passenger fight. The November 11 flight was operated by an Airbus A321neo N688FR.

“Our forward lav sink has sprung a leak and it’s spraying so much water, it’s flooding, uh, the cabin area in the back. We’re worried about electronics. We’d like to divert to Chicago O’Hare.”

Frontier flight 3566 declares an emergency over a flooding lavatory — November 11, 2026

The pilot reads back a clearance directly to O’Hare, asks to begin descending while the crew prepares for the arrival, and then reads back an instruction to descend to 24,000 feet.

The just begs for potty jokes, but the leak was spraying water, not a passenger clogging the toilet. And there wasn’t apparently sewage flowing through the aircraft.

The reason to get the aircraft on the ground before water finds its way into the avionics is well-established. The NTSB concluded that a Delta Boeing 767 investigation faced freezing flight control components as a result of leaking water that froze, limiting control over the aircraft’s ailerons. Here, the Frontier aircraft landed safely.

I covered a Delta flight in June where passengers were told to hold their bags in their laps for landing as water spread through the cabin approaching San Francisco. And the closest comparison is an Alaska Airlines flight from Honolulu to Anchorage that turned around after a sink overflow. Passengers reported two to four inches of standing water. Flight attendants tried to soak it up with paper towels. And some of you still walk into airplane lavatories barefoot.

#6174. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

Every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only showed up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):

So this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

It’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

American had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

What do you make of this American pilot being arrested?

#6173. AI Will Dehumanize the Job Hunt

I had been raised on stories of how the go-getters get going. You show up, you demonstrate desire to work, you list your skills and your aptitude, and someone out there, desperate for good, reliable help, will give you a chance. Bob Iger was a weatherman in Ithaca, then in 1974 started as a studio supervisor — a very low-level production job. He built a reputation for hard work and eventually became the CEO of Disney. Barry Diller started in the William Morris Agency mailroom. He got curious about how the entertainment business worked and used free time to read the agency’s files. He would eventually rise to higher positions, invent the “Movie of the Week,” and go on to run Paramount and Fox. Often these stories involve finding an older, experienced person as a mentor. Sol Price, the founder of FedMart, took Jim Sinegal under his wing. Sinegal had started at FedMart by unloading mattresses at 18. Sinegal rose through the company and co-founded Costco. We have tear-jerking movies about this, such as The Pursuit of Happyness.

All those stories highlight that market relations, careers, and success are not just a kind of abstract exchange and extraction of value, but really stories of human endeavor, development, and relationships. The market isn’t just the exchange of “utils,” money, and labor; at its best, it is a kind of theater for human virtue and adventure. Greed, grasping, or manipulation are sinful; hard work, creativity, and the courage to put yourself out there are our participation in the great good work of Providence.

Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

Buckley Jr.’s legacy, supports the National Review mission, and advances the principles of a free society through educational and outreach programs. #6172. Scoop: Frontier Airlines Plans First Class Service—Not Just Bigger Seats

Frontier Airlines is planning more than a bigger seat for first class. A new memo tells flight attendants that first class service standards are coming for flights beginning March 5, 2027, the same day its new front cabin launches. This follows my original scoop, since confirmed by the airline, that Frontier’s first class rolls out March 5, 2027. Under “Onboard service,” the airline now says: Our standard onboard services apply through March 4, 2027. New First Class service standards will be released for flights on and after March 5, 2027. This is a move toward a real first class service, and away from the Spirit Airlines ‘Big Front Seat’ approach to just selling more space. This hasn’t been announced publicly yet. The airline’s first class frequently asked questions, updated just yesterday, still says food and beverages are available for purchase. Specific standards are still to come. Frontier Has Confirmed The March 5 Launch Frontier originally announced first class in December 2024 for late 2025. Last month I reported that aircraft conversions were beginning, with the bigger seats sold as UpFront Plus during the transition. So getting the seat before the March 5 official launch doesn’t mean getting new service with it. Frontier publicly announced first class reservations on November 10, confirming March 5 travel and targeting that date for completion of the seating conversion: Eight first class seats: two rows in a 2-by-2 configuration, with up to 37 inches of pitch. More extra legroom: rows three through eight will offer up to 34 inches of pitch. UpFront Plus, with its blocked middle seat, continues in select rows. A First bundle advertised from $129 one way: first class seating, a carry-on, two checked bags and priority boarding. A Premium bundle advertised from $90 one way: extra legroom seating, a carry-on and priority boarding. The introductory offer requires buying the flight and bundle together by November 16, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. And these seats still don’t recline. Frontier describes them as “pre-reclined,” which means you can’t adjust the seatback. Power And Wi-Fi Are Coming Frontier now says USB-C charging will be offered in the first eight rows, not throughout the full coach cabin. Both power and Starlink wi-fi will roll out during 2027. Frontier’s new renderings show the charging setup: I’ve said that the lack of inflight internet has kept me from flying Frontier. Giving up hours of work can make the cheapest ticket actually more expensive. A bigger seat, power and working wi-fi make a big difference in my willingness to buy travel from them. Their operational reliability, however, is still a caution. Including drinks and food makes sense as it tries to have a product customers interested in a better experience will buy. They’ve had largely the cheap offerings but not the revenue opportunities from further upsells. It’s still not clear what the service standards will mean or translate into in the cabin. Unfortunately, for bookings made starting January 1, 2027, elite frequent flyers will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades to first class if they buy a bundle. And top tier Diamonds only qualify 24 hours prior to departure (18 for Platinum, 8 for Gold, and 4 for Silver). They’ve had largely the cheap offerings but not the revenue opportunities from further upsells. It’s still not clear what the service standards will mean or translate into in the cabin.

Unfortunately, for bookings made starting January 1, 2027, elite frequent flyers will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades to first class if they buy a bundle. And top tier Diamonds only qualify 24 hours prior to departure (18 for Platinum, 8 for Gold, and 4 for Silver).

More About Gary »

Problem is the greyhound bus crowd you have to travel with.

So… Big Front Seat AND premium snacks? Or, are we getting “a fresh, local guinea pig served on a honey-glazed or coffee-encrusted stick.”

@ Gary — Giving up hours of work can make you happier.”

Predicting consumer behavior is difficult, but I think offering first class is too big a leap for Frontier at this point. They need to first become an acceptable airline for higher income Americans to fly. First do things like improve customer service, hold staff to higher standards, add wifi and power to the aircraft, improve their website and app, and offer a larger number of “normal legroom ‘ coach seats. Then we could talk about Frontier having a first. class.

“I’ve said that the lack of inflight internet has kept me from flying Frontier”

Analogously, do you rent cars rather than take Uber/Lyft/Blacklane?

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

If you typically fly with American Airlines and its partner airlines, earning elite status in the AAdvantage program can unlock many perks, from complimentary upgrades to priority boarding.

In 2022, American AAdvantage revamped the method for earning elite status to a system based on Loyalty Points.

Nowadays, members earn Loyalty Points through eligible flights, credit card spending and purchases with participating partners.

Here’s what you need to know about American Airlines elite status, including how to earn it and what benefits it brings.

American Airlines elite status gives perks to AAdvantage members who interact with the program and its partners. The program lets you earn Loyalty Points toward elite status through many activities unrelated to travel, including shopping, dining and spending on cobranded American Airlines credit cards.

You can earn each American Airlines elite status tier by accumulating a set amount of Loyalty Points during the elite-qualification year that runs for 12 months from March 1 through the end of February. Once you reach the threshold, your status takes effect immediately and remains valid through March 31 of the following full year.

Note: Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles are not the same thing (but more on that below).

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning American AAdvantage elite status

You’ll find four published tiers of American Airlines elite status that you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points during the 12 months starting each March 1:

In addition to these tiers, there’s also the exclusive, invite-only Concierge Key status. However, American AAdvantage doesn’t publish any specific requirements for this status.

You’ll also earn Loyalty Point Rewards as you reach specific Loyalty Point thresholds, including some that fall between elite status tiers. You’ll earn your first Loyalty Point Rewards choice after earning 15,000 Loyalty Points within the 12-month qualification period beginning March 1.

Related: Your guide to American Airlines Million Miler status

To qualify for American Airlines elite status, you must earn the required number of Loyalty Points during each 12-month qualification period following March 1. As discussed, you’ll need to earn 40,000 Loyalty Points for Gold status, 75,000 for Platinum, 125,000 for Platinum Pro and 200,000 for Executive Platinum each qualification period.

We have a full guide to earning Loyalty Points. But, in short, you'll earn two types of American Airlines miles: base and bonus. And while both base and bonus miles are redeemable, generally only base miles earn Loyalty Points. The exception is the elite status bonus on flights, which also counts (more on that below). So, each time you earn a base mile with AAdvantage, you'll also earn a Loyalty Point.

You can earn American AAdvantage base miles through many different activities. Here’s a noncomprehensive list of some ways you can earn base miles (and hence Loyalty Points):

There are many other ways to earn American Airlines miles. However, check whether you’re earning base or bonus miles before you get too excited about how many Loyalty Points you’ll earn. Bask Bank mileage accounts are one example of an activity earning only bonus miles — hence, no Loyalty Points. Basic Economy fares on American don't earn Loyalty Points either.

Note: American and Hyatt ended their enhanced loyalty partnership in 2026, so World of Hyatt status is no longer offered as a Loyalty Point Reward. You can still earn 500 AAdvantage miles per eligible Hyatt stay by giving your AAdvantage number at check-in.

Related: Be careful: 9 times you won’t earn American Airlines Loyalty Points, even if you earn miles

American Airlines elite status comes with some valuable benefits. Here’s a look at some of the most noteworthy benefits, including how they differ by status tier.

American Airlines elite members receive complimentary upgrades on eligible flights to select destinations within North America, the Caribbean and Central America, subject to availability. Depending on the aircraft, these upgrades can move members from Main Cabin to premium economy, from Premium Economy to business or domestic first class, or directly from Main Cabin to business or domestic first class (on aircraft without a Premium Economy cabin).

These upgrades are automatically requested and are available on paid tickets and award tickets. Members can also receive a complimentary upgrade for one companion traveling on the same flight. However, Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, aren't eligible for complimentary upgrades.

American will start processing these upgrades at different times depending on your American Airlines elite status tier. Executive Platinum members may have their upgrades confirmed as early as 100 hours before departure, Platinum Pro members as early as 72 hours, Platinum members as early as 48 hours and Gold members as early as 24 hours.

American Airlines prioritizes upgrades — including complimentary upgrades, mileage award upgrades and systemwide upgrades — in the following order:

Members with American Airlines elite status — and up to eight passengers traveling with you on the same reservation — can select Preferred seats without any extra fees during booking or anytime after booking (based on availability). Preferred seats have standard legroom but are located in more desirable locations throughout the economy cabin. This benefit does not apply to Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026.

Main Cabin Extra seats, which offer additional legroom, are also complimentary for AAdvantage elite members and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation (based on availability). Executive Platinum, Platinum Pro and Platinum members can select these seats at booking, while Gold members must wait until within 24 hours of departure. Basic Economy tickets purchased on or after May 18, 2026, are not eligible for complimentary Main Cabin Extra seats.

American Airlines elite members get a mileage bonus as follows when flying on eligible flights:

The status bonus is added to the base miles earned on eligible flights, and unlike most bonus miles, it counts toward Loyalty Points as well. For example, on flights marketed by American, a member without status earns 5 miles and Loyalty Points per dollar, while an Executive Platinum member earns 11. That makes it easier for higher-tier members to requalify through flying.

AAdvantage elite members enjoy priority access at check-in, security and boarding on eligible American Airlines flights. Specifically, Executive Platinum members board in Group 1, Platinum Pro in Group 2, Platinum in Group 3 and Gold in Group 4. Boarding with any of these groups might mean there’s still space in the overhead bin for your carry-on suitcase.

AAdvantage status members also get priority when standing by for a different American Airlines flight on the same day of travel (and can standby for a later flight the same day) on eligible flights within the U.S. and between the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Executive Platinum and Platinum Pro members — and up to eight companions traveling with them on the same reservation — can enjoy complimentary same-day confirmed flight changes on American when flying to or from the U.S., Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

AAdvantage elite members also enjoy complimentary checked bags when flying American Airlines: Gold members get their first checked bag free, Platinum members get their first two checked bags free, and Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum members get their first three checked bags free. Best of all, this checked baggage allowance is also offered to guests traveling with the status member on the same reservation.

American Airlines elite status offers a variety of other perks, including the following:

Finally, American Airlines offers additional rewards at specific Loyalty Point milestones. Though these rewards are separate from AAdvantage elite status, you’ll inherently unlock them as you accumulate Loyalty Points toward the program's elite status tiers.

Here’s a look at the Loyalty Point Rewards you could choose as you progress toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required for Executive Platinum status:

Related: Why (and how) I'm earning AAdvantage Platinum Pro elite status and not going for AAdvantage Executive Platinum

Having a cobranded American Airlines credit card is extremely helpful if you want to earn American Airlines elite status. Although the sign-up and category bonuses provide bonus miles — which won’t give you Loyalty Points — you’ll earn 1 Loyalty Point per dollar spent with all U.S.-issued AAdvantage credit cards. This means you can boost your Loyalty Point balance as you use your card for purchases and even qualify for American elite status from credit card spending alone.

If you value Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is an excellent choice. Meanwhile, existing cardholders who had the AAdvantage® Aviator® World Elite Silver Mastercard® and were transitioned to the (see rates and fees) can still earn up to 15,000 additional Loyalty Points by meeting specific spending thresholds during the qualification year ending Feb. 28, 2027. Unfortunately, this benefit is not available to new Globe card applicants.

The information for the Aviator Silver card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

American Airlines elite status is worth it for some travelers. I've held Platinum Pro or Executive Platinum status since 2016 because I value the domestic upgrades, waived checked bag fees, Priority check-in lines and Oneworld Emerald status these tiers provide.

But, after reconsidering what I value in American Airlines elite status, I've only strived to qualify for Platinum Pro in recent years. In short, I decided the incremental value of Executive Platinum over Platinum Pro didn’t justify the extra costs I’d incur to earn the higher status.

It’s important to consider how much you’ll use your AAdvantage perks and the cost of earning American Airlines status. If you’ll organically earn American Airlines status through flights, then it’s likely worth earning. But if you’ll have to earn a significant number of Loyalty Points through other means, such as using the AAdvantage eShopping portal or spending on an AAdvantage credit card, there’s an opportunity cost to doing so.

Finally, if you’ll only use your American Airlines elite status perks occasionally or only need a specific perk, consider whether you can get what you seek through booking premium-cabin fares or applying for a credit card that offers that particular benefit.

Related: Which credit card should you use for American Airlines flights?

American Airlines offers four elite status tiers you can earn by accumulating Loyalty Points: Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro and Executive Platinum. These tiers offer perks including Preferred seats, complimentary space-available upgrades on eligible American Airlines flights, and Oneworld perks on select partner airlines.

If you frequently fly with American Airlines, British Airways or Iberia on expensive paid fares or spend a significant amount on American Airlines credit cards or when shopping through the AAdvantage eShopping portal, you’ll likely find it easy and worthwhile to earn American Airlines elite status. Otherwise, it's smart to consider whether the value you'll get from American Airlines status is worth the cost you'll incur to earn it.

#6168. 6 Reasons Why Citi Strata Elite Beats Amex Platinum And Sapphire Reserve

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Citi Strata Elite earns 50% more points on unbonused spending than Amex Platinum or Chase Sapphire Reserve, and those points can become American Airlines miles. It also costs $200 – $300 less per year.

I’ve written a lot about the card’s enormous first-year value. But the more I’ve used the hotel benefit, the more I think there’s a case for the Citi Strata EliteSM Card (See rates and fees) beyond the initial bonus. Here are six things it does better than Amex Platinum and Sapphire Reserve – both excellent cards and I have them both.

Banks advertise how many transfer partners they have. A long list can include many I even actively avoid (Aeromexico, Thai Airways). Most banks are also limited in whom they can work with because major airline and hotel cobrand card agreements usually include exclusivity provisions that limit what competing banks can offer. American Express has Delta. Chase has United. Citi has American. Of those three, I’d take American AAdvantage. Strata Elite points transfer to American at 1:1. And American still offers some terrific partner redemptions. However, some of my best American redemptions are just regular domestic coach trips. I’ve written about getting 4 cents and even 8 cents per mile from economy awards. American will sometimes make a flight cheap in miles while keeping the cash fare high. You don’t need to want a first class suite halfway around the world to get value from this program. Citi still has international partners I want, including Air France KLM Flying Blue, Singapore Airlines and Qatar Airways. Chase’s Hyatt transfers are a real advantage on the hotel side. (I still wish Bank of America had its own transferable points program, with Alaska’s Atmos Rewards as a partner.) 2. The Hotel Credit Works Beyond A Short List Of Luxury Properties Strata Elite offers up to $300 off prepaid hotel stays of two nights or longer booked through Citi Travel each calendar year. The discount comes off when you book, and applies to the room cost before taxes and fees. You can use it at ordinary hotels and independent properties, without restricting yourself to a luxury collection. Amex Platinum’s $600 annual hotel credit is split into two $300 periods and requires Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings. Sapphire Reserve’s $500 The Edit credit is limited to that collection, with a maximum of $250 per qualifying booking. Chase also has an additional 2026 hotel credit, but that one is restricted to selected brands. Those programs can provide real value through breakfast, property credits and hotel loyalty benefits. Citi’s advantage is the much broader choice of hotels where I can use the discount. And I haven’t found that using Citi’s credit requires giving back the savings through a higher room rate. In January, I compared the Marriott at LaGuardia Airport: Citi Travel was $156 before taxes, while Marriott’s own member rate was $176. That’s $20 less per night before applying the credit. I still compare the room and cancellation terms, but Citi Travel has been competitive or even cheaper. I’ve also had little difficulty getting Marriott hotels to add my Bonvoy number at check-in and honor on-property benefits. Earlier this year I used the Strata Elite credit at a Marriott and received club lounge access. I similarly had no problem getting status recognition on a bank portal booking at a Westin this month. These third-party bookings generally aren’t supposed to be eligible for hotel points, elite-night credit or elite benefits. 3. It’s A Better Card For Everyday Spending Strata Elite earns 1.5 points per dollar on spending outside its bonus categories. Sapphire Reserve and Amex Platinum earn just one. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. You can do better with any bank pairing its primary card with a second card that offers different earn. Generally you’re permitted to pool those points. 4. Six Points Per Dollar On Weekend Evening Dining Is Fantastic Citi Nights earns six points per dollar at restaurants from 6 p.m. Friday until 6 a.m. Saturday, and again from 6 p.m. Saturday until 6 a.m. Sunday, all times Eastern. This works at restaurants generally, including qualifying restaurant delivery services. You don’t have to pick from a bank’s restaurant reservation list. Citi uses the time the purchase is authorized, so a Friday dinner doesn’t lose the bonus just because the charge posts on Monday. Outside Citi Nights, restaurant spending earns 3x. And Citi’s other big accelerators are 12x on hotels, car rentals and attractions booked through Citi Travel, and 6x on airfare booked there. You don’t earn points on the hotel spending covered by the $300 benefit. For airfare booked directly with an airline, Amex Platinum’s 5x and Sapphire Reserve’s 4x beat Citi’s 1.5x. Big Useful Credits Instead Of Many Small Ones I’ve laid out how to use the Strata Elite credits, but the basic approach is pretty simple: book a hotel stay and buy an American Airlines ticket. In addition to the $300 hotel benefit, there’s a $200 annual Splurge credit. Select American Airlines as one of your eligible merchants before purchasing, and a ticket billed directly by American qualifies. You don’t have to find incidental fees to use it on, as with Amex Platinum’s airline fee credit. The other choices are Best Buy, 1stDibs, Live Nation and Future Personal Training. You can activate up to two merchants at a time and use the credit over multiple eligible purchases. For me, American makes this easy. If the hotel benefit and Splurge credit replace $500 you’d have spent anyway, they leave just $95 of Citi’s $595 annual fee to cover. And both benefits run by calendar year, without dividing the money into monthly allowances. There’s also up to $200 a year for Blacklane, divided into $100 for January through June and $100 for July through December. 6. The Annual Fee Is Lower The annual fees are $595 for Citi Strata Elite vs $795 for Sapphire Reserve and $895 for Amex Platinum. You still get a premium travel card: Priority Pass lounge access with up to two guests, four Admirals Club passes each calendar year for eligible American or oneworld travel, travel protections, and up to $120 for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application every four years. And the first year still offers a lot. The current offer is 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 in the first three months. At 1.5 cents apiece, that’s $1,125 in points before counting what you earn from the spending itself. Someone opening the card now can use the hotel and Splurge benefits during the rest of 2026 and again in 2027, before their first anniversary. That’s up to $1,000 from those two benefits alone. If those credits replace spending you’d make anyway, the bonus plus the credits less the $595 fee comes to $1,530 in first-year value, before Blacklane, lounge access or points earned from purchases. But for year 2, the real question is “what does this card offer me that is worth putting up with getting value out of these coupons”.

Unless you eat out quite a bit on weekends, or you really value 4 AA passes, the answer is probably not a lot. For Amex and Chase, the answer is some hotel/car rental status together with lounges. Yes one can argue that overcrowding and food quality negate the value of those cards, but the lounges are nonetheless the pot of gold at the end of the coupon clipping rainbow.

Agree AA is a great transfer partner and still probably better than UA (although UA has actually been decent this year domestically), but can get the $95 Citi Strata Premier to unlock AA at 1:1. Pair that with a DoubleCash and you’ve got an ThankYou point earning machine.

And BofA announced transfers with Atmos coming in 2027, so your parenthetical is now almost a reality.

Card will be coming up for renewal soon. Really struggling on whether to keep it. While the math above makes sense, I’m not sure I can justify the annual fee to basically earn it back. AA miles are valuable to me, but I also like to earn Hyatt points through chase sapphire reserve.

I have a zillion American miles from those endless Barclays promotions. Keep booking flight flights and they keep canceling them. Atrocious airline

Oof. Gary. Listen. I’m as Citi Nights as they come, but isn’t it a bit tone deaf not posting this after 6PM EST on a Friday or Saturday evening? (@L737! Just a week away!)

I’m trying to decide if I should PC a useless AA card into this card. I had it previously, so not eligible for the SUB. But if I can still double dip the hotel and splurge credits, it might be worth it.

What I really want is the Strata Premier, but they won’t allow that as a PC.

I parked my IRA at Citi to get CitiGold banking tier. That makes the AF only $445, and gives you free banking services (ATM reimbursed, free checks, free wires, free safety deposit box). Also gives you Citi culture pass for numerous free museums, and $200 in free subscription services (Costco, Amazon Prime, Hulu, others). Also gets you better customer service.

Paired with a Custom cash or 2 if you were smart enough to grab them before it was shut down, and you have a sweet setup. Everything else goes on the DoubleCash.

Amex has nice lounges if you travel solo, but Citi lets you bring a friend or two along. And 12x on hotels in the portal is best in class. So is 6x on weekend dining.

The credits are great. Even Blacklane, which is expensive but underrated, I love the service. The other credits are super easy to use. As a coupon book goes, this one needs no spreadsheet.

Transfer partners are awesome, as good or better than Amex/Chase in many ways. Lastly, the card itself is beautiful. Perhaps the best one out there. I hope they continue to enhance it.

#6167. Visit Oslo Follows Its Viral Anti-Ad With a Horror Christmas Musical

Photo Credit: A still from Visit Oslo's "It's Totally Even a City" video.  Visit Oslo, Visit Norway, YouTube

Visit Oslo needed a unique twist to its "Is It Even a City?" sequel to help fill hotels in the winter. Its project manager says the final result is almost as popular as the original.

Visit Oslo is betting its viral anti-ad can work twice, this time to fill hotels in the low season.

Halfdan, the protagonist from Visit Oslo’s “Is It Even a City” campaign, went viral in 2024 for his deadpan take on the destination, telling viewers: “I wouldn’t come here.” The video has more than 25 million organic views across platforms and won a Silver Lion at Cannes Lions, according to Visit Oslo.

The destination marketing organization’s team had a high bar for any follow-up campaigns, according to Tord Baklund, a Visit Oslo project manager who worked on both videos. It had to be set in the winter to help fill beds during the city’s low season, the team had to sign on the same actor to pla

Visit Oslo has released a sequel to its viral 2024 "Is It Even a City" anti-ad, this time set in winter and styled as a horror musical, with the goal of filling hotel beds during the city's low season. The original video, built around deadpan protagonist Halfdan telling viewers "I wouldn't come here," drew more than 25 million organic views across platforms and won a Silver Lion at Cannes Lions, according to Visit Oslo. ForwardKeys reported a 17% bump in flight searches to Oslo in the five weeks after that launch, and Visit Oslo project manager Tord Baklund said Norwegian reported a 14% increase in bookings. The new "It's Totally Even a City" video has reached nearly 1 million YouTube views a month after its October launch, approaching the original's 1.9 million. Baklund said October through March is a higher-priority season for the destination marketing organization, and that while Oslo does not have an overtourism problem, the city center is packed in midsummer. Paid ads have run in the UK and Germany, markets with direct flights, but Baklund said most views have been organic, with the U.S., Sweden, and Denmark also among the top viewing markets.

#6164. First look: JetBlue ups its premium game with new 'BlueFirst' seats

JetBlue’s newest premium seats are ready for takeoff.

The airline just unveiled its new domestic first-class product called “BlueFirst.” It’s set to debut on flights next month, but TPG got a sneak peek at the seats ahead of the launch.

The new first-class seats will take up the first few rows on most of JetBlue’s planes, going forward.

Eventually, JetBlue flyers will see first-class on all of the carrier’s aircraft — except for jets that already have its lie-flat Mint cabin.

And with complimentary upgrades on the horizon for JetBlue’s Mosaic elite members, the addition of BlueFirst should offer TrueBlue loyalists some enticing new status perks in the near future.

Read more: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades, new elite benefits for 2027

JetBlue plans to offer three — or four — rows of BlueFirst, depending on the plane.

Like most domestic first-class products in the U.S., the seats are arranged in a 2-by-2 configuration.

JetBlue outfitted its BlueFirst seats with a handful of thoughtful touches, such as “flex foam” cushioning from mattress and bedding company Tuft and Needle.

The headrest also sports a special BlueFirst logo.

Beyond that, expect a host of seating upgrades from JetBlue’s core cabin. These seats have cocktail trays, extra storage and a large tray table with a personal device holder.

The 13-inch seatback screens are the first in JetBlue’s fleet to offer Bluetooth connectivity, which means passengers will be able to connect their wireless headphones, such as Apple AirPods.

The screens also offer a unique twist on ordering drinks inflight. “Mixologist Mode” allows BlueFirst flyers to customize their cocktail order with a base and mixers.

JetBlue is also rolling out a new “soft product” around the BlueFirst seats, including a new line of inflight food, drinks and amenities.

While the carrier won’t offer hot meals (no ovens!) on its domestic aircraft, there’s an array of creatively assembled bento box meals. Options range from sesame beef noodles with crispy wontons and Szechuan dip to tortellini pasta salad and a pastrami sandwich (and more).

JetBlue has a strong track record for its on-board food. And while the lack of ovens probably means its BlueFirst food won’t stack up to what you’d get on a long-haul Mint flight, the spread the airline showed off this week looks impressive — even if it will be served chilled.

BlueFirst service will also include a new array of wines curated by New York-based Parcelle Wine — plus a fresh lineup of amenities, glassware, and coasters designed by a local artist.

JetBlue’s new first-class product will debut on Dec. 8, on its service from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL).

The airline has dozens of routes already slated for the new seats, which will continue to roll out across its fleet as JetBlue retrofits its planes.

Among the biggest winners in its first-class launch: JetBlue frequent flyers with elite status.

All TrueBlue Mosaic members will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades.

Plus, customers who carry JetBlue’s top-end premium credit card will also be able to join the upgrade queue.

High-level Mosaics will also be eligible to use their confirmable upgrade certificates on BlueFirst (However, you can also still use those to upgrade to Mint, which will remain the airline’s top seat).

You can read all about JetBlue’s new upgrade policy and updated Mosaic benefits in our latest story about the TrueBlue program.

The launch of BlueFirst marks a new chapter for JetBlue’s on-board product.

The carrier began flying at the turn of the century with all-economy cabins.

It first waded into the premium space in 2014, when it launched Mint. Now, it's time to add domestic first-class to the mix — a cabin executives described Wednesday as “very JetBlue.”

‘Cheap chic’: How JetBlue’s first 25 years of flying helped reshape US aviation

It comes as U.S. travelers are about to see a wave of new first-class seats hit the market — from JetBlue to budget airlines Frontier and Allegiant.

There are some drawbacks to JetBlue’s new seats at the front of the plane.

To make room for the new recliner seats, the carrier’s long-celebrated economy legroom will shrink on some planes.

There’s also no divider between first-class and coach — and, as we noted, the meals won’t be hot.

But BlueFirst will certainly raise the bar on JetBlue's top-level service on domestic flights, and serve as a worthy complement to its popular Mint product.

Also, the chance for complimentary upgrades will be a key new perk for Mosaic elites.

And for an airline hoping to give customers more reasons to prioritize its TrueBlue loyalty program, the new seats could prove a meaningful addition for years to come.

#6163. The Nvidia Scandal Is a Warning Shot

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to the media on the day he attends a meeting between Chinese Premier Li Qiang and U.S. business representatives at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, May 14, 2026.

Many Americans have their doubts about our cutting-edge AI, but as the drama now surrounding Nvidia seems to suggest, the Beijing regime does not feel the same way.

As a reminder, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, put out a statement in which he admitted to having had an extramarital affair. The “other woman” has been identified in numerous reports as Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese national.

Ms. Huang joined Megaspeed, a Singaporean company at around the time it moved into the data-center business shortly after a Biden-era tightening of export controls on advanced chips. She was briefly its managing director and sole shareholder and is believed to retain an executive role. She has not commented publicly on Mr. Huang’s admission. Her current whereabouts are unknown.

The principal focus of Megaspeed’s operations has been described as renting out computing power relying on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities) to its customers, enabling them to use it remotely. This is allowed, with exceptions, under U.S. law. What is not permitted is for the most advanced chips of this type to be exported to China. Little is known about Megaspeed’s client base (other than that it included Alibaba, the Chinese technology and e-commerce group), ultimate ownership (Ms. Huang had meanwhile sold her interest), or funding.

Megaspeed and, reportedly, Ms. Huang have attracted the attention of the U.S. authorities. Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling contraband chips to China. U.S. intelligence is said to have been aware of Ms. Huang’s relationship with Nvidia’s CEO and identified her as a Chinese spy, information reportedly passed on to senior officials in Washington. Megaspeed has denied the allegations against it (investigation of which was abruptly transferred from the Commerce Department to the Justice Department). Up until now, Nvidia has said that it found nothing amiss. China has rejected allegations of any spy plot.

Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation. Mr. Huang has said he will cooperate. The FBI is also digging, and Congress is taking a closer look. The investigations will reveal what they will reveal. Mr. Huang’s obligations as a husband are a matter solely for him and his family. As a CEO, however, it looks as if, to put it mildly, he has taken risks that he should not have. Unless he made some preemptive disclosures, the affair posed obvious intertwined questions about conflict of interest (Megaspeed was a large client after all), national security, and the threat of blackmail, all issues of which he must have been aware. Even if he has broken no laws, he appears to have put Nvidia into a position in which it should not have been. This story, as we know it so far, also raises issues about Nvidia’s corporate governance (who, if anyone, was keeping an eye on Huang?) and its relationship with the government. Who knew what and when, and what did they do, if anything, about it?

Handling this will be complicated by the nature of the AI “arms race” with China. It is a competition in which the U.S. is primarily participating through its private, not public, sector. To be sure, private companies were heavily involved in the Cold War’s arms and space races but mainly as government contractors, a relationship in which Washington, as the customer, set the agenda — and the rules. This time around, the private sector is leading the way, driven by its ambition to compete commercially. It is ahead of China to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. China wants to win the AI race. So must we, and we must act accordingly.

That will require recognizing how critical Nvidia currently is. It supplies about 90 percent of the microchips used for training AI and 70 percent of those needed to run LLMs, and it is using its cash to play an important part in funding the development of America’s AI ecosystem. Its role will become less dominant — free markets and changing market leadership go hand in hand — but for the government to apply a wrecking ball to the company now would be madness.

There clearly need to be changes to the way that Nvidia, which is unusually dependent on one man, Jensen Huang, is run, and there needs to be accountability for what has taken place. But assuming his missteps turn out to be a matter of a terrible lapse and nothing more, the changes needed will probably be evolutionary rather than revolutionary. We should not want the disappearance of the executive energy that has made Nvidia the colossus it has become.

We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Mr. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

Finally, it must be hoped that politicians do not exploit the fresh indignation now being stirred up about an already unpopular industry for their own purposes. To do so risks hobbling American AI. And that would hand Beijing a win far greater than anything that Megaspeed or Ms. Huang might have delivered.

#6161. Delhi’s Smog Collides With India’s Peak Tourism Season

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Dehli is often hit by severe fog and pollution during winter months.  Wikimedia

Air quality in northern India has plummeted as the so-called pollution season gets underway. It is now a regular feature of traveling to the region in winter. Masks have emerged as a solution — a Band-Aid to a structural problem fueled by emissions.

Smog fills Delhi and northern India every winter, casting a shadow on Diwali celebrations and hitting peak tourism season.

The region’s position on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, where the Himalayas block air from flowing north, leads to trapped pollution from late October to February. Air quality in Delhi is then often made worse by firecrackers used in Diwali celebrations.

October to March is also the busiest window for foreign visitors to India, and Delhi is often used as an entry point.

On Saturday morning, November 7, Delhi had a U.S. Air Quality Index (AQI) value of 581, according to reports citing data from Swiss air monitoring company IQAir. That made it the most polluted major city in the world at that moment.

IQAir uses the U.S. AQI, which runs from zero upward; readings of 301 and above are considered hazardous. At the time of writing, Delhi’s AQI hourly reported value has come down to 176, putting it second only to Lahore in P

Delhi's winter smog is again colliding with India's peak inbound tourism season, and hotel operators are starting to see it in demand. On November 7, Delhi recorded a U.S. Air Quality Index value of 581 — above the 301 threshold considered hazardous — making it the most polluted major city in the world at that moment, according to reports citing IQAir data. October to March is the busiest window for foreign visitors to India, and Delhi is the common entry point. Radisson's VP of operations in India, Ashwani Kumar Goela, said some guests defer or postpone visits until conditions improve, that air quality concerns are more pronounced than the same period last year, and that they are likely contributing to softer demand. Intrepid Travel said its operations are continuing as planned with no cancellations, though its tour leaders now carry N95 masks and cut back outdoor time on the worst days. India's Supreme Court limited Diwali firecrackers to "green" versions within set hours, but pollution still spiked: PM2.5 hourly concentrations peaked at around 10 times India's daily limit of 60 micrograms per cubic meter on Diwali night, according to the Center for Study of Science, Technology & Policy. The backdrop is 9.2 million foreign tourists in 2025, down 9.4% year over year, against a government target of 100 million international arrivals by 2047.

#6160. U.S. Pilot Arrested At London Heathrow Airport, Admits Cocaine Possession—Passengers Owed Over $150,000 Compensation

A 64-year-old U.S. pilot arrested at London Heathrow has pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. Wayne Sigler, from Louisiana, was remanded in custody and faces two additional charges involving alleged drunkenness or unfitness for duty. According to the BBC’s report of information confirmed by the Metropolitan Police, Sigler was arrested on Sunday, November 1. He appeared in court on Saturday, November 7, and pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine. His next hearing is scheduled for December 7 at Isleworth Crown Court. Those charges fall under the Railways and Transport Safety Act 2003. The law also covers preparing to fly, duties after reporting for work, and standby. The charges don’t establish that he flew passengers while impaired. Reporting on the incident doesn’t identify the airline or flight, but there’s a Wayne Sigler who identifies as an American Airlines pilot in federal campaign donation records, and online discussion pegs him as an American pilot who came to the airline via America West and US Airways. On November 1, American Airlines 39 to Miami and American AIrlines 91 to Chicago O’Hare were both cancelled, and American 85 to O’Hare departed nearly 5 hours late. What Delayed Passengers Are Owed A flight departing Heathrow is covered by U.K. passenger compensation rules regardless of where the airline is based. For a journey over 3,500 kilometers, such as London to the U.S., a qualifying arrival delay of more than four hours means £520 per person (~ US$690.42). A three-to-four-hour delay falls into the £260 band. An airline can avoid the compensation payment when extraordinary circumstances caused the disruption. But the U.K. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Lipton v BA Cityflyer rejected that defense in the case of a pilot’s illness. And paragraph 170 specifically addresses a pilot who drinks enough to be unfit to report for work. If that causes a cancellation, the court says the reason is “inherent in the airline’s activity and operations.” A plane with 250 passengers at £520 each would mean £130,000 in compensation or $172,500. There was a British Airways pilot who bragged about using cocaine during a Johannesburg layover. A flight attendant reported his messages, he was kept from operating the return flight, and the airline fired him. Delta makes the most money. United has the swagger. And American? By size, it’s actually No. 1: American flies more passengers and operates more flights than any other U.S. airline. But by almost every other measure, it’s behind, and it has spent the past year trying to make up ground.

Profits? Last year, Delta Air Lines made $5.1 billion, and United Airlines $3.3 billion. American earned just $111 million. This year, American is on track to lose money.

Its shares are still down more than 50% from their 2019 high. Since November 2023, Delta and United shares have more than tripled, while American’s are up less than 30%.

A series of big and small missteps ranging from scrapping seatback screens on domestic narrowbodies to a weaker international network explain some of American’s lagging profitability.

American Airlines carries more passengers and operates more flights than any other U.S. carrier, but it trails Delta and United on nearly every financial measure, and it has spent the past year trying to close the gap. American earned $111 million last year against Delta's $5.1 billion and United's $3.3 billion, and it is on track to lose money this year. Its shares are down more than 50% from their 2019 high. A Skift review of press releases and earnings calls since early 2025 found at least 50 announced changes, built around four pillars: elevate the customer experience, grow the global network, drive premium revenue, and lead in loyalty. CEO Robert Isom has begun describing American as a "global premium airline," and the carrier is bringing back seatback screens, installing Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, ending involuntary bumping, launching the 777-300ER and A321XLR with new European routes, raising co-brand card fees, and rebuilding hubs in Chicago, Miami, Philadelphia, and Phoenix. The gap also shows up in paychecks: American set aside $55 million in profit sharing, about 0.3% of annual earnings, compared with Delta's $1.3 billion. In January, the flight attendants' union issued a vote of no confidence in Isom. Executives said there are early signs the push toward higher-spend customers is working, and chief customer officer Heather Garboden said 2027 will bring even more launches.

If you carry the (see rates and fees) in your wallet, chances are you appreciate its premium travel perks and valuable rewards.

But even a card with a $795 annual fee can't cover every spending category or travel need. That's where a second credit card can come in handy.

I carry the Sapphire Reserve myself, but it's not the only card I reach for. Whether you're looking to maximize everyday spending, enhance your airline experience, or pick up hotel-specific perks, the right pairing can help you get more out of your wallet.

Here are seven cards worth considering alongside the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Here's a quick look at seven options, including how much you'll pay in combined annual fees.

The Capital One Venture Rewards is a solid option for Sapphire Reserve cardholders looking to earn more on everyday purchases.

Why the pairing works: One area where the Sapphire Reserve falls short is everyday spending that doesn't qualify for a bonus category. Those purchases generally earn just 1 Ultimate Rewards point per dollar spent, while the Venture Rewards earns at least 2 Capital One miles per dollar spent on all purchases, regardless of category.

For example, you could use your Sapphire Reserve for purchases that earn bonus points, then reach for your Venture Rewards when shopping for clothing, furniture or other purchases that wouldn't earn elevated rewards with the Reserve.

For a $95 annual fee, the Venture Rewards also gives you access to Capital One's 15-plus transfer partners, opening up additional redemption opportunities beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards.

Key drawbacks: While the Venture Rewards has a relatively modest annual fee, it still brings your combined annual fees to $890.

You'll also be managing two separate rewards currencies, since Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Capital One miles can't be combined directly. While this opens up more redemption opportunities across different rewards programs, just make sure you're comfortable managing two rewards currencies before committing to both cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Venture Rewards.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

If you regularly fly United, pairing your Sapphire Reserve with the or can help you enjoy additional airline-specific perks.

Why the pairing works: The Sapphire Reserve offers valuable travel benefits and flexible Ultimate Rewards points that you can transfer to United MileagePlus at a 1:1 ratio. However, it doesn't offer some of the perks that come with carrying a United credit card, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

Both United cards can help fill that gap, but they cater to slightly different types of travelers.

With a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 annually, the United Explorer offers:

Meanwhile, the $350-per-year United Quest offers additional benefits for more frequent United flyers, including:

The Explorer may be enough if you only fly United a few times a year, while the Quest makes more sense for travelers who can take advantage of its additional benefits.

I personally carry both the Sapphire Reserve and United Quest, and I appreciate being able to earn flexible Ultimate Rewards points while still enjoying United-specific benefits when I fly.

Key drawbacks: Both cards add another annual fee to your wallet (the Explorer after the first year), so you'll want to make sure you fly United often enough to take advantage of their benefits. There's also some overlap in travel protections and rewards earning, particularly on United purchases.

And while you can transfer Ultimate Rewards points to United MileagePlus, you can't transfer United miles back to Chase, so it's worth considering which rewards currency you'd rather earn on each purchase.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer and our full review of the United Quest.

The and  are two great options for Sapphire Reserve cardholders looking to earn more Ultimate Rewards points without paying another annual fee.

Why the pairing works: Both Freedom cards offer opportunities to earn more rewards on purchases that might otherwise earn just 1 point per dollar with the Sapphire Reserve.

The Freedom Unlimited earns 1.5% cash back on purchases outside its bonus categories, making it a solid choice for everyday spending. Meanwhile, the Freedom Flex earns 5% cash back on up to $1,500 in combined purchases in rotating bonus categories each quarter you activate (then 1%).

Although both Freedom cards are marketed as cash-back cards, they technically earn Ultimate Rewards points, with each point worth 1 cent when redeemed for cash back.

For example, $1,000 in nonbonus spending would earn 1,500 points with the Freedom Unlimited, compared with 1,000 points on the Reserve.

The biggest advantage of either pairing is that you can combine the rewards earned with your Freedom card and Sapphire Reserve, allowing you to redeem them as transferable Ultimate Rewards points.

You could even take things a step further by carrying all three cards, creating a version of the Chase Trifecta. This strategy allows you to maximize rewards across different spending categories without adding another annual fee.

Key drawbacks: The Freedom Unlimited's 1.5% earning rate isn't the highest available for everyday spending, while the Freedom Flex requires you to track and activate quarterly bonus categories to maximize its rewards.

Both cards also have some overlapping bonus categories with the Reserve, so you'll want to pay attention to which card earns the most on each purchase.

Ultimately, I'd lean toward the Freedom Unlimited if you prefer a simple, consistent earning strategy, or the Freedom Flex if you're willing to put in a little extra effort to maximize rotating categories.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited and full review of the Chase Freedom Flex.

The is worth considering if you want to earn bonus rewards on business expenses.

While the travel category overlaps with the Sapphire Reserve, the other categories can be useful for business owners who regularly spend on advertising, shipping or telecommunications.

For example, $10,000 in eligible advertising purchases would earn 30,000 points with the Ink Business Preferred, compared with 10,000 points at the Reserve's standard earning rate.

You can also combine eligible Ultimate Rewards points earned with both cards, helping you build up your balance faster for future travel redemptions.

Key drawbacks: The Ink Business Preferred adds another $95 in annual fees, and you'll need to qualify for a business credit card to apply.

Because of the overlap in travel earning, this pairing makes the most sense if you have enough spending in the Ink Business Preferred's business-specific bonus categories to justify the additional cost.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

If you frequently stay at Hyatt properties, the can help you unlock hotel-specific benefits that your Sapphire Reserve doesn't offer.

Why the pairing works: The Sapphire Reserve gives you access to World of Hyatt through 1:1 Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers, while the World of Hyatt Credit Card provides additional perks for Hyatt stays.

Key drawbacks: The Hyatt card earns World of Hyatt points rather than flexible Ultimate Rewards points, so you'll want to compare the value of each currency before deciding which card to use for Hyatt purchases.

And if you don't regularly stay at Hyatt properties, you may have a harder time getting enough value from the card's benefits to justify its $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the World of Hyatt Card.

There's no single best card to pair with the . The right choice depends on where you spend the most and what you want from your next credit card.

Personally, I'd start by looking at where my Sapphire Reserve falls short, whether that's earning rewards on everyday purchases or offering airline-specific benefits that could make my travels easier.

After all, the goal isn't necessarily to have more credit cards. It's to make sure the cards you do carry work well together.

Before adding another card to your wallet, consider how it fits into your overall credit card strategy.

If you're applying for a Chase card, keep the issuer's unofficial 5/24 rule in mind, as well as any welcome bonus eligibility restrictions. You'll also want to weigh the combined annual fees against the additional rewards and benefits you're getting.

Finally, think about whether you'd prefer to pool more Ultimate Rewards points with another Chase card or diversify into a separate rewards currency, such as Capital One miles.

The offers plenty of value on its own, but pairing it with the right card can help you earn more rewards and enjoy benefits you might otherwise miss.

Before adding another card to your wallet, consider where your Reserve falls short, your spending habits and whether the additional rewards and perks justify any extra annual fee.

Scandic paid €500 million for a business that fills more rooms and earns more per room than its own operation. The first combined numbers back the deal. The test now is whether it can integrate slowly enough to protect the occupancy that made Dalata worth buying.

Dalata’s hotels fill 80% of their rooms. Scandic’s fill 65%. That gap is a big part of why Scandic paid €500 million (about $555 million) for it, and its third-quarter update on Tuesday, the first since the deal closed, showed what it adds up to: a 24% lift to pro forma earnings per share.

Scandic had run Dalata’s 57 hotels in Ireland and the UK under a management agreement for a year before completing the purchase eight days ago. On a pro forma basis, which treats the two companies as if they had been combined for the full 12 months to September 30, the group generated SEK 30.4 billion (about $3.05 billion) in revenue and SEK 3.35 billion (about $336 million) in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), an 11% margin.

An aerial view of a 49.5-megawatt, three-level data center under construction in Vernon, Calif., April 14, 2026. Inset: Taylor Frazier McCollum

Mario Tama/Getty Images, Screenshot via Electric Llama/YouTube

Meet Taylor Frazier McCollum. McCollum just led a successful movement to block the construction of a $5 billion data center campus in Prince George’s County, Md. Simultaneously, McCollum is upset that her county’s government will not pay for a new roof for her grandfather’s home. Somehow, McCollum cannot see the connection between these two things. In an interview with NPR, she explained that the data center project prompted her political “awakening” and boasted that “so many people are depending on this fight to be successful.”

Are they? Prince George’s County is not in good shape. It has a budget deficit of more than $130 million. Unemployment is high. Last year, the Six Flags amusement park there closed permanently, and in the next few years, the Washington Commanders NFL team intends to move out. The FBI is also trying to leave. McCollum’s father believes that his daughter is a hero in the mold of Medgar Evers, who was killed trying to integrate Mississippi’s schools, or of Martin Luther King. “People like Taylor,” he says, “jump out here so the people behind them get to make progress.”

#6147. Why Policy Will Make a Comeback in 2028

Within both major parties, dramatic ideological battles will play out in the presidential race.

With the midterms now behind us, the political world has already shifted to speculation about the next presidential race. While I am not quite ready to make any horse race bets, I will venture to make an even bolder prediction: 2028 will be the election when policy makes a comeback.

At risk of being accused of romanticizing the past, I will freely acknowledge that there was never any golden age in which presidential campaigns were focused on sober-minded discussions about the finer points of policy. Go back through the decades, and in every election, you will find complaints about how elections were much more focused on personalities and trivial matters than serious issues.
